News.title: West Mersea live: 'Family tragedy' at Mersea Island as coastguard scrambled
News.content:
Essex Police said emergency services are at the scene of an incident in West Mersea, Colchester

Emergency teams are responding to a 'tragic incident' involving a family at the Seaview Avenue and beach area of West Mersea, near Colchester, Essex

Emergency teams are responding to a "tragic incident" involving a family at an Essex beach.

Police, firefighters, paramedics and coastguard teams were called to the Seaview Avenue and beach area at West Mersea on Wednesday evening.

The West Mersea Coastguard Rescue Team said on Facebook early on Thursday: "We have responded to a tragic incident on West Mersea beach. Our thoughts are with the family involved." It added that it would not be making any further comment.

No further details about the incident have been released at this stage.

News.title: GTA 6 players warned they'll need a driving licence before they can play blockbuster game
News.content:
GTA 6 players warned they'll need a driving licence before they can play blockbuster game

After waiting 13 years for GTA 6, some players could face one final hurdle before jumping into Rockstar's blockbuster game of hedonistic delights

View 3 Images GTA 6 is priced at £69.99 - but there's a way to get it cheaper. (Image: Rockstar Games)

Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally on the horizon – and gamers around the globe can barely contain themselves after waiting more than a decade for the next instalment.

‌



The blockbuster game lands on November 19, marking the end of a 13-year gap since GTA V first hit shelves way back in 2013. For millions of fans, that red-circled calendar day will likely become one of the biggest gaming events of all time. For anyone who has somehow missed the GTA craze over the past 30 years, the series throws players into huge open-world cities where they can follow the main storyline, steal cars, go to XXX bars and nightclubs, wreak havoc, or even just drive around listening to the famously bizarre in-game radio stations. Think crime, fast cars and plenty of mayhem. Unless you're one of those ironic players who find it funny to drive by the road rules.

‌



There's just one catch come the release this November: you'd better have a real-life driver's licence to play.

‌



In Australia, that is. As per new online safety laws introduced in March, Aussies wanting to play GTA 6 - especially if they wish to enter its online multiplayer mode - will have to complete mandatory age verification checks. The most common form of ID used for that process is a driver's licence.

So, essentially, gamers could find themselves needing an actual valid licence before they can properly get behind the wheel in Rockstar's latest virtual playground of hedonistic delights.

‌



But, before you scoff at a faraway problem for faraway people, the issue may not stay confined in Down Under for long. Since the country introduced its controversial social media restrictions, several other nations have signalled they could bring in similar measures – including the UK.

View 3 Images Gamers are getting excited about GTA 6 Ultimate Edition content already - this is the Grotti Cheetah car (Image: Rockstar Games)

In June 2026, then-prime minister Sir Keir Starmer announced plans for a ban on social media use by children under 16, which is expected to come into force in spring 2027. The proposals also include a default overnight app curfew between midnight and 6am for under-18s.

‌



France is also moving in the same direction, with lawmakers approving a ban preventing children under 15 from opening social media accounts from September 1.

Australia, one of the first countries where GTA 6 will be available, already requires any R18+ content to verify that users are adults. The government has also doubled penalties for companies that fail to comply, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese saying tech firms are "not doing enough" to protect children online.

View 3 Images GTA 6 pre-orders are slowly going live across the world - starting with New Zealand (Image: Rockstar Games)

Article continues below

There is at least some good news for Aussie gamers. Rockstar has already launched an age verification system for existing GTA Online players, and it is expected to carry over to GTA 6 when the game launches.

So if you are planning to dive into GTA 6 online from day one, getting your licence verified early might be the smartest move you make all year.

News.title: 'I died giving birth and woke up in afterlife where I was given ultimatum'
News.content:
'I died giving birth and woke up in afterlife where I was given ultimatum'

A woman who came close to death as she gave birth returned to life after being handed an ultimatum by a mysteriosu figure

View 4 Images Patty related her amazing story (Image: YouTube/NDE Diary )

A woman plagued by fears of death throughout her childhood briefly died during the birth of her own baby and her near-death experience completely changed her. "The biggest, most important thing is that I'm no longer afraid to die," Patty Ellen says. "And the weird thing is that I can't wait to go back."

‌



In a video for the NDE Diary YouTube channel, Patty described the moment that she "died" on the operating table as doctors attempted the emergency caesarian section. She explained: "I remember being wheeled in... I remember hearing the sound of the heart monitor beeping.

‌



"Then I remember it going flat. And at at the very same moment that I heard it go beep, I rose out of my body and I was like just hovering there. I remember seeing a body. I remember seeing the doctors. I remember seeing everything that was going on."

‌



But within moments she was no longer in the operating theatre, but "somewhere else". She found herself at the centre of a 360-degrees "video screen" on which she was shown the key events of her life.

"It was stopping at certain points in my life," Patty recalled. "Some were good, some were not so good in the way I treated people."

View 4 Images Patty could hear the doctors conferring as they fought to save her life [stock image] (Image: skaman306 via Getty Images)

‌



Because the replay of her life seemed to be pausing at her worst moments, Patty began to worry that it could be the beginning of an eternity in Hell. She continued: "I think we all have done some things that that we were not proud of, or treated people badly or said an unkind word or something like that.

"Those are the things that I'm talking about, that [the replay] was stopping at. For [music] a split second, I thought to myself, 'I'm going to Hell... they're showing me this because they're going to say to me 'You're going to Hell'."

But at that point, Patty became aware of someone standing next to her: "I felt them put a hand on my shoulder and tell me that I was doing okay and not to worry."

‌



She claimed the message of comfort was transmitted to her telepathically, adding: "All you have to do is think something and the other person knows it... I wish that we could communicate like that now."

View 4 Images Patty was offered the choice of returning to her life (Image: YouTube/NDE Diary )

While the replay of her life seemed to focus on her failings, the message that came across most strongly was one of forgiveness. Patty claimed: "I believe it's so important for our soul, for our spirit, and not only to forgive other people, but to forgive ourselves. I had a really really hard time forgiving myself.

‌



"I've worked on that a lot. It's definitely a learning thing where we're meant to... it's definitely to teach us where we can do better, where we've done good and where we need to improve."

As the strange out-of body experience came to an end, Patty heard her baby's first cry: "The very same moment that he was crying, the person that was with me, who I didn't recognise, I felt like he loved me forever and ever. It was almost like he just loved me for eternity from back from before I was born until my future. I just felt like he he loved me forever and is going to love me forever.

"That was very comforting. I only wish that I knew who it was. I have no clue."

‌



View 4 Images She was shown her life on a huge 360º screen [stock image] (Image: Mads Perch via Getty Images)

The mysterious presence telepathically spoke to Patty one last time, giving her the choice of remaining where she was or going back to her life. Knowing that her baby had just been born, Patty immediately chose to go back and be with him.

She continued: "I was brought back brought back to the hospital room where I saw doctors and nurses, about six or seven {of them]. I believe that they were giving me CPR because I remember them saying, 'She's not breathing,' At that moment when the person asked me, "What do you want to do?" I was immediately shot back into my body when I said, "I want to be with my baby." The next day, I was in so much pain. My chest was hurting so badly."

Article continues below

Patty says she returned to her body with a valuable lesson: "The biggest thing that I took back from this is that what I was told is that we're here to learn unconditional love, compassion, forgiveness, kindness, acceptance, you know, all these things is what I was told. This is what we are here to do."

News.title: Michelin-starred chef faces jail after serving 49,000 'illegal ants' on menu
News.content:
Michelin-starred chef faces jail after serving 49,000 'illegal ants' on menu

The double-michelin star winning restaurant has been called 'excellent' and 'worthy of a detour' by the coveted fine-dining Michelin Guide - but its menu has attracted unwelcome attention by the authorities

View 3 Images Michelin-starred celebrity chef faces jail for sprinkling dessert with ants

A double Michelin-starred chef is facing the prospect of prison in South Korea after being accused of serving ants as a dessert garnish at a high-end Seoul restaurant.

‌



Australian chef Joseph Lidgerwood earned his second Michelin star in 2025 for his South Korean restaurant Evett, in the capital city's swanky Gangham neighbourhood, where he serves Korean cuisine cooked over a wood fire.

‌



Alongside the alleged use of ants, his menu had previously featured an array of adventurous yet seasonal ingredients such as golbaengi - moon snails - and haesam - sea cucumber - all foraged from South Korea's east coast.

‌



Speaking to Australian broadcaster the ABC in 2025, Lidgerwood said: "Most of the time, what we source, especially like a really unique ingredient, we'll probably just try to highlight it in a couple of different [ways]. So, [for example,] we do a pickling of it, a roasting of it."

View 3 Images Prosecutors have accused Lidgerwood and the restaurant of importing and serving as many as 49,000 ants to feed to customers since 2021

Evett received its first Michelin star for high-quality cooking just 12 months after opening in 2018, serving Seoul's discerning diners. The restaurant was awarded a second star in 2025, a remarkable turnaround for Lidgerwood, who once received a failing grade in his high school cooking class back in Australia.

‌



Recalling the experience, he said: "I got 'not competent' on my grade 11 home economics class … I still remember that. It still haunts me to this day."

If convicted, however, that may not be the only thing haunting him. Lidgerwood, who appeared on Netflix's Culinary Class Wars. He has been accused of importing and serving up to 49,000 ants to feed to customers since 2021. Prosecutors are also seeking a ₩20 million fine against the restaurant's parent company, while the chef could face up to a year behind bars over the alleged ant dishes.

View 3 Images Joseph Lidgerwood appeared on Netflix's Korean cooking show Culinary Class Wars (Image: Netflix)

‌



Prosecutors allege serving ants breaches South Korea's food safety laws. Under the regulations, only 10 insect species are approved for human consumption, including grasshoppers, locusts and two-spotted crickets. Businesses wanting to serve insects not included on the approved list, such as ants, must first obtain permission from authorities, which prosecutors claim the upmarket Seoul restaurant failed to do.

Authorities are said to have discovered the alleged ant-topped desserts after social media videos and photographs showed the unusual dish — a sorbet palate cleanser.

Evett has that the Aussie chef used "ant acidity in dishes while working in the US and Europe, and was unaware that it was illegal in Korea". The restaurant owner has also admitted that ants were being served, but said that they made up a "small part" of the eateries' fancy 15-course foodie menu. Diners could also opt for non-ant related toppings, instead using fermented vinegar and edible flowers to have on their dessert.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

The restaurant added said that slightly more than half of diners opt for the ant option, thus disputing the assertion by Korean prosecutors' that the swanky food joint made ₩120million (£61,000) off serving the ant dessert at the centre of the scandal.

To make matters worst for the fine dining hotspot, health authorities also found the ants used in the meals at Evett contained "up to 55 times more heavy metals than typical edible insects". Heavy metals, like arsenic, lead and mercury, are not dangerous in trace amounts, like in an ant, for instance. But, with prolonged exposure, or if consumed in large amounts, they can be harmful, especially to children and pregnant women.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Ants, however, are eaten across the world and are prized in several Asian, African and Latin American nations. They are also eaten in Australia by the country's First Nations people as 'bush tucker', as it is called locally. Eating ants in Australia goes back at least 60,000 years, with various types of native ants—like green ants and honeypot ants—as traditional food and medicine for millennia.

In Thai and Cambodian cooking weaver ants and their eggs are used in cooking. Queen ants are prized as caviar in Colombia. In Tokyo, the celebrated Danish chef Rene Redzepi, who co-founded the world-famous Noma restaurant, created a tasting menu dish covered in live ants at a pop-up.

Article continues below

Brazilian chef Alex Atala, who owns the Michelin-starred DOM restaurant, once offered a dish of a pineapple cube topped with a raw Amazonian leaf-cutter ant.

News.title: Burglar told police 'I don't give a f**k' when found hiding in bush with socks on hands
News.content:
Burglar told police 'I don't give a f**k' when found hiding in bush with socks on hands

James Dean, from Birkenhead, was found hiding under a hedge in a nearby garden after burgling St Peter's Catholic Primary School in Noctorum, Wirral, and causing £10,000 worth of damage

View 2 Images James Dean has been jailed (Image: Merseyside Police)

A burglar said he "didn't give a f**k" about stealing from pupils when he was found hiding in a bush with socks on his hands.

‌



Merseyside Police were called to St Peter's Catholic Primary School in Noctorum, Wirral, shortly before midnight on May 24 this year after a teacher who lives opposite the premises was alerted to a burglary in progress by security alarms, Liverpool Crown Court heard.

‌



Defendant James Dean, 45, from Birkenhead, was discovered hiding beneath a hedge in the garden of a nearby home while wearing socks on his hands.

‌



Olivia Randell, prosecuting, said Dean was also found to have items including the school's CCTV hard drive and two cash boxes beside him at this time, with £652.16 in cash recovered from him as he confessed: "I'm nicked. I done it."

View 2 Images Liverpool Crown Court (file) (Image: Liverpool Echo)

British Airways flight makes emergency landing after fault discovered mid-air READ MORE :

Dean, who said he had "drank a few cans of beer", also went on to state that he would admit to a further six burglaries if his sentence would be limited to no more than 12 months. Under interview, he told detectives that he "didn't know why he did it, but it was most likely for money".

‌



Judge Katherine Pierpoint said: "I have seen the body worn footage in this case. He started to say that he wasn't responsible, that he had found the items, that he had seen some other lads get off. He then started to shout abuse at members of staff who had obviously been alerted by the alarm, calling them grasses. When police said he was accused of stealing from children, his response was 'I don't give a f***'."

Ms Randell set out how the main door of the school had to be replaced at a cost of more than £7,000 after being kicked. Dean caused £1,500 of damage to internal fire doors, while the CCTV system would cost around £1,000 to replace.

It came after an earlier spree of burglaries on April 5, in which Dean targeted Sylvan Home Care Services, Gossip Coffee and Wine Bar and Voltage bar, all on Allport Lane in Bromborough. While no items were taken during these break-ins, he was said to left behind a trail of destruction which cost more than £4,000 to repair.

‌



Dean has a total of 59 previous convictions for 127 offences, including more than a dozen burglaries. His criminal record saw him handed a three-year sentence for a break-in at a pub in 2019 and four years for robbery in 2022, reported the Liverpool Echo.

Chris Macmaster, defending, told the court: "Mr Dean does not seek to excuse his behaviour. It is clear that Mr Dean has active diagnoses of depression, anxiety and ADHD and has a history of psychotic symptoms, including auditory hallucinations. Some of the things he says when intoxicated should be treated, in my respectful submission, in that context, in the context of a gentleman who has some complicated and substantial issues.

"In another circumstance, there may be an argument, serious though these matters are, where the court could perhaps look at some other options. Mr Dean is a man in his mid 40s who, palpably, does need some help."

‌



Dean pleaded guilty to one count of burglary and asked for a further three offences of burglary to be taken into account in sentencing. Appearing via video link to HMP Liverpool wearing a grey Reprimo t-shirt, he was jailed for two years and eight months.

Sentencing, Judge Pierpoint said: "The total damage was nearly £10,000 of damage of a public building. You got into the office area, where you had taken two money boxes and also damaged the CCTV system and taken the hard drive with you.

"You made good your escape and hid in someone's garden, under a bush. You had socks on your hands, which shows some degree of planning because you did not want your fingerprints to be found. You were issuing threats to people who were nearby.

‌



"I do have regard to the diagnosed mental health issues that you have. That may explain, to some extent, the way you were acting at the scene. You clearly were, at that time, under the influence of alcohol.

"It will have taken a lot of time, effort and money to sort out what you did in only a few moments. It is not just the financial impact that this kind of offence has. It is also the impact it has on the teachers, on the children and on the wider community.

"I hope it is right that, in the sober light of day, you are thoroughly ashamed that you broke into a school where you have family members who go to or have been to that school. I hope you are thoroughly ashamed of what you did. You have an appalling record. I count well over a dozen offences of burglary and associated offences up to 2016.

Article continues below

"I hope it is right that you are remorseful and shameful for what you have got yourself in and that you want to try to turn your life around. If that doesn't happen, you will either end up damaging yourself or serving lengthier and lengthy sentences in custody."

News.title: Longevity expert's five health tips for people in their 30s to do now
News.content:
Longevity expert's five health tips for people in their 30s to do now

Leslie Kenny says your 30s are a great time to invest in your health in later life

View 4 Images Leslie Kenny says 'many of the changes we associate with ageing are influenced by habits we build decades earlier' (stock image) (Image: SWNS)

An expert has revealed the five key habits people need to start in their 30s to be fit and healthy in their 50s and beyond. Leslie Kenny says that many of the changes we associate with getting older are 'influenced by habits we build decades earlier'.

‌



"People often think ageing is something that just happens to us," longevity expert, Leslie Kenny said. "Your 30s are one of the best times to invest in your future health because you’re laying the foundations for the next 20 or 30 years."

‌



Today, Leslie - who co-founded the Oxford Longevity Project, a non-profit that educates the public on ageing breakthroughs - shares the five most important habits to start building in your 30s that will keep you strong and healthy into older age.

‌



View 4 Images Leslie said people should 'focus on feeding their cells' (Image: SWNS)

1. Don't obsess over calories - feed your cells

"Rather than obsessing over calories, I’d focus on feeding your cells," Leslie said. "Aim to eat plenty of colourful vegetables, berries, legumes, mushrooms, nuts and seeds. These foods are rich in the natural compounds your body uses to repair itself and protect against inflammation.

"Don’t neglect protein either. Most of us don’t need huge amounts in our 30s, but we do need enough. It helps maintain muscle, supports our immune system and provides the building blocks for healthy skin, bones and organs.

‌



"I’d also eat fermented foods such as yoghurt, kefir, kimchi or sauerkraut several times a week. Looking after your gut microbiome today can pay dividends for your immune system, metabolism and even brain health later in life."

2. Start 'banking your bone'

"The biggest mistake I see is people thinking exercise is only about burning calories," said Leslie, CEO of Oxford Healthspan. "In your 30s, you should be building muscle. Muscle is one of the best predictors of healthy ageing because it helps regulate blood sugar, supports balance and mobility, protects your bones and even releases beneficial molecules that communicate with your brain.

"For women especially, this is the decade to bank your bone. We naturally begin to lose bone density as we get older, particularly around menopause, so every strength workout you do now is like making a deposit into your future.

‌



"Think of it as a savings account for your skeleton. The stronger your bones going into your 40s and 50s, the more resilient you’ll be for the decades that follow.

"Strength train at least two or three times a week. Add regular walking, cycling, or swimming for cardiovascular fitness, and don’t forget balance and flexibility. These are the things that help keep you active and independent decades from now."

View 4 Images Leslie urges everyone to wear sunscreen (Image: SWNS)

‌



3. Wear sun cream every day

"One habit I wish more people took seriously is protecting their skin from ultraviolet light," Leslie said. "Your skin is your body’s largest organ and UV exposure is one of the biggest drivers of visible ageing."

Leslie says she has noticed women tend to do a much better job at protecting their skin than men. I see so many (men) who never think twice about spending hours in the sun without protection," she added.

"Many will wish they hadn’t when they reach their 50s and 60s, when the wrinkles, sunspots and skin damage begin to catch up with them. The bonus is that protecting your skin isn’t just about looking younger. It also reduces your risk of skin cancer."

‌



During the summer, it's recommended people wear a sun cream with SPF50 protection every day.

View 4 Images Leslie says people should strength train at least two or three times a week, and add regular walking, cycling, or swimming for cardiovascular fitness (Image: SWNS)

4. Target 60-90 minutes of deep sleep a night

"If there is one thing people consistently underestimate, it’s sleep," Leslie said. "Sleep is when your brain clears away waste products, your immune system resets and your body carries out much of its repair work.

‌



"It’s one of the best investments you can make for your future brain health, not to mention your body's overall recovery and repair."

There are different stages of sleep that are all responsible for different areas of our mental and physical health.

"Aim for seven to nine hours of quality sleep and, and, if you wear a sleep tracker, target 60-90 minutes of deep or slow wave sleep as this is when the waste clearance system activates and growth hormone for muscles is produced," Leslie added.

‌



"Try to go to bed and wake up at similar times each day. Limit bright screens before bed, keep your bedroom cool and dark and get outside into natural daylight within an hour of waking. These simple habits help keep your body clock working properly."

5. Stack everyday habits to keep consistent

"People often ask me what supplement or treatment will help them live longer," Leslie said. "My answer is always the same. Build the habits first.

"Strong muscles, healthy bones, protected skin, a resilient heart, and a healthy brain don’t happen overnight. They are the result of thousands of small choices made over many years.

Article continues below

This is often referred to as 'habit stacking.' Adding small, manageable habits into your everyday routine can make it much easier to stay consistent.

"The wonderful thing about longevity science is that it shows we’re not simply victims of our genes. We have far more influence over how we age than most people realise. Starting in your 30s simply gives you a longer runway to enjoy the benefits."

News.title: Dr Amir Khan shares how to 'reverse' pre-diabetes with 5 ‘powerful’ steps
News.content:
Dr Amir Khan shares how to 'reverse' pre-diabetes with 5 ‘powerful’ steps

More than six million people in the UK are living with pre-diabetes

View 3 Images Doctor Amir Khan has explained how you can "reverse" pre-diabetes (Image: Dr Amir Khan/Instagram)

A doctor has revealed how to “reverse” a potentially dangerous health condition with five steps. According to the expert, these lifestyle changes are “incredibly powerful”.

In a video uploaded to his Instagram page, Doctor Amir Khan explained that it is possible to reverse pre-diabetes. Pre-diabetes means your blood sugar levels are higher than they should be. If you have pre-diabetes, you have a high risk of type 2 diabetes. According to Diabetes UK, around 6.3 million people in the UK are living with pre-diabetes - although not all of them will be aware they have it.

Dr Amir, who is best known for his appearances on ITV, said: “If you've just been told, you're pre-diabetic, don't panic. This is one of those moments you can genuinely change the future.”

One in four adults worldwide has metabolic syndrome, frogs vs cancer, tucking into a low-inflammation diet can cut the risk of developing dementia, and why you hate other people - all this and more in our science newsletter

He explained more about what pre-diabetes actually means. He said: “In the UK pre-diabetes usually means your HbA1c, that's your average blood sugar reading, is between 42 and 47 millimoles per mol.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

“It means your blood sugar is running higher than we'd like but not yet high enough to diagnose type 2 diabetes. The good news is for many people, this stage is reversible.

“Now what's happening is your body is becoming insulin resistant. Insulin is the hormone that acts like a key helping glucose move from your bloodstream into your muscles, liver and fat cells to be used or stored for energy.

“But with insulin resistance, those cells stop responding as well. So your pancreas has to produce more and more insulin just to keep blood sugars under control.

“Eventually, it can't keep up and blood glucose starts to rise.”

View 3 Images Prediabetes means your blood sugar levels are higher than they should be (Image: Getty)

Reversing pre-diabetes

However, Dr Amir admitted that this may not be easy for everyone. “Now, I do need to acknowledge something here.

This isn't simply about willpower, genetics play a role, so does age, ethnicity, polycystic ovarian syndrome now known as PMOS, menopause, poor sleep, certain medication, chronic stress and living in environments where healthy food or safe places to exercise aren’t easily available.

“Health inequalities do matter, you know this and this is harder for some people than others, but if you can make changes, now the evidence shows they're incredibly powerful.”

Walk after eating

He said: “So what I would suggest is move more, especially after meals, even a 10 to 15 minute walk after eating can significantly reduce the blood sugar rise after that meal.”

Build muscle

“I've been saying this for months, resistance exercise two or three times a week makes your muscles more responsive to insulin,” he continued.

“Muscle is one of the biggest places your body stores glucose.”

View 3 Images Going for a walk after eating could be beneficial, he said (Image: Getty)

Eat more fibre and protein

Dr Amir said: “They help you stay fuller for longer and reduce those sharp spikes in blood sugar. Think beans, lentils, vegetables, nuts, yoghurt, eggs or tofu. I love them all.”

Lose weight if you need to

He said: “If you're carrying excess weight, losing even five to 10 per cent of your body weight can dramatically improve insulin sensitivity, and reduce your risk of progressing to type 2, diabetes.”

Article continues below

Look after your sleep and stress levels

“Finally, don't neglect sleep and stress, he said. “Poor sleep and chronic stress make insulin resistance worse so looking after your mental health is part of looking after your metabolic health too.”

He added: “Remember pre-diabetes isn't a life sentence, think of it as your body's early warning light, listen to it. Make changes where you can ask for support if you need it and in many cases, you can get your HbA1c back to the normal range before type 2 diabetes develops.”

If you are concerned about your blood sugar levels, you should speak to your GP.

News.title: UK weather maps show 7C bitter August chill after scorching 37C heatwave
News.content:
UK weather maps show 7C bitter August chill after scorching 37C heatwave

Temperatures in the UK are expected to fall dramatically with rain on the cards just days after another scorching heatwave is forecast to grip the nation with highs of 37C

View 3 Images UK weather maps show lows of 7C as chill incoming (Image: WXCharts)

Weather forecasts predict a new heatwave on the horizon as the Met Office warns temperatures could become "very warm again", however after the initial hot period there is set to be a cold snap.

‌



Weather maps produced by WXCharts using GFS data show a 7C chill after the scorching 37C forecast just days earlier.

‌



Temperatures are expected to plummet on Tuesday, August 4 with lows of 7C in Scotland and Wales.

‌



View 3 Images The Met Office also warns there could be rain (Image: Getty Images)

However, on July 31, some areas of the UK will be a whopping 30 degrees warmer. These highs are forecast to remain into August, with warms of 34C.

On Saturday August 1, temperatures will still sit in the 30s, with London warming up to 33C according to the weather maps. Suffolk and Norfolk are also likely to see highs of 34C.

‌



Even in cooler areas temperatures are expected to be 27C.

View 3 Images The cool conditions will follow extreme heat in the UK (Image: WXCharts)

The stark difference in weather may serve as a shock for many Brits. Weather maps show the coolest conditions in the Highlands of Scotland, however areas of Yorkshire will only be 8C.

‌



In the South West some parts of Devon are forecast to sit at 9C.

London and surrounding areas are forecast the warmest temperatures of 13C according to the maps, still a harsh drop from days prior.

The Met Office warns in its longer range forecast from July 27 to August 5 that the UK will see 'changeable' conditions but does state that temperatures will largely be above average.

‌



A spokesperson for the Met Office said: "A changeable period is likely overall, with many areas likely to see a mixture of bright or sunny spells and some rain at times.

"Northwestern areas are more likely to see the focus of rainfall, but southeastern areas should also see some showers. Confidence becomes lower into the start of August, but there are hints that high pressure could return for a time, which would mean dry conditions resuming, especially in the south.

"Winds will be mostly light or moderate, but occasionally fresh or strong around some coasts, mainly in the north and west.

Article continues below

"Temperatures will be near or above normal, warmest in the south, and perhaps becoming very warm again by the start of August."

News.title: Police officer was violent rapist who attacked women over 14 years, BBC reveals
News.content:
A police officer who took his own life in May was a violent rapist who carried out a spate of sexual attacks and attempted murders of women over at least 14 years, the BBC can reveal.

PC Alan Greer's first known victim was a woman he raped in her home in Glasgow in 2012 after she had called the police to report being the victim of a crime.

The woman reported the sex attack by Greer late last year, sparking one of Police Scotland's biggest ever anti-corruption inquiries.

Detectives have so far uncovered a further eight victims, five of whom were sex workers, attacked while Greer was off duty.

It has emerged that Greer used hundreds of prostitutes throughout his police career, and it is anticipated more victims of his violence will be identified.

Assistant Chief Constable Lynn Ratcliff, gold commander for the investigation, said what the inquiry had found was "truly shocking".

She said: "This officer has clearly abused his power and has revisited someone that he's encountered in the course of his duties.

"But this victim was brave enough to come and speak to us, and that really was the trigger point for us starting our investigation.

"That's allowed us to proactively identify eight further victims."

News.title: 'What was their crime?': BBC visits Iran school where strike killed 120 children
News.content:
The school day had begun as usual, Amaineh says.

Because it was the Islamic holy month of Ramadan, the children gathered inside the prayer hall to recite the Quran, she recalls, before she began teaching her pupils a new letter of the Persian alphabet.

But, as the first attacks of the war unfolded across Iran, she says the headteacher announced the school would be closing, and teachers began contacting parents, urging them to collect their children.

Only five of Amaineh's 15 first-grade pupils were left in her classroom on the upper floor, she says, when she first heard an explosion not far from the school. She says she was in the corridor and rushed back for the children.

"Just as I went to leave, a missile struck the school," says Amaineh. "Something hit my head and my students' heads - we were all sent flying."

Then, she says, thick black smoke filled the classroom: "I couldn't even see the pupils I was holding in my arms. We couldn't breathe."

She says she remembers hearing another explosion, as well as the sounds of screaming, children crying and then the school itself collapsing â "destroyed all at once".

"Blood was pouring from me and the students," she adds.

News.title: Airport drop-off fees up by a third - here are the priciest
News.content:
Drop-off fees at the UK's major airports have risen by a third on average since last summer, new analysis has found.

The RAC motoring group looked at the cost of pulling up to the closest point to terminals at the 20 busiest airports, 16 of which had put up their prices since last year.

London airport Gatwick topped the list by charging a "farewell fee" of Â£10 for 10 minutes. Stansted also charges Â£10 but drivers are allowed 15 minutes at its "express set down" outside departures.

Airports UK, the trade body, said that free drop-offs were available and fees were part of airports' business models and climate change objectives.

The RAC said that the price of dropping people off in "kiss-and-fly" areas rose by an average of Â£1.70 to Â£7 compared to this time last year.

London City Airport, which only started making people pay this year, is the most expensive on a per-minute basis. Its Â£8 charge for five minutes works out at Â£1.60 per minute.

Birmingham is the cheapest, charging Â£7.00 for 15 minutes which equates to 47p per minute.

In contrast, none of the top 10 airports in the EU charge for drop-offs, according to RAC research.

News.title: Life-changing MS drug to help people walk now on NHS in England
News.content:
The first drug to help people with multiple sclerosis walk is being made available on the NHS in England.

Fampridine boosts nerve signals to make it easier for some people to move and live independently.

Aysen Slack, who used to pay for fampridine privately until it became too costly, said the decision would make a "huge difference".

Up to 5,000 people in England could benefit each year. The drug is already available elsewhere in the UK.

Multiple sclerosis is caused by the immune system attacking the protective covering around nerve cells - known as myelin.

This damage impairs the ability of nerves to carry electrical messages from the brain to the rest of the body - including those needed for the precise control of muscles needed to walk.

Fampridine is known as a "signal booster" as it helps those electrical messages still get through.

Clinical trials showed around four in 10 people taking the drug had improvements in their walking speed and in how long they could walk for.

This could be the difference between getting around the house or needing help at home or enabling people to go out and see friends and family.

Current NHS support includes physiotherapy and walking aids.

The drug has previously been rejected for use by the NHS in England as it was not considered value for money, although it did become available in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

News.title: Glasgow set to welcome the world for scaled back Commonwealth Games
News.content:
When the fastest man on the planet won Commonwealth relay gold for Jamaica in 2014, more than 50,000 fans cheered him home at Hampden.

But the athletes seeking to emulate Usain Bolt when the Games return to Glasgow - including mile world record holder Josh Kerr - will be competing at Scotstoun Stadium in front of 11,000 spectators.

This time round almost everything is on a smaller scale but organisers are confident fans will create a Tartan Army-style atmosphere for the 3,000 competitors who will be chasing glory.

From Friday until 2 August, 215 gold medals will be up for grabs - compared to 261 when Scotland last staged the Games - but Glasgow 2026 will see a record 47 para-sports events.

News.title: Rain to return this weekend as parts of UK on brink of drought
News.content:
If you cannot remember the last time it rained, you are probably not alone.

June was actually wetter than average in the UK, which might come as a surprise given our recent run of weather, but for England and Wales the majority of that rain came down in the first two weeks of the month.

Since 15 June, most of England has recorded less than 10mm of rain with large areas of central southern England seeing 3mm or less. Meanwhile, Wisley in Surrey has had no rain at all for 36 consecutive days.

Most of Wales has seen less than 25mm (1in) of rain since the middle of June, but it has been particularly dry in the north-east with Rhyl in Denbighshire recording only 3mm.

A Thames Water hosepipe ban came into force on Thursday, adding to other bans already in place for customers of other water companies across the south of the UK, as parts of southern, central and eastern England were declared to be close to drought.

Northern Ireland had a very wet June, recording 67% more rain than average, and it was also very wet in western Scotland. However, July has been much drier than average in Northern Ireland and most of Scotland, though the rain has continued in the Highlands, with Aultbea already reaching the July average rainfall, and with more on the way.

News.title: Most sewage spills in England may be illegal, new research suggests
News.content:
Most of the sewage spills into England's waterways in the last two years may have been illegal but gone unpunished, according to new analysis.

UK law states that raw sewage should not be released during "normal" weather conditions, yet until now the regulator has not clarified exactly what that means.

But campaigner Prof Peter Hammond obtained a definition in secret court papers, and said it shows that for more than 80% of the time sewage was being spilled, the weather was "normal", making the spills possibly illegal.

The water companies and the regulator, the Environment Agency (EA), rejected the analysis and said they were working to reduce spill numbers.

News.title: Firm hacked by rogue OpenAI models says it is 'a wake-up call'
News.content:
The co-founder of Hugging Face, a technology start-up that was hacked after some of OpenAI's most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models went rogue, said on Thursday that the incident is "a wake-up call" for the industry.

Thomas Wolf told BBC's Newsday radio programme that "this will be one of the most common types of cyber attacks we see", but that most firms are not aware that the "game has changed".

The BBC has contacted OpenAI for comment.

The ChatGPT-maker said on Tuesday that its AI models broke out of a secure test environment during a trial and launched a cyber attack. The firm said the incident was "unprecedented" and that it was conducting an investigation with Hugging Face.

AI agents are able to operate alone to accomplish tasks after human instruction.

Wolf said that Hugging Face initially had no idea where the attack originated when signs of it surfaced in mid-July but that the company was able to contain the breach.

Hugging Face is one of the world's largest open-source hubs for sharing AI models and is often used by tech developers and researchers.

Wolf said the breach was "very different" from the usual cyber attacks that Hugging Face often faces and that OpenAI quickly informed the company that its models were behind the hack.

In a "very short time" there were 17,000 attacks on Hugging Face's network from various IP (Internet Protocol) addresses, said Wolf, who is also the firm's chief science officer.

Wolf said it was a warning to other companies that they must strengthen their cybersecurity defences to counter such attacks.

The hack is "worrying" because it suggests OpenAI's models ignored the typical safeguards that would prevent an AI program from committing a cyber attack, said Nate Soares from the Machine Intelligence Research Institute.

"In some sense, it knew that this was not what the creators intended. It just didn't care," he added.

News.title: Coastguard called to 'tragic' West Mersea incident
News.content:
The Coastguard said it was called to a "tragic incident" on West Mersea Beach, with people being asked to stay away from the area.

Essex Police, the RNLI and the East of England Air Ambulance were also in attendance in the seaside town, near Colchester, on Wednesday evening and were seen searching the coastline and the water.

In a post on Facebook, West Mersea Coastguard Rescue Team said it had been called to a "tragic incident" on the beach and its thoughts were with the family involved.

Police have asked the public to avoid the Seaview Avenue and beach area.

News.title: Murder probe after man injured in stabbing dies
News.content:
A murder investigation has been launched after a man was fatally stabbed in Leicester.

Leicestershire Police said an officer in a police car was flagged down in London Road, close to Saxby Street, by a man who had "significant injuries" to his chest and stomach at about 22:45 BST on Wednesday.

Paramedics were called and the man, who was in his 20s, was taken to hospital, where he died in the early hours of Thursday morning, the force added.

Following initial inquiries, police believe the man may have been stabbed in De Montfort Place - at the rear of a number of properties in London Road.

No arrests have been made so far and detectives are appealing for any potential witnesses, including anyone with dashcam footage, to come forward.

A scene preservation is in place at the location while a forensic examination is carried out.

Det Insp Lorna Granville, from the East Midlands Special Operations Unit Major Crime Team, said: "Our investigation is in the very early stages, and we are currently working to establish the full circumstances and identify those who may have been involved.

"We believe the injured man may have been stabbed minutes before he was able to stop an officer who was driving in the area.

"We have a number of enquiries underway but would ask anyone who was in that area of London Road last night, between 22:45 and 23:00, to contact police."

News.title: Main ferry out of service for longer than planned
News.content:
The Isle of Man's main ferry will be out of action for longer than anticipated while "essential works" are carried out.

The island's ferry operator said "further necessary repairs" were needed after the Manxman entered drydock last week for scheduled maintenance.

The vessel has been replaced on the Douglas-Heysham route by former flagship ferry Ben-my-Chree, the Isle of Man Steam Packet Company said.

Back-up freight vessel MV Arrow is also set to return to the island while the Manxman is out of action. The operator said it was "reviewing its operational plans to minimise disruption" to passengers wherever possible.

The Ben-my-Chree had been due to take over as sole operator on the firm's Larne route from Friday.

That sailing will now be carried out by the fast craft Manannan.

News.title: Jet pioneer celebrated with new Royal Mail stamps
News.content:
The pioneering work on the jet engine by Sir Frank Whittle has been celebrated with a new set of stamps from Royal Mail.

Whittle, who was born in Coventry and founded Power Jets in Rugby to build the aircraft engines he designed, before going on to continue his pioneering work in Gloucestershire, died 30 years ago this year.

The stamps come in two sets, the first featuring four images of Whittle and his engines, while the second shows eight iconic British jet aircraft.

His son, Ian, said "It is a fitting tribute not only to my father's pioneering achievements, but also to the generations of engineers, designers and aviators who helped shape Britain's world-leading contribution to aviation."

Whittle was born in Coventry in 1907 and joined the RAF in 1923, training as an aircraft mechanic and graduating from RAF Cranwell as an officer in 1928.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe public memorial to be held later this year, family says
News.content:
A public memorial for Ann Widdecombe will be held later this year, her family has said in a statement.

Former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman Widdecombe, 78, was found dead in her Dartmoor home with serious head injuries earlier this month.

Her family thanked the public for "the wide expression of condolences" but asked that her private service, to be held in the coming weeks and for which invitations have already been sent, is "limited to those closest to Ann".

"We understand that there is significant public interest in the funeral of Ann Widdecombe," the statement said.

"A private service for family and close friends will be held in the coming weeks, and invitations for this ceremony have been distributed.

"A more public memorial will follow later in the year, the details of which will be released in due course.

"While we are very grateful for the wide expression of condolences, the family would ask that this initial service is limited to those closest to Ann."

Tributes poured in to Widdecombe from TV stars and across the political spectrum following her death.

Anton Du Beke, who was her partner on Strictly Come Dancing in 2010, said he was devastated , which he called the "saddest of news".

"I had the most brilliant time with Ann on Strictly Come Dancing, she became a real friend, she was fun, she was upbeat, she was positive, she was supportive, she was game, wanted to enter into the spirit of the whole thing," he said in a video on X.

Kemi Badenoch, leader of the Conservative Party for which Widdecombe served as shadow home secretary from 1999 to 2001, said the party was "reeling".

She described Widdecombe as "a very fun and feisty woman who spoke her mind", while the then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer said Widdecombe was a "distinguished politician".

In a video posted on social media, Farage said Widdecombe was "an extraordinary woman" and "someone who gave her life to public service, to fighting for the things she believed in".

He described her as "a devout Christian and somebody with strong socially conservative views. Perhaps not popular in modern Britain but that is what Ann believed in".

News.title: Police formally investigate woman after Brit stabbed to death in French village
News.content:
A woman has been placed under formal investigation over the death last year in France of a British-South African mother-of-four.

Karen Carter, 65, was found lying near her car with stab wounds by a friend in TrÃ©molat, the Dordogne village where she had lived for over a decade and managed two holiday rental homes.

Prosecutors say the 70-year-old woman was originally taken into custody in 2025 as part of preliminary inquiries before being released.

Jacques-Edouard Andrault, the investigating judge in the case, said in a statement on Wednesday that "the investigations conducted as part of the judicial inquiry opened on 7 May, 2025, have led the investigating judge to formally charge her".

Being placed under formal investigation in French law means an investigating judge has to decide whether or not there is enough evidence for the case to go to trial.

At the time of the killing in April last year, Karen Carter's husband, Alan, said that he first heard of her death through a cousin who had read about it on a local community Facebook page.

He said he received confirmation of the death after his assistant phoned local police.

Describing his wife as an outgoing, friendly person who "wouldn't hurt a fly", he said her death has been "traumatic" for his family.

"I'm an introvert, and she's the exact opposite. She's an extrovert, she loves people, she loves to have fun. People love her, she has a good heart," he said.

"She's the one who would bring home the lost dog, or cat, or whatever. She's that sort of person. Everyone liked her. That's why I married her. She's just lovely."

News.title: No helicopters to fight wildfires as 'crisis management' plans activated in Wales
News.content:
The Welsh government has activated "crisis management arrangements" due to the number of wildfires across the nation.

It comes amid criticism from residents over a lack of resources like helicopters to tackle the fires, some of which have been burning for days across north and south Wales.

The Welsh government said North Wales Fire and Rescue had received extra resources but aerial support was not available anywhere in the UK.

However, it said "urgent discussions are now underway both within Wales and at a UK level to identify how this can be resolved".

Meanwhile, firefighters are tackling a big blaze in south Wales for a fourth day, with the smoke travelling as far as Cardiff.

News.title: PC Harper's widow criticises early prisoner release plan as Burnham to review scheme
News.content:
The widow of PC Andrew Harper has described the possible early release of prisoners as "deplorable", following reports that two of his killers could be freed early.

Lissie Harper said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham earlier said he would review the Sentencing Act policy that from September would see thousands of offenders in England and Wales eligible to be released earlier.

Speaking on Wednesday, Burnham said: "I can't say that I can change the policy completely, but I will look at it in detail before we go further forward."

He acknowledged that there was "pressure on prisons places" and that a failure to invest in the prison system in the past had created "an unacceptable situation".

Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter but could be released early under the new Sentencing Act.

PC Harper was killed after he was dragged to his death behind their getaway car. The car's driver, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for manslaughter but would not be eligible for early release.

Burnham's comments came after the mother of police officer Andrew Harper said the potential early release of two of her son's killers felt like an "insult".

In a separate statement released later on Wednesday, PC Harper's widow Lissie Harper said: "It has taken me years to rebuild a life that was torn apart in a matter of moments. Years to pick up the pieces left behind by three men whose actions robbed Andrew of his life and stole our future.

"It is deplorable to me that we have reached a point where releasing prisoners early is even considered acceptable. We speak of justice, accountability and standing with victims, yet decisions like this do the opposite."

The overcrowding of the prison estate has been a problem for several years and successive governments have released prisoners early in a bid to free up space.

Tens of thousands of inmates have been let out of prison to create more space in jails since 2024.

The Sentencing Act, which was passed by Sir Keir Starmer's government earlier this year, was designed to ease pressure on prisons, and will see some offenders spend less time in prison before release.

Burnham said: "I want to assure myself that everything has been looked at before this policy proceeds, and I can give that assurance that every single part of this I will look into with the justice secretary."

Concerning the case of PC Harper, he said: "I feel for the family it's an appalling crime that was committed."

He said the "main perpetrator" of his death would not be eligible for early release.

Burnham also said it was not acceptable to joke about early releases and that it was right Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had apologised for comments he made that were caught on camera.

Emergency services have urged people to avoid part of a beach in Essex after what the coastguard rescue team has described as a “tragic incident”.

The West Mersea Coastguard Rescue Team said on Facebook early on Thursday that they had been called to an incident near Seaview Avenue in West Mersea, Colchester, on Wednesday evening.

“We have responded to a tragic incident on West Mersea beach. Our thoughts are with the family involved,” the post said, adding they would not be making any further comment.

Pictures show a huge emergency services presence on West Mersea beach in Essex on Wednesday evening, and a cordon remains in place on Thursday morning.

The nature of the incident has not been disclosed.

Essex Police said in a Facebook post: “While we remain on scene, we would ask the public to avoid the Seaview Avenue and beach area.

“We appreciate that this will cause some local issues, but would ask for your patience and understanding as we may be there for some time yet.”

Carl Powling, Conservative councillor for Mersea and Pyefleet, told BBC Essex: "Without knowing exactly what's happened there, it's very difficult to speculate but people are very concerned.

"It's definitely a tragic incident and it does highlight the dangers of the tidal area we live in and the sea and what can happen."

Local MP Sir Bernard Jenkin said he is "sad and very shocked" about the incident in a statement to the BBC.

"We don't think of West Mersea Beach as a dangerous beach,” he said.

"I mean, there are tidal currents but thousands of people use it as this time of year and generally feels like a very safe place.

"We don't have the details of what happened... clearly, something unusual occurred but we'll have to wait and see what it was."

This is a breaking story. More to follow...

A multi-millionaire tailor who claims leaky fridges at his luxury flat caused his £1m collection of fine French wines to go "mouldy" is suing for more than £550,000.

Master tailor Tom Reimer, who once kitted out opera legend Luciano Pavarotti, is a wine lover with a 20,000-strong collection of prime bottles, housed at his homes in London and Germany.

But Mr Reimer claims that the value of his collection in London was ruined due to faults with three special wine chillers installed as part of a refurb of his £8m Marylebone apartment in 2021.

A 1cm-wide gap on the doors of the three units allowed cool air to escape and warmer air to enter, he says, leading to condensation and mould growth on the labels and some of the vintages "probably" becoming "corked" massively reducing the value of his 1,500-bottle London collection.

Experts say rare wines are much less valuable on the collectors' market if their labels are damaged as purchasers are wary of taking a risk on the wine itself being ruined.

open image in gallery Two of the wine coolers at centre of Tom Reimer's moudly wine court case ( Champion News )

At Central London County Court, the tailor is now suing the outfitting company who installed the chillers for about £500,000 for the reduced value of his collection, as well as another £50,000 in other costs and losses.

However, Croydon-based International Food Services Equipment Ltd is fighting the claim, denying they designed the doors or the no more than "hairline" gap, which was nevertheless an “industry standard design feature”.

They also blame any label damage on Mr Reimer for repeatedly turning the units off when his neighbours complained about their noise, and say they wouldn't have taken the job on at all if they had been told the alleged value of the collection.

Tom Reimer, a scion of a wealthy German family, carved out a highly lucrative career as a top tailor in Hamburg, where in the 1990s his company kitted out Pavarotti with a white silk tailcoat as a contrast to his customary black tails and white tie.

open image in gallery Tom Reimer outside Central London County Court after hearing in case against International Food Services Equipment Limited ( Champion News )

As an avid wine collector, he has built a colossal hoard of 20,000 bottles over the years, many of them ultra-prime Bordeaux and Rhone Valley reds and cellared mostly in Germany.

However, while carrying out a major refurb of his £8m apartment in The Regent, Marylebone, he decided to install special chillers to “house some bottles” in the UK, his barrister, Ololade Saromi, told Recorder Sarah Ellington.

Mr Reimer’s architect contacted International Food Design, which specialises in restaurant design, asking whether it could supply cooled wine storage for the flat, which was being transformed into a “high-end residential apartment”.

The company ultimately installed a wine cooling system, featuring glass sliding doors and remote condensers, at a cost to Mr Reimer of about £23,000.

They were installed in March 2021, with two fridges with a total capacity for 195 bottles in the kitchen, and a third catering for 1,188 bottles on the first floor patio.

However, Mr Reimer says disaster struck because a 1cm gap on the fridge doors, extending to their full height, resulted in cool air leakage from the units, and warm air to enter.

The “constant exchange of warm and cold air” produced temperature fluctuation which was fatal for wine fridges required to maintain a steady temperature of 12-13 Celsius, he says.

“To maintain the required temperature, the fridges had to work harder," said his barrister.

“The condensers which performed the cooling function were continuously working as opposed to starting and stopping as required because the gap caused a constant exchange of warm and cold air. This produced temperature fluctuation and instability for which the condensers tried to compensate.

“The gaps in the fridge doors caused the loss of environmental control, excessive condenser operation, vibration, overheating, condensation and consequent damage to the claimant’s wine collection.

“The condensation settled on the stored wine bottles and caused the moulding and disintegration of the wine labels.

“This probably also resulted in cork disintegration and damage to the wine content."

open image in gallery A bottle of Chateau Petrus Pomerl 2012 which features in Tom Reimer's moudly wine court case ( Champion News )

Overall, Mr Reimer is claiming £499,452 under the Consumer Rights Act for the alleged reduced value of his £1m London wine collection, due to the label damage.

Many of the collection were elite “first growth” clarets from the Bordeaux and Rhone Valley regions, including bottles of 1982 Chateau Mouton Rothschild, which can sell for over £1,000, and 2012 Chateau Petrus Pomerol, which retails over £2,000.

He also wants further compensation to cover expenses such as over £14,000 subsequently spent on commercial wine storage and the roughly £23,000 he paid for the coolers to be installed.

But lawyers for the fitting company say any air loss through the “hairline” gap, designed to allow for movement between the doors, would have had no impact on temperature in the chillers, and deny that they designed the cooler doors in any case.

"The defendant did not design the wine fridge door system – it is simply part of a standard unit and the airgap complained of is a necessary element of a properly functioning sliding door system," said defence barrister, Matthew Winn-Smith.

And on top of suggesting that Mr Reimer courted disaster by turning off the units to pacify his neighbours, the company says they would never have tangled with the project in the first place had they known about the value of the wine collection.

open image in gallery Bottle of Chateau Mouton Rothschild 1982 which features in Tom Reimer's moudly wine court case ( Champion News )

The £23,000 price tag for the cooler installation was “extremely modest” compared with top notch wine storage specialists and cellarists, which would have charged £190,000, said Mr Winn-Smith.

“Nothing was communicated about the intended storage of circa £1 million of fine wine," he told the judge. “Nor was anything communicated about the need for especially quiet running condensing units.

“Had it been suggested before the contract was concluded that it was intended the fridges would store £1m worth of wine, it is almost certain that the defendant would not have entered into the contract.

"It is simply not what their goods are ever supplied to do.”

Emphasising that the company had no part in designing the wine fridge door system, Mr Winn-Smith suggested any damp or condensation was simply due to the coolers being regularly turned off.

“The defendant believes that any damage caused to the claimant’s wine collection was the result of Mr Reimer - or his agents or a third party - turning off the wine fridges because they were too noisy for his residential setting,” said the barrister.

Expanding his point, he said Mr Reimer was "under pressure from both his landlord and his neighbours.

"This explains why he, or someone else, would have turned off the units," he said.

"Had they been left on then, on our case, the wine would have been adequately refrigerated, and the moisture levels would have been fine, causing no condensation damage to any of the wine bottle labels.”

Mr Reimer, however, denies shutting off the coolers to placate his neighbours, although claiming that noise and vibration cranked up to “excessive” levels due to condensers on the units working overtime “due to constant demand generated by the gap”.

The trial is continuing.

Scotland is raring to boogie once more as the 2026 Commonwealth Games get underway with its opening ceremony on Thursday.

The Games return to Glasgow just 12 years after they were first hosted in the Scottish city, with a showpiece event at the Hydro expected to set the tone for the 10 days of action that will follow.

Medal events will run from Friday 24 July to Sunday 2 August, which will see more than 3,000 athletes from 74 nations and territories competing for 215 golds.

But before competition gets going, they will all come together at the opening ceremony, with each nation and territory sporting an individual batons customised to represent their culture.

Here’s everything you need to know about the opening ceremony.

When is the opening ceremony?

The opening ceremony starts at 8pm BST on Thursday 23 July at the Hydro in Glasgow.

How can I watch it?

Viewers in the UK can watch the opening ceremony on TNT Sports 2, with coverage starting at 6:30pm BST. It can also be streamed on HBO Max.

Who will be performing?

A number of artists will take to the stage to provide the musical entertainment, headlined by Tom Walker, who is most famed for his track Leave a Light On.

KT Tunstall, Callum Beattie, Nina Nesbitt and Valtos will also be performing, as well as Scottish collaboration Nathan Evans and Saint PHNX.

Six-time Olympic gold medallist Sir Chris Hoy will also take part in the opening, serving a poignant moment nearly two years on from his stage-four cancer diagnosis.

Thousands of people living with multiple sclerosis (MS) in England are set to benefit from a new twice-daily pill that significantly improves walking ability, which is now being rolled out on the NHS.

Hailed as "life-changing," fampridine marks a significant advancement as the first drug specifically designed to address walking difficulties associated with the incurable autoimmune disease.

MS, which affects the brain and spinal cord, can manifest through a range of debilitating symptoms including tiredness, dizziness, tingling sensations, muscle cramps, vision problems, and memory issues.

Until now, patients struggling with mobility have primarily relied on physiotherapy, walking aids, or supportive devices for their feet.

The drug, also known as Fampyra, functions by acting as a signal booster within the nervous system.

It works to restore electrical signals along damaged nerves, thereby enabling muscles to function more effectively and improving overall mobility for patients.

open image in gallery It is expected that a once-a-day weight loss pill will offer a more convenient treatment for obesity ( Alamy/PA )

Professor Frankie Swords, NHS national medical director, said: “Walking difficulties can have a huge impact on the freedom and independence of people with MS, so this signal-boosting pill could be life-changing for thousands of patients.

“Fampridine helps electrical messages travel along nerves damaged by MS, giving people the chance to walk more easily and helping them be more mobile to do more of the everyday things that matter to them.

“For some, even a modest improvement could mean getting around the house more easily, going out with greater confidence and living more independently.”

Officials estimate that around 5,000 people with MS will be eligible for the drug in the first year.

It is recommended for MS patients with certain Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores.

The EDSS is a tool used by medics to monitor disability caused by MS.

Those with a score of between four – able to walk without an aid or rest for around 500 metres – and seven, which include patients who use wheelchairs or are unable to walk further than five metres, will be offered fampridine.

Patients will try the drug for two to four weeks, with walking ability assessed before and after treatment.

open image in gallery Thousands of patients in England will be eligible for fampridine, which has been hailed as ‘life-changing’ ( Getty )

Those who show progress will continue to take the medicine and will be reviewed regularly.

Fampridine trials found the drug improved walking speed in 43 per cent of patients and helped people walk for longer.

Aysen Slack, 65, from Eastbourne, previously paid for fampridine privately, but stopped due to costs.

She said: “Fampridine seemed to be working well for me, but paying for the medication was a significant expense and I could not keep doing that forever. So I had to make the difficult decision to stop taking it.

“I would definitely like to try fampridine again on the NHS. My mobility has decreased a lot and even in my flat I have to use sticks now. It would make a huge difference to my life if I were able to improve my walking.”

Ceri Smith, head of policy and evidence at the MS Society, said: “We’re delighted that fampridine has now been approved for use on the NHS.

“Over 120,000 people live with MS in England and Fampridine is the only licensed treatment that helps improve walking ability and speed for some of these people.

“For many of them, it’s life-changing, allowing them to live more independently or stay in employment.

“It’s vital that MS services now have the support they need to make fampridine available to all people with MS who could benefit from it, regardless of where in England they live.”

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Arsenal identify new targets after Saliba blow, Liverpool hijack PSG’s bid for winger
News.content:
Arsenal are set to sign a centre-back this summer after it was confirmed that Premier League title winner William Saliba has been ruled out for an “extended period” with a back injury. The Gunners could turn to Aston Villa’s Ezri Konsa or former Manchester City centre-back John Stones, who is available as a free agent.

Arsenal are also set to step up their pursuit of Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes but the Magpies are said to be frustrated by the lack of contact from the Premier League champions in what could turn into a protracted transfer saga. Newcastle are holding out for a fee similar to Sandro Tonali’s potential £100m move to Tottenham Hotspur.

Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola has set out his targets for the transfer window and has confirmed the Reds “definitely need to sign a winger”. Liverpool have now reportedly turned their attention towards Monaco’s Maghnes Akliouche, who is also wanted by Paris Saint-Germain, while PSG’s Bradley Barcola is also still a target.

Manchester United are still interested in adding another midfielder after signing Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans and are said to be in talks with Roma for France international Manu Kone, while Chelsea have agreed to loan Alejandro Garnacho to Aston Villa after their record signing of Morgan Rogers.

Norway’s state oil company almost doubled its quarterly profits as the US-Israeli war on Iran choked off supplies from the Gulf and sent oil and gas prices soaring, allowing it to offer more cash to shareholders while cutting back on renewables.

Equinor reported adjusted earnings before tax of $11.48bn (£8.6bn) for the three months to the end of June, up from $6.54bn in the same period last year, slightly ahead of the $11.37bn average forecast in a poll of 17 analysts compiled by the company.

The quarter covered the most disruptive period for global oil supply in years as attacks on shipping cut traffic through the Strait of Hormuz – the channel between Iran and Oman that carried about a fifth of the world's oil before the war – to a fraction.

With Gulf exports curtailed, buyers turned to suppliers outside the region and Brent crude swung between $75 and more than $100 a barrel over the three months, against $60 to $70 in the same period last year.

Equinor, which supplies oil and gas to Europe, was among the main beneficiaries. The average price it received for its oil reached $97.90 a barrel in the second quarter as against $63 a year earlier, while the price for its European gas rose 32 per cent to $15.79 per million British thermal units. Its US gas price, meanwhile, fell 16 per cent to $2.30.

Production volumes rose 3 per cent in the same quarter last year and the company held to its full-year target of 3 per cent output growth and its planned investment of $13bn.

"Strong production in the second quarter enabled us to capture value from higher prices, contributing to strong cash flow and financial results," Anders Opedal, Equinor's president and chief executive, said in a statement.

The Stavanger-based company said last month that it would return $3bn to investors through share buybacks over the course of 2026, twice the amount previously planned, while reducing spending on renewable energy because of weak demand, according to Reuters. Buybacks are a means of returning cash to shareholders alongside dividends.

The company’s trading and refining arm, which buys and sells energy on world markets, made $777m in the quarter, more than the $623m analysts had expected and nearly double its own guidance of $400m, while adjusted net profit reached $3.44bn as against an average forecast of $3.36bn, Bloomberg noted.

The Hywind Tampen floating offshore wind farm is situated between energy company Equinor's oil and gas fields ( AFP/Getty )

Equinor's shares have risen 54 per cent since the start of the year, outstripping a 30 per cent gain across European energy stocks, according to Reuters.

The disruption has continued into the current quarter. Brent crude traded around $93 a barrel on Wednesday, its highest in six weeks, after the US military carried out an 11th consecutive night of strikes on Iran and Yemen's Houthi government announced a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, closing off the Red Sea pipeline route the kingdom had been using to bypass Hormuz for a some of its exports.

The latest strikes, and Iran’s retaliation against US military installations in the region, further weakened any hope that the interim ceasefire signed last month could be salvaged.

Equinor is the UK’s largest single supplier of gas, delivering about a quarter of the country's imports through pipelines from the Norwegian continental shelf at a time when British households face high energy bills due to the supply disruption caused by the Russian war against Ukraine.

The Norwegian company is seeking approval to develop the Rosebank oilfield west of Shetland, the largest undeveloped field in British waters, in partnership with Ithaca Energy.

The project was granted consent in 2023, but a Scottish court ruled the approval unlawful last year because it failed to account for the emissions produced when the extracted oil was burned. The two companies have since resubmitted their plans.

Oil companies across Europe are expected to report sharply higher earnings for the quarter, with Shell, BP and Total Energies due to publish results in the coming weeks.
