World.title: Greer joins USMCA talks in Mexico City to push for stronger automotive rules of origin
World.content:
The U.S. government, which announced on July 1 that it had declined to renew the United States-Mexico-Canada-Agreement (USMCA) in its current form, is seeking stronger automotive sector rules of origin (ROOs) in the North American free trade pact.

In a report submitted to U.S. Congress this month, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer stated that his office, the USTR, “intends to examine carefully the USMCA’s automotive rules of origin to identify areas where stronger rules can directly benefit U.S. manufacturers and workers.”

In the foreword of the same report — titled “Report to Congress on the Operation of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement with respect to Trade in Automotive Goods” — Greer said that “the automotive industry remains a significant contributor to the U.S. and North American economies” and “the USMCA has had a positive impact on the global competitiveness of the regional auto industry.”

“… Yet, the United States has run a persistent, substantial, and growing trade deficit in autos and parts with Mexico for over 30 years,” the U.S. trade representative stated.

“In 2024, that deficit peaked at [US] $138.2 billion. In recent years, analysis indicates that the share of U.S. content within Mexico’s automotive exports to the United States has been declining, while the share of Chinese or other Asian content in those goods has been increasing.”

In the July 1 report, the USTR stated that the North American automotive industry “has faced external supply chain shocks, increased competitive pressures from China, and evolving U.S. trade policy.

“Further, evidence shows that U.S. content in vehicles produced in Mexico and Canada is declining, while automotive trade deficit with Mexico remains persistently large. The 2026 USMCA Joint Review will provide the United States the opportunity to assess and strengthen the USMCA automotive ROOs to incentivize the use of additional U.S. and North American content,” the USTR said.

“… In 2017, industry estimated 85 percent of the auto parts content for vehicles built in Canada originated in the United States, and more than 60 percent of the auto parts content of vehicles assembled in Mexico originated in the United States. But in 2024, industry reported that the estimated U.S.-origin content of vehicles built in Canada and Mexico dropped to 50 and 35 percent, respectively,” Greer’s office stated.

In an article published on Wednesday under the headline “U.S. insists on strengthening USMCA rules of origin,” the newspaper El Economista wrote that the USTR was seeking to bolster automotive ROOs in the three-way trade pact even though the rules are already “the strictest of any trade agreement in the world.”

In its report, the USTR noted that the USMCA “raised regional value content (RVC) requirements to 75 percent for passenger vehicles and light trucks, compared to 62.5 percent under the NAFTA,” the North American Free Trade Agreement that was superseded by the USMCA in 2020.

In accordance with the USMCA, clearing the 75% RVC threshold is one necessary condition for the tariff-free trade of vehicles within North America. However, U.S. President Donald Trump — who is determined to protect and grow the U.S. auto industry — last year imposed 25% tariffs on vehicles made in Mexico and Canada. The U.S. content in those vehicles — but not regional content — is exempt from the tariff, lowering the effective duty for most cars exported to the U.S. from Mexico.

Despite the United States’ decision not to extend the USMCA until 2042, the free trade pact remains in effect.

However, it is now set to be reviewed on an annual basis until 2036, although the three signatories can decide at any time to extend it for an additional 16 years.

Mexico-US trade talks continue in CDMX

The focus on possible changes to automotive ROOs in the USMCA comes as Mexican and U.S. officials engage in USMCA review talks in Mexico City. Mexico’s top USMCA negotiator, Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard, is already participating in the bilateral discussions, which began Monday, and Greer is set to join them.

“Ambassador Jamieson Greer will travel to Mexico from Wednesday, July 22, to Friday, July 24, to continue bilateral discussions related to the Joint Review of USMCA,” the USTR said in a statement last week.

“During the bilateral meetings, Ambassador Greer and Secretary Ebrard will discuss a range of topics including steel and aluminum and derivative products, automobiles, economic security, labor, agriculture, and electronic payment services,” the USTR said, noting also that Greer will meet with President Claudia Sheinbaum at the National Palace. That meeting is scheduled for this Thursday.

One of Mexico’s main aims in its negotiations with the United States is to secure the reduction — if not the elimination — of U.S. tariffs that currently apply to Mexican vehicles, steel and aluminum. Among the measures the Mexican government has taken that could help it secure concessions from its northern neighbor is the imposition on Jan. 1 of new and higher tariffs on imports from China and other countries with which it doesn’t have free trade agreements. The government reported on Monday that the new tariffs approved by Congress in December 2025 had reduced imports across 1,463 product categories by 23.2% between January and May. The most impacted country is China.

Segundo día de trabajos con el equipo de USTR , vamos avanzando. pic.twitter.com/pHKvZp6olF — Marcelo Ebrard C. (@m_ebrard) July 22, 2026

Underscoring the United States’ desire to strengthen automotive ROOs in the USMCA, Greer said on Wednesday that doing so was a “key objective,” according to reporting by the news agency Reuters.

However, the U.S. trade representative, who appeared before the U.S. Senate Finance Committee in Washington, D.C., before departing for Mexico, said that the resolution of the automotive ROOs issue would “take a little more time” and involve discussions with U.S. Congress “in the following year.”

However, Greer said he hoped to strike ​some interim trade agreements with Mexico and Canada this year, according to Reuters.

“We are moving with all due speed on this,” he said.

Reuters reported that Greer “did not specify what separate ‘potential interim arrangements'” with Mexico and Canada “would look like, but said he wanted ​to have options for Trump, Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to consider by the end of this year.”

Sheinbaum said last Thursday that at this week’s talks with the U.S., Mexico would be aiming to “reach some agreements that give us greater stability in the coming years.”

She has stressed that “at any time,” Mexico, the United States and Canada can agree to extend the USMCA for 16 more years, something that the Mexican and Canadian governments wanted to do this month but which the Trump administration rejected.

Mexico and the United States are each other’s largest trade partners, while Canada is the second-largest market for Mexican exports. Most trade between Mexico and the United States occurs tariff-free under the USMCA, which governs North American trade worth around $2 trillion annually.

With reports from El Economista and Reuters

World.title: Cueva twins dominate Zapopan Diving Cup, cinching gold over China for the first time ever
World.content:
Mexico has long excelled in diving, and the latest gold-medal triumph of the 14-year-old Cueva twins from the Bajío state of Jalisco demonstrates the country’s potential.

Mexican divers finished their participation in the 2026 Zapopan Diving Cup, held between July 16 and 19, with 10 medals: three gold, four silver and three bronze. Mía and Lía Cueva Lobato defeated Chinese partners Shan Lin and Yiping Long to win gold in the synchronized 3-meter springboard final, marking the first time the duo had defeated Chinese competitors in an international competition.

Mexico’s Rut Páez and Yunuen Parra finished in fourth place in the same event.

“I felt very happy,” said Lía Cueva after receiving her gold medal. “It’s the first time we’ve beaten the Chinese, and it gives us a lot of motivation to do it again at the Olympic Games.”

“We know we still have a lot of work to do, but I’m convinced that we will continue training very hard so that results like this… become more and more frequent and visible,” added Mía Cueva. “They can expect us at the Olympic Games.”

The win followed previous success at the World Aquatics Diving World Cup in Jalisco’s capital of Guadalajara, held in April 2025, in which the Cueva twins took silver in the women’s 3-meter synchronized springboard final.

Meanwhile, Mexicans Randal Willars and Kevin Berlín delivered a strong performance on the men’s synchronized 10-meter platform, beating Great Britain and Colombia to take the gold medal, with a score of 414.72 points.

In the women’s 10-meter platform event, Mexico’s Suri Cueva took the silver medal, with 303.10 points, while Samantha Jiménez took bronze with 302.15 points. China’s Zhixin Qu took first place with 369.40 points.

The Metropolitan Aquatic Center hosted representatives from nine countries in preparation for the Santo Domingo 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games, to be held from July 24 to August 8. On Monday, President Sheinbaum presided over an official send-off for the more than 600 athletes who will compete across disciplines including diving, archery, gymnastics, boxing and more.

With reports from Cronica and Grupo Animal

World.title: México state security strategy has slashed homicides in half: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📍 Mañanera held in Toluca: President Sheinbaum took her Wednesday press conference to Toluca, capital of México state, Mexico’s most populous state with around 17 million residents.

President Sheinbaum took her Wednesday press conference to Toluca, capital of México state, Mexico’s most populous state with around 17 million residents. 📉 Homicides down sharply in México state: National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported an average of 2.8 homicides per day in the state in June, a 58% drop compared to September 2024. She said a “unified command” strategy launched in 15 high-crime municipalities last year contributed to the decline.

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported an average of 2.8 homicides per day in the state in June, a 58% drop compared to September 2024. She said a “unified command” strategy launched in 15 high-crime municipalities last year contributed to the decline. 📅 Lowest homicide rate in 19 years: Figueroa said México state saw an average of 2.9 homicides per day in the first half of 2026, down 31% from 2025’s daily average and 68% below the 2013 rate.

Figueroa said México state saw an average of 2.9 homicides per day in the first half of 2026, down 31% from 2025’s daily average and 68% below the 2013 rate. 👮 Over 3,300 arrests since Sheinbaum took office: Security Minister García Harfuch said 3,367 people have been detained for high-impact crimes in México state since October 2024, alongside seizures of 1,219 kg of drugs and 819 firearms.

Security Minister García Harfuch said 3,367 people have been detained for high-impact crimes in México state since October 2024, alongside seizures of 1,219 kg of drugs and 819 firearms. 🎯 No timeline on Iván Archivaldo Guzmán capture: Asked how close authorities are to detaining the Chapitos faction leader, García Harfuch declined to speculate, instead pointing to the recent killing of an alleged Culiacán plaza boss as a sign of progress against the faction.

Asked how close authorities are to detaining the Chapitos faction leader, García Harfuch declined to speculate, instead pointing to the recent killing of an alleged Culiacán plaza boss as a sign of progress against the faction. ⛓️ El Mayo’s prison transfer uncertain: Asked whether Ismael Zambada could serve his life sentence in a Mexican prison, García Harfuch said that would depend on whether Mexico’s Attorney General’s Office pursues extradition, though a transfer appears unlikely.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Wednesday morning press conference in Toluca, capital of México state.

Located in central Mexico, the state, commonly abbreviated as Edomex, is Mexico’s most populated with just under 17 million residents when the last census was conducted in 2020.

A good number of the state’s 125 municipalities are located in the greater metropolitan area of Mexico City. They include two municipalities that are among the 10 most populated in the country: Ecatepec (1.64 million residents in 2020) and Nezahualcóyotl (1.07 million).

México state is also home to popular tourism destinations including the Teotihuacán archeological site and the magical towns of Valle de Bravo and Malinalco.

Security in the state — Mexico’s fifth most violent in the first half of the year in terms of total homicides — was a key focus at today’s mañanera, with officials presenting the latest data on homicides and arrests.

Like the vast majority of Mexico’s 32 federal entities, México state has seen a significant reduction in its homicide rate this year. Thus, federal and state officials, including Governor Delfina Gómez, who attended today’s mañanera, have statistics to back up their argument that their security initiatives are working.

Beyond the presentation of the latest security statistics, Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference was significant as Security Minister Omar García Harfuch responded to questions about Iván Archivaldo Guzmán Salazar, a Sinaloa Cartel leader and son of convicted drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, and about Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, a Sinaloa Cartel kingpin who on Monday was sentenced to life in prison in the United States.

Homicides decline significantly in México state

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa told reporters that the security strategy in México state has prioritized “intelligence, coordination and the territorial presence” of security forces.

She noted that a specific “unified command” strategy was implemented in 15 high-crime municipalities in eastern México state in March 2025, contributing to a reduction in homicides in the state that borders Mexico City to the north, east and west.

Figueroa presented data that showed that there was an average of 2.8 homicides per day in México state in June, a reduction of 58% compared to the daily average in September 2024, the final month of the presidency of Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

She also reported that the homicide rate in México state in the first six months of 2026 was the lowest in the past 19 years. There was an average of 2.9 homicides per day between January and June, a reduction of 31% compared to the daily average across 2025.

Compared to 2013, when there was an average of 9.1 homicides per day, the reduction in the first six months of this year was 68.1%.

Figueroa noted there was an average of 116.1 reported high-impact crimes per day between January and June, a reduction of 19% compared to 2025. Among the offenses classified as high-impact crimes are murder, kidnapping, extortion and violent robbery.

More than 3,300 arrests in México state since Sheinbaum took office

At the start of his presentation, García Harfuch said that “México state is an example of how the coordination between the three levels of government yields results.”

The security minister also said that since the current government took office in October 2024, it has worked closely with the México state Attorney General’s Office and Security Ministry “to develop investigations, carry out joint operations and detain those who generate violence in the entity.”

“This coordinated work,” García Harfuch said, has resulted in the arrest of 3,300 people who allegedly committed high-impact crimes.

Data he presented showed that the exact number of people arrested between Oct. 1, 2024, and June 30, 2026, was 3,367.

In addition, authorities seized 1,219 kilograms of drugs and 819 firearms in the same period.

“These results reflect a strategy based on intelligence and investigation, but above all operational coordination that has allowed us to disrupt criminal structures, provide faster assistance [when crimes are committed], … detain priority targets and strengthen the safety of Mexican families,” García Harfuch said.

Are authorities closing in on Iván Archivaldo Guzmán?

A reporter for the newspaper Milenio noted that Milenio recently published a report stating that Iván Archivaldo Guzmán, leader of the Chapitos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, is in a “situation of tactical vulnerability and extreme isolation.”

“How close is the security cabinet to detaining Iván Archivaldo?” the reporter asked García Harfuch.

“In order not to speculate and say how close or how far [we are from detaining Guzmán], I prefer to talk about the progress the security cabinet has made [in Sinaloa],” the security minister said.

García Harfuch noted that an individual nicknamed “El Texas” — an alleged plaza chief in Culiacán for the Chapitos — was recently killed in a clash with the army in the Sinaloa capital.

The slain man, identified in media reports as Cristhian Guadalupe Pérez Pérez, was one of the “main generators of violence in Culiacán and this entire area,” the security minister said, referring to Sinaloa.

“He was a key person for this organization, for this criminal leader,” he said, referring to Iván Archivaldo and the Chapitos.

García Harfuch said that federal security forces carry out operations in Sinaloa every week “to continue weakening” the Chapitos and “the other faction of the Sinaloa Cartel.”

He was referring to the Mayos faction, which is engaged in a long-running and extremely bloody feud with the Chapitos that intensified after Joaquín Guzmán López, another son of El Chapo, kidnapped El Mayo in July 2024 and forced him onto a private plane that flew him to New Mexico where he, and Guzmán López, were detained by U.S. authorities.

Could El Mayo be transferred to a Mexican prison?

The same Milenio reporter highlighted that Zambada’s lawyer, Frank Pérez, said in an interview that his client wants to serve his prison sentence in Mexico. He asked García Harfuch whether a transfer to a Mexican prison was possible.

The security minister said that the Federal Attorney General’s Office would have to determine whether or not it would seek the extradition of Zambada, who was also wanted in Mexico when he was arrested in the U.S. two years ago.

A transfer of the 76-year-old drug trafficker to a prison in Mexico appears extremely unlikely.

Joseph Nocella Jr., U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of New York, said Monday that Zambada would “spend the rest of his life in a U.S. prison, exactly where he belongs.”

El Chapo, who founded the Sinaloa Cartel with El Mayo and others, escaped twice from prison in Mexico, once in a laundry cart in 2001 and again in 2015 via a tunnel that connected to his cell. He is now serving a life sentence in the Florence Supermax prison in Colorado.

World.title: Corozal man fined $30 for drinking Belikin stout in public; Cops stopped him with his bottle halfway – Could have bought 10 stouts
World.content:
Corozal man fined $30 for drinking Belikin stout in public; Cops stopped him with his bottle halfway – Could have bought 10 stouts

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Corozal man was fined $30 after pleading guilty to drinking alcohol in public on Orange Street in Belize City.

Twenty-seven-year-old Alex Ronaldo Soler, a resident of the Altamira area of Corozal Town, appeared unrepresented in court and pleaded guilty to public drinking. He was fined $25, along with $5 in court costs.

Soler has until July 31, 2026, to pay the fine or serve one week in prison. The court informed him that the payment may also be made at the Corozal Magistrate’s Court.

According to the prosecution, Corporal Mario Chin was conducting foot patrol on Orange Street at around 4:00 p.m. on Sunday, July 19, when he saw Soler walking toward Albert Street while drinking from a brown Belikin Stout bottle.

Police said Soler attempted to conceal the bottle when approached. The bottle, which reportedly still contained about half of its contents, was seized as evidence.

Soler was escorted to the Precinct One Police Station, where he was formally charged with drinking in public.

World.title: Alex Noralez sexual assault appeal set for September 25
World.content:
Alex Noralez sexual assault appeal set for September 25

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The appeal of a former San Pedro teacher convicted of sexually assaulting two students is scheduled to be heard in the High Court on September 25, 2026.

Alex Jason Noralez, 47, appeared before Justice Candace Nanton on Wednesday through attorney Leeroy Banner, who substituted for his attorney, Richard “Dickie” Bradley.

The appeal could not proceed because the necessary documents had not yet been filed. Noralez’s grounds of appeal must be submitted by August 14, while the respondent has until August 28 to file a response.

Noralez remains remanded at the Belize Central Prison after being denied bail and a stay of execution pending the outcome of his appeal.

On January 21, 2026, Noralez was convicted of two of three counts of sexual assault involving students at a San Pedro high school. He was acquitted of a third count involving another student.

Noralez maintained that he did not sexually assault the students, telling the lower court that any hugs were innocent.

He was sentenced to 18 months in prison on each count, but the sentences were ordered to run concurrently, meaning he is serving a total of 18 months.

World.title: Two years probation for mother who woke up to $47,935 in bank account and went on spree with Boledo money
World.content:
Two years probation for mother who woke up to $47,935 in bank account and went on spree with Boledo money

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City mother who admitted retaining and spending money mistakenly deposited into her bank account has avoided immediate imprisonment and was instead placed on two years’ probation.

Thirty-four-year-old Kamera Kathleen Belisle, of the Lake Independence area, pleaded guilty to dishonestly retaining a wrongful credit after BZ$47,935.45 belonging to the Belize Government Lottery was mistakenly transferred to her Belize Bank account in March 2024.

Justice Candace Nanton imposed the probation sentence on Wednesday after considering a report from the Community Rehabilitation Department, which had recommended a suspended sentence rather than imprisonment.

Belisle must report to the Community Rehabilitation Department, comply with all instructions from her assigned officer and participate in any programmes considered appropriate. The judge recommended that she undergo financial-literacy training and financial counselling.

The court warned that Belisle could be brought back for sentencing and face up to two years in prison if she commits another offence or breaches the conditions of her probation.

The money was intended for Lowe’s Supermarket in Ladyville, a sub-agent of the Belize Government Lottery, but was sent to Belisle’s account after an incorrect telephone number and bank-account information were provided to Nando’s Wholesale LLP, the lottery’s sales agent.

Investigators found that BZ$28,592.35 had already been removed through bank transfers, ATM withdrawals and point-of-sale purchases before the Financial Intelligence Unit froze the account. A remaining balance of approximately BZ$20,030.81 is expected to be returned to the complainant.

Belisle, who was represented by attorney Norman Rodriguez, told the court she was remorseful and described the incident as a life lesson.

“I am really sorry that this happened, and I do apologize,” she said.

World.title: International News: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to face trial in June 2027
World.content:
International News: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to face trial in June 2027

By Zoila Palma: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are scheduled to go on trial in New York on June 1, 2027, over alleged weapons and drug-related offenses, which both deny.

U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein set the trial date on Wednesday and scheduled a pre-trial hearing for November 17 to consider motions from both sides.

U.S. forces reportedly seized Maduro and Flores during a nighttime raid on their compound in Caracas on January 3 before bringing them to the United States to face prosecution.

Maduro’s defense attorney, Barry Pollack, has indicated that he may argue that his client is protected by sovereign immunity, a legal principle that can shield heads of state from prosecution.

The court hearing drew significant public attention, with spectators reportedly waiting for hours to catch a glimpse of the former Venezuelan leader.

Maduro appeared in court wearing a beige jail uniform but was not handcuffed. He and Flores used headphones for translation as their attorneys met with the judge, and Maduro later waved to members of the public before being escorted from the courthouse by U.S. Marshals.

World.title: International News: Over 1,000 firefighters battle massive wildfire in Southern France
World.content:
International News: Over 1,000 firefighters battle massive wildfire in Southern France

By Zoila Palma: More than 1,100 firefighters are battling a major wildfire that has scorched approximately 2,500 hectares in the mountainous Var region of southern France, northeast of Marseille.

Today, officials said that they were working to extinguish remaining fire pockets before strong Mistral winds, expected later in the day, could intensify the blaze.

The regional government reported that four people suffered minor smoke inhalation, while 10 homes were destroyed and about 50 others damaged.

Firefighters, however, managed to prevent the flames from spreading to hundreds of additional homes. The emergency response includes four firefighting aircraft, three helicopters, around 350 vehicles and reinforcements from neighboring regions.

The wildfire forced about 500 residents from threatened villages to spend the night in emergency shelters.

Hundreds of households near the villages of Cotignac and Pontevès remain without electricity, and several roads have been closed as crews continue to battle the flames.

World.title: Dominica’s Fort Young Hotel is hiring, and Belizeans can now work there freely
World.content:
Dominica’s Fort Young Hotel is hiring, and Belizeans can now work there freely

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A job opportunity from across the Caribbean may be within closer reach for Belizeans than ever before. Fort Young Hotel and Dive Resort, the historic waterfront property in Roseau, Dominica, has announced vacancies across its operations, with applications open until July 31, 2026.

The openings span the full range of hotel work: Plumber, Painter, Carpenter, Commis, Demi Chef, Chef de Partie, Houseman, Food and Beverage Server, Bar Supervisor, Spa Therapist, Dive Master, and Maintenance Technicians in both HVAC and Electronics.

General requirements include previous experience in a similar role as an asset, a valid Food Handler’s Certification where applicable, consistent attendance and punctuality, willingness to work assigned shifts including weekends and public holidays, clear communication with guests and team members, and adherence to hotel policies.

What makes this notable for Belizeans is the enhanced CARICOM free movement arrangement in effect between Belize, Dominica, Barbados, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines, which allows nationals of these countries to live and work in each other’s territories without a work permit. Applicants should verify current travel and documentation requirements before making plans.

Applications go to [email protected] before the July 31 deadline.

World.title: Atlantic Bank brings a loan fair with same day approval to San Pedro Saturday
World.content:
Atlantic Bank brings a loan fair with same day approval to San Pedro Saturday

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Islanders thinking about a new home, a vehicle or a personal loan have a date to mark. Atlantic Bank’s San Pedro Branch is hosting a Loan Fair this Saturday, July 25, 2026, from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. on Barrier Reef Drive, San Pedro Town.

The one day event invites residents to apply for a home loan, a vehicle loan, or any other personal loan, with the bank’s team on hand to walk applicants through their options. The standout feature is same day approval, meaning qualified applicants could walk out of the fair with an answer rather than waiting weeks for a decision.

For Ambergris Caye, the timing and the offer fit the island’s realities. Housing demand in San Pedro continues to climb, and a vehicle loan on the island often means the golf cart that keeps a family or a business moving. A single Saturday to sit with a lender, ask questions and get a decision on the spot removes much of the friction from taking that step.

Applicants are encouraged to come prepared with their personal and financial documents to make the most of the visit.

The fair runs Saturday, July 25, 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m., Barrier Reef Drive. For more information, visit www.atlabank.com or call 223-1212.

World.title: National Basketball team represents Belize at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in Dominican Republic
World.content:
National Basketball team represents Belize at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in Dominican Republic

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s National Basketball Team is set for the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic.

Team Belize carries pride and passion that have made Belize proud time and time again.

“This talented group has already delivered memorable performances for Belize on the international stage, and they are prepared to do it again as they take on some of the region’s top basketball nations.

Team Belize is ready to leave it all on the court,” Belize Olympic and Commonwealth Games Association said.

The 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games (Santo Domingo 2026) are scheduled to take place from July 24 to August 8, 2026, in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic.

This sporting event is highly historic, marking the exact 100th anniversary since the regional games were first inaugurated back in 1926.

World.title: A light extinguished
World.content:
Shawna Williams-Stevens (left) shows off trophies her niece, 10-year-old Shani Coke, received from Troy Primary School. Looking on is Shani’s mother, Ackeem “Kim” Williams. Kasey Williams

TROY, Trelawny — Huddled on the verandah of their family home, relatives of 10-year-old Shani “Kaidra” Coke, whose partially nude body was found with her throat slashed on Tuesday, remembered the child for her brilliance and radiant smile.

“Shani was born here and lived [with her grandparents], because her [mother] has to work. When Shani goes to school she doesn’t play around. She took her education seriously. From Shani a go basic school she was always first [in her class]. She was always putting out her best. She is from an educated background. Her father is educated and so is her mother,” the child’s aunt Shawna Williams-Stevens told journalists on Wednesday as she stood beside her grieving sister, Shani’s mother Ackeem “Kim” Williams.

The aunt’s hands could not hold the many academic trophies and certificates earned by Shani during her tenure at Troy Primary School.

“From grade one her teachers rewarded her, whether with a stamp in her book or sweets, or you know the teachers always try to elevate her for her to know that she does good. Her mother would always buy her gifts to encourage her,” said Williams-Stevens.

“Right now she was [among] the top students at Troy Primary. If school was keeping it would have to lock today, because of Shani,” added the aunt, while pointing out that up to last Friday Shani was recognised for her participation in summer school.

“All last week she got her certificate to show her brilliance. When you look at her you see the next doctor, lawyer, and they just took her life, just cut her off. Right now we are devastated. Right now we don’t know our head from our feet. Last night we nuh sleep. This is traumatising. Maybe Kaidra was going to come and take her mother out of poverty and they cut her life short and kill her,” Williams-Stevens said before breaking down in tears.

According to a police report, as well as the account of residents, mid-afternoon Tuesday Shani was walking home from a shop along a roadway near her home when she was abducted.

Later, a farmer, who had gone in search of his cow after hearing strange sounds from bushes, made the grisly discovery and raised an alarm.

Police said following the discovery of the child’s body, there was a mob attack on a father and son in the community.

Residents told the Jamaica Observer that the two men are Shani’s relatives. Angry residents accused the son of raping and killing the child. He was beaten, chopped and stoned to death, while his father, who was also attacked by the mob, was admitted to hospital.

Police identified the dead man as Delroy Coke, but did not provide any other information.

Shani’s father, Aston Coke, otherwise called Junior, told journalists that his daughter was well-loved and admired by many in her community.

“Her grandmother sent her to the shop and she did not make it back home. Someone stopped her on the street and disturbed her somehow and slashed her throat… She was loving and caring in the community growing up. Everybody knows her. She knows everyone. She can see you and call you by your full name. She had a sense of humour. She was doing well in school and she got a lot of academic awards,” said the heartbroken father.

“She decided that she wanted to make something out of herself growing up, because we were driving that into her head, but things just happened overnight,” added Coke as he alleged that the man believed to have killed his daughter was a habitual offender.

“It is an act that should never have happened in this neighbourhood,” declared Coke, who is battling his own health problems.

He recounted the last encounter with his daughter over the weekend.

“She came by Saturday afternoon and my uncle was putting on a back-to-school treat up by the community centre and she went there to get bags and food. She was very polite. She stopped by and I said to Kaidra, ‘What you doing here? Aren’t you supposed to be up by the treat?’ She said, ‘Yes, Daddy’ and she walked off and said, ‘Daddy, later when I am coming back I will show you what I get.’ I called her back and went in my wallet to give her money to buy juice,” Coke said.

“That was the first time my uncle and some of my aunts met her. I didn’t get to see her Sunday morning when she went to church and I didn’t get to see her yesterday (Tuesday), because she didn’t come all the way out here to the store,” he said as he reflected on the precious memories and proud moments he spent with his daughter.

“She was always smiling and you never saw her sad. You always saw her happy. Those are the things I remember about her at all times. When it comes to the academics you go by her grandmother’s house, trust me you will see a lot of achievements — trophies — that she got at school. Even sometimes when her mother and grandmother are not around I go by the church to collect them,” he said.

“It is a very sad story to know that this neighbourhood of Troy, Trelawny, has come to this. I don’t know if it is because it reached my doorstep [why] I feel it so pressuring, but things have been happening around here a long time and nobody gets justice,” charged Coke.

World.title: Too late to explain?
World.content:
Chairman of Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee Julian Robinson speaks during Wednesday’s sitting of the parliamentary oversight committee.

PERMANENT secretary in the Office of the Prime Minister Ambassador Rocky Meade has defended the Government’s decision to preserve Hurricane Melissa cash donations for longer-term recovery, insisting the auditor general’s finding that only 1.8 per cent of the funds had been spent did not reflect the Government’s full recovery strategy.

However, after hearing the detailed explanation from Meade during Wednesday’s sitting of the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), Chairman Julian Robinson argued that the explanation should have been communicated much earlier and clearer to prevent the public alarm and loss of confidence that followed the audit report.

The discussion emerged as the committee reviewed the auditor general’s compliance audit into governance and procurement under the Hurricane Melissa relief programme, which found that the National Disaster Fund Committee had been non-functional for more than two years.

As members questioned officials about how the committee now operates, the conversation shifted to the controversy sparked by a separate auditor general’s report showing that only 1.8 per cent of the roughly $1.44 billion in Hurricane Melissa cash donations had been spent by February 23, prompting Meade to again defend the Government’s recovery strategy.

Seeking to place those findings in context, Meade told the committee that the Government deliberately prioritised distributing food, medical supplies, building materials and other items donated in kind during the immediate aftermath of the hurricane, while preserving cash donations to support the country’s transition from emergency relief to long-term recovery.

“The point about the percentage of donations that were deployed needs to be put into context. We were getting donations in kind and we got cash donations. The decision that was taken was in the immediate aftermath of the hurricane, while persons were in need of physical items, giving them money would not help them at that time necessarily. They were interested in getting physical items. The funds that we had, the idea was to reserve those funds to acquire and provide for these [modular] units that would give people the recovery,” he explained.

He argued that focusing solely on the amount of cash spent failed to capture the extensive use of donated goods, which he said formed the backbone of the initial relief effort.

“The bottom line to the point is that the totality of the donations we got included cash and kind, and the priority was to use up the resources in kind first. So by reporting that at a certain point, only a small percentage of the donated funds were used, it doesn’t capture the fuller picture that of all the donations, including the kind… we did substantially use up the donations in kind to provide for the immediate need, and it was a part of the plan that most of the funds that were donated would be used for the more medium-term sustainable recovery, including the housing solutions, [and] that’s the context,” he said.

While acknowledging that approach, Robinson said the public had not been given sufficient information to understand why the money remained largely untouched months after the hurricane.

“It’s important to note because people did fundraisers, people went out of their way, and so if you hear eight months post a hurricane that only two per cent of the money has been used, come next hurricane, people aren’t going to be inclined to run and support a fund of this nature… So the communication on that particular issue, I believe, should have been done earlier, probably immediately after the report came out so that there was some greater understanding of what the plan was,” said Robinson.

Meade accepted that the Government could have done more to communicate its strategy, although he maintained that information had been shared through several channels.

“I certainly accept the point that if you saw a gap in communication, it means we didn’t do enough. I can assure you that communication was done, but clearly if there are persons who didn’t hear it, we didn’t do enough… I accept your point in principle, and we will do even more than we did,” said Meade.

Updating the committee on the recovery programme, Meade said the cash donations are now being used to support the modular housing initiative, including the construction of foundations and installation of utilities.

He disclosed that the Government had initially targeted the procurement of 2,500 modular units, with about 1,200 already in Jamaica for families who suffered total or near-total loss of their homes during Hurricane Melissa.

World.title: For the love of music
World.content:
Veteran dancehall selector Supa Twitch has credited his enduring passion for music, discipline, and unwavering respect for sound system culture as the keys to a career that has remained relevant for nearly four decades.

Fresh from a standout performance at the recent Joyride event, Supa Twitch said the atmosphere was a reminder of why the music of the 1990s and early 2000s continues to resonate with fans across generations.

“Joyride was special. The crowd came to feel the music, not just hear it. You could feel the nostalgia in the air, with people singing every lyric from my 90s set like it dropped yesterday. When I touched the stage the energy was electric. It was pure love, which is the magic of a real dancehall crowd,” he said.

Born in Hartford, Connecticut, and raised in east Kingston, Supa Twitch attended St Aloysius Primary School before moving on to St. George’s College. He relocated to New York in 1991 and is now based in Miami, although he describes the road as his true office.

“I was in love with dancehall from the age of 10 and used to sneak out just to listen to sound systems,” he recalled.

His professional journey began in 1988 with the east Kingston-based Supersonic sound system before moving to Black Stone the following year.

Inspired by legendary selectors Rory of Stone Love and Webba of Black Stone, Supa Twitch said he quickly realised that selecting was about much more than playing records.

“A selector doesn’t just play tunes; a selector moves people. I wanted to move people,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

After migrating to New York, he joined Afrique Soundstation, where he worked alongside respected figures including Jagga B, Crazy Richie, and the late Supa Claude.

“That was school for me. They taught me versatility and showed me how to take dancehall global without losing my roots,” he shared.

Reflecting on his longevity in one of the world’s most competitive music cultures, Supa Twitch said staying true to the music has always come first.

“You have to respect the music, evolve without selling out, and bring 100 per cent every time you perform. Most importantly, you have to keep loving the music. Once that love disappears, it starts feeling like a job,” the selector charged.

While acknowledging that today’s dancehall industry offers artistes unprecedented global opportunities through digital platforms, he believes something valuable has been lost.

“The talent is definitely there today, but the golden era had more artiste development and stronger connections between artists and sound systems. Back then, a tune had to pass the dance test before it hit radio. Now a song can trend and disappear in two weeks,” the veteran reasoned.

For Supa Twitch, events like Joyride play a vital role in preserving Jamaica’s rich sound system heritage.

“Joyride acts as both an archive and an amplifier. It reminds the new generation where the music comes from and reminds my generation why we fell in love with it in the first place. Sound system culture is Jamaica’s original social media,” he said.

One of the biggest highlights of his Joyride performance came when he playfully convinced female patrons he was about to play only hard-core dancehall selections before surprising them with classic soul and R&B favourites.

“I had them singing every single word. That created the biggest vibe of the entire night,” he told the Observer.

Among his proudest achievements are founding Supa Sound in 2005, winning the 2014 International Reggae and World Music Awards (IRAWMA) for Florida’s Most Popular Dance DJ, and successfully touring Japan annually between 2013 and 2019.

Looking ahead, Supa Twitch revealed plans for an extensive international touring schedule, including Europe, Canada, and a return to Japan later this year, with Australia targeted for 2027. He is also expanding his acting career following his appearance in the 2025 film Unbelievable.

World.title: Final push to get PEP students high school-ready
World.content:
Permanent secretary in the Ministry of Education Dr Kasan Troupe delivers her remarks at the handover ceremony of nine CIBC Caribbean prepaid cards to principals affected by last October’s Hurricane Melissa at the bank’s corporate office in New Kingston.Garfield Robinson

THE Ministry of Education is expecting at least 80 per cent of the 1,341 students enrolled in its special summer numeracy and literacy programme, for those who did not attain mastery scores in their Primary Exit Profile (PEP) examinations, to meet that benchmark before they enter high school in September.

After PEP results were released in June, the education ministry reported that of the 31,677 students who sat the exam, 75 per cent achieved mastery in numeracy assessments, while 79 per cent demonstrated mastery in literacy.

At the time, portfolio minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon indicated that those students who performed at near mastery and non-mastery levels would be sought out by the ministry to ensure that no child is left behind.

On Tuesday, permanent secretary in the ministry Dr Kasan Troupe told the Jamaica Observer that those students are now being engaged in an intense three-week, Government-funded, summer programme that runs until the end of July and which will target their weak areas and reassess their level of competence upon its completion.

“Right now, as indicated by our minister, the plan is for us to have a majority of our students, if not all, go to high school literate. As you know, we have been working on that as an education system,” said Troupe at the handover ceremony of CIBC Caribbean prepaid cards to nine principals affected by last October’s Hurricane Melissa, at the bank’s corporate office in New Kingston.

“We saw a 10 per cent improvement in the level of mastery for literacy this year. The same students who we assessed this year, when they got their mastery scores in grade four it was 69 per cent, and this year it is 79 per cent, and we identified some students who are on the cusp. If it was a little bit more we would have got them there. So, the thrust now is to run them through an intensive literacy and numeracy initiative,” said Troupe.

The permanent secretary explained that the first week of the programme was used to conduct assessments that identified where students were on their journey of becoming numerate and literate. She noted that the information garnered from those tests was then used to form their learning plan for the next two weeks.

While acknowledging that attempting to achieve mastery in three weeks would be a challenge, she argued that the ministry is well equipped to provide students with the material needed to help them along the way.

“Some persons would say what we didn’t do in six years we’re going to try to do in a summer. That’s not absolutely true; it is like an intensive programme. And we are deploying literacy software and licenses that we have procured, [so] we are using that as well, and we have our Jamaica Learning Passport that is built around literacy and numeracy support, so we are pulling in the ICT [information and communications technology], we are pulling in the readers, and we have equipped the regions,” she said.

Troupe told the Observer that students are being thoroughly monitored throughout the programme, and those who are still unable to secure mastery will undergo a Government-funded psychoeducational assessment which will then help to shape their curriculum at the high schools they attend in September.

“We are now working with those receiving schools to ensure that the learning programmes are developed in response to the gaps identified in those learners. We are restructuring some of those learning programmes in some of those high schools to limit the number of subjects the students are exposed to; to increase the amount of time that they will need in literacy, numeracy, language arts, mathematics, ICT, physical education, and I think social studies and personal development,” she said, explaining that students will matriculate to other subject areas once they improve.

She added that students were grouped in selected nearby schools or other institutions closest to them so that they have ease in accessing the summer programme. Troupe added that the initiative was designed to minimise spending for parents.

“We have also looked at providing nutritional support through Nutrition Products Limited for the students, we provided the teachers or the tutors — and that is something that the Government is fully funding — so the parents are not contributing to summer school in any way — we are paying. It’s fully funded by the Government. We have our principals who are coordinating, we have our literacy coaches and specialists who have been deployed into the field,” she said.

Troupe also called on parents to make the extra effort to send their children to summer school, charging that persistent commitment to their child’s improvement is what will eventually make the difference.

“We are asking our parents to make the sacrifice. And if they can’t afford whatever it is, let us know because we will make the sacrifice and put the resources in place — because the end game is for all of our students to be literate before they go to high school,” declared Troupe.

World.title: Back the Girlz!
World.content:
Members of the Reggae Girlz team celebrate their fourth goal against Antigua and Barduda during their Group B match in the Concacaf Women’s qualifiers at the National Stadium on April 10, 2026. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

FIFA Consultant and Women’s Football Division Advisor Jose Andres Portabella believes the long-term growth of women’s football in Jamaica hinges on meaningful support for the Reggae Girlz in their bid to reach a third successive FIFA Women’s World Cup.

In less than four months, the national senior women’s team will take on Costa Rica in the quarter-finals of the Concacaf W Championship in Texas, USA, with victory securing a place in next year’s World Cup in Brazil.

It would continue a historic run for the team, which stunned the world at the 2019 tournament in France and the 2023 tournament in Australia and New Zealand.

Despite their impressive performances over the past decade, the Reggae Girlz have struggled to attract consistent, lucrative sponsorship and sustained fan support, although more than 6,500 supporters turned out at the National Stadium for their 2-0 win over Guyana in April.

Portabella told the Jamaica Observer that stronger backing for the Reggae Girlz would not only boost the team’s success but also help drive the long-term development of the sport locally.

“I would love to see the whole country rally behind the Reggae Girlz. They have a beautiful opportunity to go three times in a row to a World Cup – that is special, it’s not every country that can say that. So I would love to see the Jamaican people come together and get behind the Reggae Girlz in a way that no one has ever seen before,” he said.

“If we see that, I think the Girlz will respond to the country in an amazing way, and it will inspire a completely new generation to really see the pathway to play football, to enjoy football and to one day excel in football at the global stage.”

Portabella was a key figure in helping the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) to develop and launch its Women’s Strategic Plan, which outlines several key objectives to be achieved in the sport by 2031.

The world governing body is prepared to provide more than $41 million in funding to support JFF programmes focused on national teams, league and club development, as well as governance and leadership.

Portabella believes Jamaica has the potential to build one of the best women’s football programmes, provided all stakeholders play their part.

“FIFA definitely sees Jamaica (with) huge potential in women’s football. Not only potential, but already a proven track record,” he said. “Your national teams have been spectacular at youth and senior level so we’re looking forward to seeing what the future holds for Jamaica, for the players here, the clubs. Your women’s Premier League is continuing to grow in a fantastic way. The future is truly bright for them and at national team level as well.”

“It’s not only the success that you see from the players, but coaches, we want to see more women coaches out there. We want to see young kids participate in the sport at a grassroots level so I think the future is quite bright for Jamaica as a whole. The JFF and the Women’s Premier League need to continue to work together with their clubs, all stakeholders, to really take things to the next level.”

JFF Projects Committee Chairperson for Women’s Programmes Carlene Edwards, who also serves on FIFA’s Women’s National Competitions Committee, says improving the club system will also prove crucial in improving the sport.

“My greatest wish for women’s football is that we get it really to a professional level,” she told the Jamaica Observer. “I think based on the strategy, we are aiming to at least get to some sort of professionalism by 2031. With what Concacaf is now doing around club licensing, I think later this year we’re supposed to be seeing the rolling out of the women’s club licence and I believe that is one element to actually get our clubs at least to a level of professionalisation.”

“I believe as we transition in 2031, I’m hoping as well that our players can be paid some sorts, I think that would be the greatest wish.”

World.title: Enter The DoughJo Ja
World.content:
The DoughJo Ja principal Kimberly Clarke. (Photo: Instagram/@thedoughjo.ja)

Sourdough lovers, celebrate! The DoughJo Ja has officially landed on the shelves of Loshusan Supermarket bringing a freshly baked line-up of handcrafted sourdough treats to locals.

Officially launched in April 2026 by principal Kimberly Clarke, the brand was born out of a personal search for gluten-friendly options using wild fermination techniques.

“It started from my search for healtheir bread that wouldn’t necessarily trigger my gluten sensitivity,” Clarke said. “I used to post TikTok videos of me making the bread and then persons eventually showed interested in them,” shared Clarke.

Within a matter of months, she has transitioned seamlessly from social media posts to online orders and, ultimately, supermarket shelves. Shoppers can now pick up handcrafted sourdough loaves in original, 100 per cent whole wheat, and sharp cheddar ranging from $1,800 to $2,200, as well as sourdough blueberry crumble muffins for $2,400.

Delighted by the enthusiastic response and the shift towards healthier choices, Clarke ensures every creation is made with meticulous care and patience.

The DoughJo Ja

World.title: Schools under scrutiny
World.content:
Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown addressing the region’s One Back-to-School Conference held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover, on Tuesday.Anthony Lewis

POINT, Hanover — The Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown has sounded the alarm over what he alleges are numerous accounting breaches in primary schools within Kingston and St Andrew.

“The breaches are too many. Here is what is happening now, colleagues. We are getting documents from the Integrity Commission (IC) for principals to be investigated… Accountability is stepping up,” he said.

Brown made the revelation, Tuesday, during the second of a three-day back-to-school conference for Region One that was held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover.

“Stakeholders in the communities are writing to the ministry. They talk about what they observe in schools. They go to a school and they get no receipt for the money they pay. They call you and ask if they should get a receipt and what it should look like,” he told an audience of educators.

The regional director said primary schools are the main offenders.

“Do you know where we tend to find the bulk of the breaches now? The primary schools. It’s a serious problem,” said Brown.

While he conceded that there may be administrative issues such as inadequate staff that impact how money is handled, he said there can be no excuse for some of the behaviour seen.

“Some simple things. Why would you keep money in excess of a million dollars locked up in a room for two, three weeks, months, and so forth? The bursar not being there caused that? So what I’m saying: I know you need those people, and we are working on that, but don’t do things to set up yourselves in the process,” added the senior officer.

Brown used the opportunity to explain proper administrative procedures when handling school funds.

“I beg you, lodge the money in a reasonable time frame. Money must be lodged intact. Can somebody please explain what the FAA (Financial Administration and Audit) Act means when it says ‘money must be lodged intact’? ‘[It means as soon] as collected,” he emphasised.

He explained that if five $100-notes are collected, that exact configuration must be deposited into the account.

“Don’t use it to make any change for anybody who wants to pay somebody something. That is what they mean [by] to lodge the money intact. If you are guilty, don’t say anything. Just sit like nothing is wrong but pray a prayer in your heart. I’m giving you 30 seconds to ask God to forgive you,” stated Brown to an outburst of laughter.

“You saved the money, but the law says treat it a particular way,” added the senior officer.

During his address Brown also expressed gratitude to the Ministry of Education for providing the region with additional professionals to conduct audits of schools within the region.

“We want to publicly say thanks to the members of the central ministry team, our CEO, [and] the permanent secretary. We spoke and they have given us a large number of people to build out the finance unit in the region. I have about five or six additional staff members now so we can do more audits. Clap the central team for that,” he said magnanimously.

World.title: Danger in John’s Hall
World.content:
A bedhead and concrete block are among items used to alert commuters to danger on the John’s Hall road in St James..

MONTEGO BAY, St James — An old bedhead and the top of a broken table used to cobble together a crude guard rail serve as warning that there is danger on the road between John’s Hall and Spring Mount in southern St James. One section appears on the verge of collapse, much like a nearby house whose foundation was eroded by Hurricane Melissa, last October, and commuters are worried.

“I’m afraid but mi just have to drive on it, can’t do better,” a shopkeeper who identified herself as Sancia told the

Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

“If little rain fall it gone, because underneath it, it’s deteriorating,” she explained.

The gaping cavern in a section of the Spring Mount Road is just a few kilometres up the hill, impassable as residents eagerly await word from the Government on when it will be repaired. Now, they have added the danger at John’s Hall to their list of urgent issues.

When contacted, community relations officer for the National Works Agency (NWA), Western Region, Janel Ricketts said they are aware of this latest development at John’s Hall. Though none were seen by the Observer, she said signs are in place to help guide motorists.

“This too, like Spring Mount, is on the radar of the NWA but in terms of an update, I don’t have that right now,” she told the Observer.

For shopkeeper Sancia and others who use the road, help cannot come soon enough as the alternative route is longer and more costly. What was once a straight route from John’s Hall to Montego Bay has now become a meandering journey to Sunderland, around Blackshop, and through Patosi.

“And the hottest part is we dropping out right at the square down there and we don’t reach Montego Bay as yet. It’s going to be more money, more gas, more everything,” Sancia lamented.

She also highlighted challenges being faced by students in that area of the community.

“Children that live here now that have to go Maldon are paying double or triple fare because they have to take taxi from here go to Montego Bay and a next taxi go and vice versa,” Sancia explained.

“It bad for everybody: Parents, children, business owners,” she added.

A roadside vendor in John’s Hall who chose not to provide his name spoke of the downturn in business he has seen as commuters from southern St James have had to find new routes.

“It rough because the road block up that side so people can’t come down. They would stop and buy drinks, food stuff, shop stuff; that’s not happening again,” he said.

He also pointed to the impact it has had on other areas of life that used to generate income, such as sporting competitions.

“Football was a thing where the different communities partake in and now them can’t come,” he said.

“Spring Mount people a bawl now because nobody can’t come down. We just want to see the road fix, the two place; because without it we don’t have any real livelihood, nobody can’t come, nobody can’t go,” he said.

A motorist who gave his name as Richard said travelling to the area has been a financial challenge and, like area residents, he is also worried about the increasing deterioration at John’s Hall.

“With this breakaway now, we would have to find a next way to go in town, it’s really pressuring. I hope they do something fast, whether it’s construction to start the new road or they find something better that we can travel on. But do something better,” Richard appealed.

World.title: Brussels is coming for Google — and the bill could be huge
World.content:
Google could be hit with the largest fine yet under the EU’s Digital Markets Act. Zoya Sheftalovich and Kathryn Carlson explain why Brussels believes the tech giant is unfairly pushing its own services in Google Search and limiting what app developers can tell customers — and why the case is becoming another source of tension with Washington.

Then, the EU’s startups commissioner, Ekaterina Zaharieva, heads to Sofia for an unusual visit to Bulgaria’s new leaders. We look at the government’s mixed signals on Ukraine, the billions in EU recovery money still at stake, and why Zaharieva’s former job as Bulgaria’s foreign minister may serve her well.

And finally, Portugal’s new digital exam-marking system leaves thousands of would-be university students waiting to find out whether their grades are correct.
