World.title: All the Keir Starmer critics landing big jobs under Andy Burnham
World.content:
POLITICO rounds up the politicians who publicly challenged Starmer’s authority and have now been rewarded.

Anas Sarwar

As Scottish Labour leader, Sarwar was the first top Labour figure to call on Starmer to quit. At a hastily arranged press conference back in February, Sarwar said scandals involving the prime minister were now becoming a “distraction” from Labour’s mission.

He told reporters there had been “too many mistakes” — his comments followed the furor over sacked U.S. Ambassador to Washington Peter Mandelson — and warned that the “leadership in Downing Street has to change.”

This was a moment of real peril for Starmer and cabinet ministers were forced to post messages of support for the then prime minister across social media in a bid to shore him up.

But six months and a whole new administration later, Sarwar’s audaciousness has paid off — he is set to take up a lifetime seat in the House of Lords and become a trade minister in the new Burnham government.

Ed Miliband

Ed Miliband was beaming when he walked up Downing Street on Monday. While missing out on the coveted chancellorship, he was about to be appointed foreign secretary — a nice promotion from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.

World.title: Moscow-linked nuclear project in northwest Germany gets green light
World.content:
The approval notice lays out extensive conditions. For example, employees of Rosatom and TVEL are barred from entering the plant. “Access is only permitted in justified exceptional cases and when accompanied by the nuclear regulatory authority,” explained a spokesperson for the Lower Saxony Ministry of the Environment.

The regulations also stipulate extensive safety inspections of the licensed machines supplied by TVEL and Framatome subsidiary ANF. Framatome employees must adhere to rules governing their interactions with TVEL and Rosatom employees, particularly regarding protection against espionage, sabotage, and recruitment attempts.

The green light comes as nuclear power is increasingly seen as essential to wean the EU off fossil fuels — while the bloc is simultaneously trying to ban energy imports from Russia in response to President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Passing the buck

According to Lower Saxony, an updated assessment by security authorities regarding Russian involvement and proposed security requirements for the project was a key factor in the decision to grant the license (as previously reported by POLITICO). The updated assessment was in a federal government statement issued in February and drawn up under the leadership of Germany’s Federal Ministry for the Environment. Under the “traffic-light” coalition government, the statements issued by the relevant federal ministries had been significantly more critical.

Christian Meyer State Minister for Environment, Energy and Climate Protection outside the Emsland nuclear power plant on the day the plant is officially shutting down on April 15, 2023 near Lingen. | David Hecker/Getty Images

Although the Lower Saxony Ministry of the Environment itself made the final decision on the project in Lingen, Lower Saxony’s Environment Minister Christian Meyer considers the federal government’s approval and the revised safety assessment to be “fundamentally wrong.” But Meyer had to accept them in a state governed by the rule of law, he said.

Meyer’s office says it asked the federal ministry whether there was still a possibility that, even with the strict conditions in place, the application might be rejected on grounds of internal and external security. Berlin’s response was unequivocal: “Based on the current findings regarding the risk potential and the conditions imposed, there is no discernible situation that would allow for a legally sound refusal of the permit.”

World.title: Germany wants combat drones. Government officials can’t agree where to get them.
World.content:
Several confidential ministry papers seen by POLITICO show officials divided between purchasing Boeing Australia's MQ-28 Ghost Bat as a bridge while European projects mature, or holding a competition first that would give German and European designs more time to develop.

A final internal memo, prepared for State Secretary for Arms Jens Plötner by the ministry's planning staff before he decides on the next steps, concludes that the 2029 target can no longer be met and recommends postponing it.

Germany’s defense ministry declined to comment.

Australian shortcut hits roadblock

The ministry's original plan was to buy 12 Boeing Australia MQ-28 Ghost Bat drones as an interim capability while simultaneously testing rival designs, giving German and European alternatives more time to mature. The officials in the ministry's innovation department that developed the proposal argued this was the only realistic way to meet the 2029 target.

The disagreement highlights a broader dilemma confronting Berlin as it seeks to rebuild armed forces weakened by decades of underinvestment: whether to buy advanced foreign equipment that could be fielded quickly, or wait for German and European industry to catch up and keep more production, expertise and sensitive technology at home.

Under the proposal, Boeing and German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall had agreed to examine how the MQ-28 aircraft could be adapted to Germany’s requirements and be partly produced in the country. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius publicly endorsed the option during a visit to Australia in March, saying a purchase of Ghost Bats was under consideration.

World.title: EU countries weigh fresh plan to salvage Russia sanctions package
World.content:
Talks ended without an agreement on Wednesday night — the latest in a series of efforts to reach consensus on a slew of energy and trade measures designed to drain Moscow’s war chest as its offensive against Ukraine grinds into its fifth year. The delay pushes discussions down to the wire and past the anticipated cut-off for legislative business. Wednesday was supposed to have been the final ambassadors' meeting until after the August summer holidays.

The package was presented by the European Commission in June, but discussions over the details have dragged on, despite significant parts — like a ban on Russian seafood imports and visa restrictions for its soldiers — being watered down in the process.

Athens has dug in its heels over a proposed ban on EU companies shipping Russian gas to consumers outside the EU, arguing it goes beyond what leaders had previously agreed and that practice would continue anyway with vessels just re-registering abroad.

The Greek government refused an earlier compromise in which European gas tankers would be allowed to export Russian liquefied natural gas to third countries until January 2029. That version also capped Russian exports and banned new contracts. Athens instead has pushed for an indefinite exception, said three EU diplomats involved in the discussions, granted anonymity to talk about the sensitive negotiations.

Greece’s permanent representation to the EU declined to comment.

Greece’s Dynagas shipping company is one of the few that operates ice-ready ships that can reach Russia’s LNG terminal on the Arctic Ocean. If the EU were to ban its companies from exporting Russian gas, the Greek government argues the ships will simply register elsewhere, reducing EU oversight.

World.title: Green homes: Which countries are making their buildings more energy efficient?
World.content:
It's a long and winding road to 2050.

 

Last week, the EU launched an infringement procedure against all members for failing to fully transpose the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD), also called the Green Homes Directive, into law. The deadline to do so was 29 May 2026.

Brussels planned to put the bloc on a common trajectory towards net-zero emissions by the first half of the century with a mandatory modernisation of buildings, Europe's largest energy consumer.

The opening of the infringement procedure, which means that each member state has been sent a letter of formal warning to complete the transposition, doesn't mean that Europe isn’t progressing on that front.

In fact, many buildings are becoming more energy-efficient, even though not as fast as Brussels may like.

Today, around one in four EU citizens lives in greener complexes than six years ago, according to Eurostat, but the speed of action varies widely across the bloc.

The highest rate was reported in the Netherlands, with 60.5%, followed by Denmark (34%), France (33%), and Slovenia (33%), with about a third each.

The figures represent a massive gap with Italy, which comes in last place for the speed of its renovation, with only 3% of buildings classified as more efficient compared to 2018.

Malta (8%) and Greece (9.5%) are not much further ahead, with less than 10% of their buildings being greener.

Making buildings more energy-efficient means, for example, improving roof and window insulation to reduce energy consumption. However, the EU aims to phase out incentives and subsidies for old gas and fossil fuel boilers in favour of heat pumps and solar panels.

Yet the plans have faced criticism, as many member states say it's too expensive to implement the changes within such a short timeframe.

"It's not a question of agreeing or not with the EU, but rather of numbers", said Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, Italy's environment and energy security minister. "How can we intervene by 2033 and make a couple of pensioners spend €50,000 to bring their home to energy class B?"

Criticism also came from Germany's former housing minister, Klara Geywitz, from the centre-left SPD party, who said it was not right to force people to renovate their buildings or sell their property to comply with energy-efficiency standards.

Eight countries have submitted a National Building Renovation Plan

Nonetheless, even if no country has yet fully transposed the full EU directive into law, something is moving on the renovation front.

Eight member states have already submitted their draft National Building Renovation Plan (NBRP) to the European Commission, marking the first concrete step in implementing the EPBD.

These countries are Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Finland, Lithuania, Romania, Slovenia and Spain.

The NBPRs are meant to set out a detailed renovation roadmap for both residential and non-residential buildings and must include an analysis of the national building stock, as well as targets for 2030, 2040 and 2050, and policies to reach those targets, including an assessment of investment needs.

"Unlike previous strategies, NBRPs follow a common EU-level template, enabling a more consistent assessment of progress across Member States.

However, while the strategies already provided gave a general direction, "they lacked a harmonised structure, common indicators and binding milestones across the Union", the Commission said.

The deadline to submit the final versions of the plans is 31 December 2026.

World.title: Wildfires rage across parts of France, Spain and Italy
World.content:
Wildfires continued to spread across parts of France, Spain and Italy on Wednesday, forcing thousands of people from their homes amid soaring temperatures.

 

In southwestern France's Gironde department, more than 10,000 people were evacuated overnight due to a blaze that's ravaged more than 2,000 hectares in the region, local authorities said.

The fire broke out in the town of Saumos on Wednesday and has advanced southwest towards the areas of Le Porge and Lège Cap-Ferret.

As of Thursday morning, 500 firefighters are tackling the blaze, with aerial reinforcements on the way.

Two firefighters were killed while tackling flames in the Mérignac suburb of Bordeaux on Tuesday.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez met with their families and colleagues on Wednesday to pay tribute to the pair.

"On behalf of the president of the Republic, the government and the entire nation, which owes them so much, I expressed our boundless gratitude and our unwavering support," he wrote in a post on social media.

Multiple departments in southern France remain under a red alert for forest fires on Thursday, per Météo-France.

A firefighter sprays water on burnt vegetation and trees during clean up operations in an area affected by a wildfire in Cotignac, France, Wednesday July 22, 2026. AP photo

Italy

Fires have also broken out in Sicily, where around 6,000 emergency responders, including firefighters, forest guards and civil protection officers have been mobilised to assist.

According to the regional government, 300 of the island's 344 reported fires had been extinguished as of Wednesday.

"The most critical blazes, where teams from the fire brigade, civil protection and the forestry corps are currently in action, are in Casaboli, Bivona, Alimena, San Cataldo, Galati Mamertino, certain areas of the Madonie Park and the Syracuse area," it said in a press release.

One firefighter named by officials as Alessandro Marchi died while responding to a fire in San Cataldo, Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi announced.

"He lost his life whilst carrying out his duty, in the service of the community. On behalf of myself and the Ministry of the Interior, I extend my deepest condolences to his family," Piantedosi said.

Spain

A major wildfire has also been declared to the southwest of the Spanish capital, Madrid, between the towns of Almorox and Villa del Prado.

Video footage posted to social media by Spain's Civil Guard showed officers going home to home as residents were evacuated from parts of the area.

As of Wednesday night, 88 firefighters, 35 vehicles, and a helicopter had been deployed to help fight the fire.

It comes after a devastating wildfire in Spain's Guadalajara province had already burnt through 32,000 hectares to the north of Madrid.

According to data from the European Forest Fires Information System, wildfires have burnt around 254,388 hectares across the EU in 2026.

This is higher than the long-term average but remains below the 270,449 hectares that burnt in 2025 over the same period, per the data.

World.title: RIP La La Hand saga: Ryan Gosling detail fixed in 10-year anniversary 'La La Land' poster
World.content:
It’s a small detail that has rubbed Ryan Gosling up the wrong way for a decade. Now, the La La Hand saga finally comes to an end...

 

Damien Chazelle’s La La Land is set to return to cinemas to mark its tenth anniversary next month. It starred Gosling and Emma Stone as a couple who meet and fall in love while pursuing their dreams in Los Angeles. Stone won the Oscar for Best Actress and Chazelle won Best Director at the 2017 ceremony, and the film was infamously announced as the winner of Best Picture before the correct winner, Moonlight, finally got the top gong.

To mark the 10-year rerelease, the film's team has decided to alter the film's poster – which features that upsetting detail.

You see, Gosling hasn't been shy or silent about how much he hates the poster. It's not the streetlights, the Los Angeles skyline, the colour grading or his snobbish "white person saves jazz" demeanour. It's his hand - specifically the position of his wrist, which is bent, with his hand poised flat in the air in the middle of a dance with co-star.

“I didn’t know this would become the poster for the movie,” Gosling told the Wall Street Journal in a 2024 interview. “We were supposed to have our hands up, and I thought it would be cool to put my hand [flat] even though everyone told me it wasn’t cool. I was sure it was cooler... It just killed the energy that way. I call it La La Hand.”

Well, he'll be able to sleep soundly once more, as Lionsgate have issued the following statement: “Over the years, Ryan Gosling has noted on more than one occasion that he would love to fix his "La La hand" from the original poster... Well, Ryan, you have been heard! Lionsgate is thrilled to announce that an updated version of the poster is now officially available below."

We're in two minds about this.

On the one hand (sorry), we're glad that Gosling is getting his way and that a minor upset has been fixed. Plus, this fix doesn't fall into the "Photoshopped-to-hell-and-back" poster atrocities we've been subjected to over the years.

On the other hand (not sorry), going back and tampering with the past in a form of revisionism will only create another Mandela Effect - the fascinating phenomenon that refers to people sharing a collective, inaccurate memory (an event, an image, a phrase) that never happened. Except it did.

RIP Ryan's limp wrist. You shall be missed.

World.title: The EU versus Big Tech, and sanctions package approval
World.content:
Hello and good morning. Angela Skujins penning your Thursday dispatch, with some hot news.

 

We just heard that after marathon talks EU ambassadors early Thursday morning approved the EU's 21st package of sanctions against Russia.

The previous hold out? As my colleague Jorge Liboreiro reports, maritime heavyweight Greece previously clung to its veto due to issues regarding a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) and its transport. We expect further reporting from Jorge today regarding the play-by-play of how this deal finally got done.

But before we go there, Latvian leader Andris Kulbergs said in exclusive comments on Euronews’ flagship morning news programme Europe Today that European politicians should ask themselves two major questions during the debate. Do they want Ukraine to win, or, "Do they want to earn money?"

"There's a choice. It's not both. So the sanctions has to be implemented," he said. Watch.

Back to Big Tech. As my colleague Luca Bertuzzi reports, the Commission's potential fine for Google rumoured to be handed down today follows a two-year investigation into how the company promotes its own services in search results, and how it stops app developers from directing users to deals outside its app store and payment system.

Why today? German financial newspaper Handelsblatt spoke to two anonymous high-ranking EU officials, who pointed to Thursday on the calendar as it follows a meeting chaired by the European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, where the fine would reportedly be rubber-stamped.

Pay the price. Fines for violating the Digital Markets Act (DMA) can reach up to 10% of a company's total worldwide annual turnover. With Google's parent company, Alphabet, reporting a record annual revenue of $402.8 billion (€353.08 billion) in 2025, the maximum penalty imposed by the European Commission could theoretically run into the tens of billions of dollars.

But Google isn’t the only party to potentially suffer. If the DMA fine for the American-based company comes to fruition, the EU risks attracting the ire of US President Donald Trump.

American retaliation? Washington has previously accused Brussels of unfairly targeting American companies through its digital policies. For example, in January, the Republican leader threatened to impose 100% tariffs on any European country that imposed a tax on digital services on US companies.

Right now, Brussels is walking a tightrope of tense transatlantic relations. Outside of the battle over big tech, the US government is preparing fresh import duties on the bloc as the current ones are due to expire this week.

The EU executive is expected to bow to these fresh import levies after the current regime lapses, according to Peggy Corlin, but many are concerned there could be additional retaliation following the DMA dispute.

“Toxic” Putin. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated in his nightly address that his country’s frontline gains and mid-range strikes are creating a “toxic” atmosphere around Russian President Vladimir Putin. But does this stench waft from Moscow to Manila?

Russian state-run news agency TASS confirms that Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is meeting with his American counterpart Marco Rubio on the sidelines of the ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) Foreign Ministers meeting in the Philippine capital. The meeting is scheduled to take place during the morning of 23 July.

In Manila, Rubio said the US remains open to playing a role in ending the conflict, “if that opportunity presents itself”. He did admit, however, the efforts have “fallen off a little bit over the last few months”.

Washington's attention has increasingly shifted to the Middle East following the conflict with Iran, particularly with news coming in overnight that the US announced a landmark nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia.

The framework allows the country in the future to produce enriched uranium, a key ingredient for nuclear fuel as well as nuclear bombs.

Fighting for peace. Kallas used her time speaking at the ASEAN forum in Manila to reiterate to partners, as well as observers, to “join the calls” that Russia should stop its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Her team confirmed to Euronews yesterday that she had no scheduled meeting with Lavrov herself.

Some extra news: a major blow to proponents of migration crackdown**.** The European Commission on Thursday refused to register a controversial European Citizens’ Initiative spearheaded by far-right activists due to “discrimination grounded on race and ethnic origin”.

The document calls on the Commission to temporarily stop all “non-Western immigration channels” including study and family reunification visas. On top of this, irregular and regular migrants who have not integrated into European society should swiftly be returned to their country of origin, the document states.

EU set to bow to fresh US tariffs after current regime lapses

The European Union is preparing to accept new tariffs the United States is expected to impose in the coming days over forced labour, as long as they do not exceed the 15 percent cap agreed under the Turnberry agreement, the European Commission said.

As Peggy Corlin reports, the White House said in early June that it would impose fresh duties on its global trading partners, arguing that insufficient efforts to curb trade in goods produced using forced labour were harming US commercial interests.

The current US tariff regime expires on Friday, and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Tuesday that implementation of the forced labour duties was imminent.

European officials are closely monitoring the level of the new tariffs, as an EU-US trade agreement signed in July 2025 in Turnberry, Scotland, by US President Donald Trump and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen caps US duties on EU goods at 15 percent.

Read more of Peggy’s analysis to understand what's at stake.

More from our newsrooms

Could Gianni Infantino really become UN Secretary General if Trump puts him forward?

US President Donald Trump can recommend the boss of FIFA, Gianni Infantino, to lead the United Nations, but not impose him over the other candidates — and the other permanent members of the Security Council would need to endorse him. Vincenzo Genovese explains.

Hungary's prosecutor resigns under pressure in political win for Magyar

Hungary's Prosecutor General, Gábor Bálint Nagy, has resigned amid mounting political pressure as Prime Minister Péter Magyar seeks to replace Orbán-era officials. The move follows allegations of political bias by lawyers for detained Ukrainian cash couriers in a cross-border cash seizure case. Sandor Zsiros and Rita Konya have the latest.

Energy and fertiliser crisis due to war will continue to drive up food inflation, UN says

Rising energy and fertiliser prices are likely to continue contributing to food inflation globally, the UN warned in its latest report. This in turn can drive up the cost of a healthy diet and threaten progress against global hunger. Read more about this story by Indrabati Lahiri.

We're also keeping an eye on

​EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas continues her trip to Manila for the ASEAN summit, and will meet with Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defence of Philippines, as well as other leaders.

The European Central Bank (ECB) holds its Governing Council meeting in Frankfurt, with President Christine Lagarde delivering a press conference at 2:45 pm.

European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius to deliver a speech at the EU Defence Night in Washington, US.

That’s it for today. Luca Bertuzzi, Vincenzo Genovese and Jorge Liboreiro contributed to this newsletter.

World.title: 7,000 km of subsea cables link Portugal to US: what is the 'Nuvem' system?
World.content:
On Tuesday morning, the official launch ceremony for Google's Nuvem transatlantic submarine cable system took place at Lisbon's Oceanarium. The project represents a new investment which, as Minister Delegate for State Reform Gonçalo Matias said in his speech at the event, aims to link "North America and Europe along a new digital corridor that crosses the Atlantic".

 

At a time when "around 95% of all the world's data travels through submarine cables", the minister explained, Portugal is stepping up to become one of the main players in a project that will be the first to connect the country directly to the United States. But what exactly is "Nuvem", what does it hope to achieve and what role will Portugal play in its development?

A new submarine cable system

The project was first announced by Google in 2023 (source in Portuguese), and was immediately described as "a new transatlantic submarine cable system to link Portugal, Bermuda and the United States".

According to the company, on the US side "Nuvem will make landfall in South Carolina", specifically Myrtle Beach. In Portugal, Sines will be the landing station, with intermediate points in Bermuda and the Azores.

With a length of approximately 7,000 kilometres, this cable system consists of 16 pairs of fibre-optic cables, for a total capacity of around 384 terabits per second, Reuters reports. (source in Portuguese)

However, according to the newspaper "ECO", (source in Portuguese) the new submarine cable system is only expected to come into operation next year.

Why are these cables important?

Fibre-optic submarine cables are the backbone of the global internet. (source in Portuguese) They are responsible for carrying around 99% of all international data traffic, from calls, messages and videos to payments. Without them, global communications, financial transactions and cloud services would be unworkable, as satellites do not have sufficient bandwidth capacity.

Unlike satellites, which can be affected by weather conditions, the cables rest on the deep ocean floor, protected by multiple layers of steel, copper and polymers that shield them from pressure, currents and even shark attacks.

Submarine cables are of course not completely immune to failures, but most occur accidentally through human activity, such as fishing or anchoring, followed by natural risks such as earthquakes, undersea landslides and tsunamis. In addition, challenges such as ageing infrastructure and complex regulatory environments can complicate efforts to maintain resilience.

Nuvem's objectives

When it announced the project, Google itself said (source in Portuguese) that Nuvem was intended "to improve network resilience in the Atlantic and help meet growing demand for digital services".

The same source added that the "route of the new cable" is designed "to add diversity to international routes and support the development of information and communication technology (ICT) infrastructure for the continents and countries involved".

On Tuesday, in his speech at the institutional ceremony for the project, Portuguese minister Gonçalo Matias said that putting this new system in place "does more than add another line" across the Atlantic, creating "alternative paths for data transmission" and reducing "Europe's dependence on a small number of congested corridors". It therefore offers "resilience", he concluded.

Who is involved?

The minister also explained in his address that the Nuvem system is a project "built on partnership, between Google and MEO, between public ambition and private investment, between two nations, Portugal and the United States, long united by the same ocean that now carries our data".

MEO will therefore also be a key player. In a statement quoted by the Lusa news agency (source in Portuguese), the Portuguese company confirmed that it will also "join the Nuvem submarine cable system", becoming "an investor and national partner in one of the most important digital infrastructures in the Atlantic".

MEO did not, however, specify what investment it will make under the project, saying only that "by establishing a direct connection between Portugal and the US, the system also strengthens the country's attractiveness for investment in data centres, cloud platforms and global technology services".

"Nuvem" follows "Firmina" and "Equiano"

This is not, however, the first investment of this kind made by Google in the Atlantic Ocean. In fact, "in 2022, Equiano helped bring Europe and Africa closer together", Portuguese minister Gonçalo Matias also recalled on Tuesday.

As described by the US tech giant (source in Portuguese), this is a submarine cable that "starts in Western Europe and runs along Africa's west coast, linking Portugal to South Africa and increasing connectivity and opportunities for engagement between European and African countries".

It was followed by the installation of Firmina, a huge submarine cable laid by the company to connect the east coast of the United States, once again via South Carolina, to South America (Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay), and therefore not involving Portugal.

Still under Google's umbrella, Portugal also expects to be, as early as next year, the focus of another project: Sol, minister Gonçalo Matias noted.

This will in turn be "a new transatlantic submarine cable system that will connect the US, Bermuda, the Azores and Spain", the US company said (source in Portuguese) when it announced the project, which thus completes the company's "unique investment" in "transatlantic resilience".

Why Portugal?

The question was in fact addressed by minister Gonçalo Matias in his speech on Tuesday. "Why here? Why Portugal? The most obvious answer is geography. We are located at the westernmost edge of Europe, at the point closest to the Americas, the natural bridge to Africa," stressed the minister responsible for State Reform. Indeed, Google itself had already highlighted this, pointing out that the country's "strategic geographical location in south-western mainland Europe" has turned it into a "hub for submarine cables".

However, the minister added that the country offers "stability, in a world where this is scarce"; "talent: engineers, researchers, a young generation versed in technology and languages"; and also "clean, competitive energy, which data centres need just as much as they need connectivity".

Portugal is in fact one of the European leaders in the energy transition. In the "Environmental Portrait of Portugal" (source in Portuguese) produced by Pordata to mark World Environment Day, on 5 June, it was noted that the country is among the four EU member states where more than 95% of energy produced comes from renewable sources (97.8%), based on 2024 data.

However, for Google (source in Portuguese), another factor has proved important: the country's "focus on strengthening the infrastructure of the digital economy".

World.title: Flash in the pants: Lamine Yamal's 6PM German boxer shorts go viral after World Cup appearance
World.content:
Spain’s youngest player in the World Cup-winning side may not have scored in the final, but thanks in no small part to his baby bath-tub photos with Lionel Messi, Lamine Yamal cemented his place as La Roja's number one player on social media. The closest contender to his leading role came from his own family with his little brother Keyne, who was at every one of Spain’s matches, the other shining star of Spain's World Cup campaign.

 

Lamine Yamal’s little brother Keyne on 19 July 2026 Yuki Iwamura/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

At 19 years and six days, Lamine Yamal became both the youngest player ever to have won the European Championship and the World Cup, and the first player under 20 to achieve this double.

Victory has many fathers as the popular saying goes, so it should come as no surprise that many people want to claim credit for their part in the older Yamal's success, or in this case support.

In many photos from the final, the boxer shorts of the teenage FC Barcelona winger can be seen. They are underwear from the streetwear label 6PM, founded in 2016 by German entrepreneur Achraf Ait Bouzalim.

6PM, the hip-hop fans’ label

Like Lamine Yamal, whose father Mounir Nasraoui comes from Morocco, Achraf Ait Bouzalim, who was reportedly born in Frankfurt am Main in 1995, also has Moroccan roots. The start-up founder dropped out of a business administration degree.

His streetwear brand is particularly popular among hip-hop music fans. 6PM initially also ventured into the music business, producing rap records together with Reezy, Stickle and Luciano. Like Yamal, 6PM embodies a young, international, multicultural identity.

Sheila Ebena, the footballer’s mother, who was 16 when he was born, comes from Equatorial Guinea. The parents, who have since separated, named their child after two neighbours, Lamine and Yamal, who gave the couple financial support in Spain.

FILE: Fun in a tub with Lionel Messi, Sheila Ebana and her baby Lamine Yamal in 2007 AP Photo/Joan Monfort

6PM is relying on its social media presence - in English - and on exclusive drops that sell out within a short time and are intended to generate strong demand and identification with the brand.

Football fever was already spreading on the streetwear label's site before Yamal boosted their fortunes as during the World Cup visitors were able to take part in a competition by submitting their predictions.

On Instagram, 6PM has 483,000 followers and is revelling in playing up to suggestions its underwear had a strong supporting role for the playmaker as Spain defeated Argentina in a final that ended in fisticuffs as tempers flared at the final whistle. Lamine Yamal has 56.2 million followers on Instagram.

The text of the 6PM post reads: "WE’RE NOT SAYING THEY MAKE YOU SCORE BETTER, BUT CONGRATS @lamineyamal ON WINNING THE 2026 WORLD CUP WITH LA ROJA"

Instagram post about Lamine Yamal 6PM

By the way, a two-pack of Lamine Yamal’s underwear costs 30 euros and, according to the 6PM website, apparently has not yet sold out.

Yamal’s boxer shorts on the German label’s website 6PM

6PM collaborates with international artists such as Nigerian graffiti artist Slawn, whose work is printed on T-shirts and hoodies.

As a football fan, Achraf Ait Bouzalim is also likely to be delighted about the Yamal hype.

World.title: Cost of pay gap in the EU: Women earn €3,900 less than men a year
World.content:
The gender pay gap in the EU is real, and it is costly according to the numbers.

 

Women's gross hourly earnings are on average 11.1% less than men's per Eurostat, meaning that for every €100 a man earns in the bloc, a woman only earns €88.9.

Annualised, the gap becomes clearer as the average woman is paid almost €3,900 less than men a year in the EU according to estimates from the European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC), also based on Eurostat data.

That means the 92.5 million women working in the EU are collectively losing more than €358 billion a year.

"The cost of pay transparency measures are small for companies but this analysis shows that inaction by national governments will cost women workers billions in lost wages,” ETUC General Secretary Esther Lynch stated.

The EU's Pay Transparency Directive covers businesses with at least 100 employees, so this estimate reflects that female workforce, which includes 43 million women.

Luxembourg is the only country in the EU where women are paid more than men, earning roughly €474 more per year.

The average employed woman loses more than €5,000 a year in Finland (€7,592), Austria (€6,854), Germany (€6,049) and Sweden (€5,116), based on 2025 data.

The annual loss is also above the EU average (€3,881) in Estonia (€4,967), France (€4,536), Czechia (€4,499) and Ireland (€4,129), all above the €4,000 level.

The estimated losses are €3,684 in the Netherlands, €3,487 in Slovakia, €3,405 in Cyprus, €3,181 in Hungary, €2,856 in Latvia, €2,591 in Greece, €2,404 in Lithuania, €2,245 in Slovenia and €2,005 in Spain.

The lowest amount is in Belgium, at just €322. It's also below the €1,000 threshold in Romania and Poland.

Among the EU's Big Four, Italy has the lowest level, at €1,557.

The EU’s Pay Transparency Directive can make a difference

The EU's Pay Transparency Directive aims to boost salary transparency and tackle the gender pay gap. It was due to take effect by 7 June 2026, but most member states missed the deadline.

"This is completely unacceptable when women have already suffered decades of pay discrimination. Time is up on the culture of secrecy which has allowed male dominated boardrooms to get away with pay discrimination for so long,”Lynch stated.

ETUC estimates show the impact would be significant, even a 10% smaller gap would make a big difference as the average employed woman would then earn around €672 more a year.

The highest gain would be in France, at €1,069, followed by €1,033 in Ireland.

An employed woman would also be paid more in Finland (€963), Germany (€867), Italy (€847) and Denmark (€802).

The annual gain would be lowest in Poland, at €221, as the gender pay gap is smaller in that country.

ETUC Deputy General Secretary Isabelle Schömann also said that any government which continues to avoid their legal responsibility to put this directive into action can expect to be taken to court.

The gender pay gap within the EU varies significantly, ranging from -0.8% in Luxembourg to 18.8% in Estonia.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: Mykhailo Drapatyi: Who is Ukraine's new commander-in-chief?
World.content:
Ukraine has a new army chief, with Mykhailo Drapatyi replacing Oleksandr Syrskyi as commander-in-chief. The change follows a cabinet reshuffle that ousted the popular defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov.

On Tuesday (July 21), Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy appointed Mykhailo Drapatyi as the new commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Zelenskyy wants him to develop a modern defense strategy and to continue the recently launched military reforms.

This comes after an unexpected cabinet reshuffle last week. Many ministers have retained their posts under new Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi, but not former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who had a major argument with former commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi about the strategic direction that Ukraine's war effort should take.



President Zelenskyy's military shakeup has been widely criticized Image: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Handout/REUTERS

The firing of the popular defense minister sparked outrage among parts of Ukraine's population. During mass protests, demonstrators not only demanded his return but also the dismissal of Syrskyi.

While the latter has now been removed from his post, Federov will not be returning. Zelenskyy has appointed Yevhen Khmara, who was previously head of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU), as the new defense minister.

'The army needs changes'

Mykhailo Drapatyi was the only general who publicly defended Fedorov after his dismissal. He wrote on Facebook that Fedorov's appointment to the defense ministry six months ago had been "a serious attempt to change conditions in the military system that were in place for years."

He added that the Defense Ministry had developed into a true partner for the army: "Cooperation between the troops and the Defense Ministry changed. There was a new willingness to listen to commanders, to take decisions more quickly and to support changes that came from the units themselves."

Drapatyj explained that many of the changes had had to be pushed through despite fierce resistance from the old system, and that there was a need to discuss problems in the army openly and honestly.

Zelenskyy fires armed forces chief Syrskyi To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who is Mykhailo Drapatyi?

Mykhailo Drapatyi (born in 1982) is a highly decorated Ukrainian major general who has distinguished himself as a battle-hardened frontline commander since 2014. At the beginning of the Donbas War, the trained tank trooper became known for his resolve during what was then called an "anti-terror operation."

After Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, he coordinated — as deputy commander of the Ukrainian Joint Forces — the successful defense of the town of Kryvyi Rih as well as the liberation of strategically important areas in the south of the country.

Thanks to his reputation as a military crisis manager, who also stopped the Russian offensive near Kharkiv in 2024, he rose through the ranks of the general staff to become head of the ground forces of the Ukrainian army and eventually Commander of the Joint Forces.

Did Syrskyj want to eliminate a rival?

On June 1, 2025, Drapatyi handed in his resignation as army commander after a Russian missile strike targeting a training ground under his command killed at least 12 soldiers and injured more than 60 others.

On Facebook, he justified his decision, citing his "personal sense of accountability for this tragedy." This earned Drapatyi a reputation for not hanging on to a position at all costs and taking moral responsibility. President Zelenskyy, however, did not accept the resignation and later appointed Drapatyi Commander of the Joint Forces.

However, when Drapatyi was tasked with defending the Kharkiv region in autumn 2025, observers remarked that this was a deliberate move to restrict his influence. Some media outlets speculated that Commander-in-Chief Syrskyi wanted to sideline the popular general as a potential rival.

A crisis of the president's own making?

Observers point out that President Zelenskyy's personnel decisions seem to have been driven by growing public pressure.

Military experts are divided when it comes to assessing the change of power. Oleksandr Khara of the Ukrainian Center for Defense Strategies views the protests as an important democratic corrective in an era in which elections cannot take place.

"The president listened to the response from civil society and the military and drew his conclusions. Society has succeeded in steering events back onto a democratic course," he said.

Speaking to DW, Oleksiy Melnyk of the Kyiv-based Razumkov Center was more critical. While Zelenskyy had the right to make personnel decisions, he had nonetheless caused a major domestic political crisis that was completely unnecessary.

"This will definitely not turn out to his advantage. It is regrettable that the president has learned nothing from previous lessons, because exactly one year ago there was a similarly triggered home-grown crisis," he said.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

World.title: Peru: 10 killed in housefire in capital Lima
World.content:
The fire was reportedly started by extortionists. Investigators are trying "to determine the point of origin, the circumstances, and the causes of this fire."

At least 10 people have died after a fire broke out at ⁠a ⁠family home in a low-income neighborhood in ​Peru's capital, Lima, police said on ‌Wednesday.

According to relatives, five of the deceased were adults, and the other five were children.

Another two people were injured in the incident, the INDECI civil defense institute wrote in a social media post.

The fire ‌broke out ​early in the morning at ​a house located in Lima's ⁠La ​Victoria ​district.

The fire reportedly spread quickly due to flammable materials and parked vehicles outside of the house Image: Ernesto Benavides/AFP

Peru's president-elect Keiko Fujimori visited the ruins Wednesday, calling the deaths "a terrible massacre."

"What people are asking for is order and security, and that is the first thing we are going to do next week," she told the press.

Investigation is underway

Peruvian news outlet El Comercio reported that nine fire units responded to the scene to extinguish the flames, which, according to preliminary reports, spread rapidly due to the presence of flammable materials and parked electric vehicles.

Local media reports said the fire was started by extortionists Image: Ernesto Benavides/AFP

Authorities have launched an investigation "to determine the point of origin, the circumstances, and the causes of this fire," police chief Oscar Arriola told the media.

According to local media reports, extortionists who were threatening local businesses started the fire.

Colonel John Lujan, who is heading up the investigation, said "a possible deliberate act or a case of extortion" is among the possible causes that are being explored.

World.title: US hits Iran as Houthis claim strikes on Saudi tankers
World.content:
Skip next section Yemen's Houthis says they targeted Saudi oil tankers in Red Sea

Published 07/23/2026 Published July 23, 2026 Yemen's Houthis says they targeted Saudi oil tankers in Red Sea

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement says it has targeted two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, escalating tensions around one of the world's key energy shipping routes.

The group identified the vessels as the Encelia and Layla, saying they were attacked with ballistic and cruise missiles for allegedly violating a Houthi naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, announced earlier this week.

A maritime security source told Reuters, the Saudi-flagged tanker Encelia sent a distress call after reporting it had been hit by a missile and caught fire near the Saudi port of Jizan.

Maritime security firm Vanguard and the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) also reported a tanker being struck by an unidentified projectile in the same area, causing a fire onboard. No casualties have been reported.

According to UKMTO, the ship’s master reported the incident approximately 70 nautical miles (130 kilometers) south-west of Al-Shuqaiq, Saudi Arabia.

Iran war: Analyzing the Houthi blockade against Saudi Arabia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Houthis also claimed to have targeted a second vessel, Layla, though that report has not been independently confirmed.

The attack comes days after the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi ports in the Red Sea, raising concerns about disruptions to global energy supplies. Ship-tracking data showed several tankers changing course on Wednesday following Houthi warnings to avoid Saudi ports.

World.title: Iran war: Trump threatens bridges over Hormuz Strait attacks
World.content:
Skip next section Signs of ships avoiding second choke point off Yemen after Houthi warnings: tracker data

07/22/2026 July 22, 2026 Signs of ships avoiding second choke point off Yemen after Houthi warnings: tracker data

Houthi supporters rallied in Sanaa in support of the announcement of a maritime blockade earlier this week [FILE: July 20, 2026] Image: Mohammed Hamoud/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Houthi threats to ships headed to or from Saudi Arabia's western shoreline could further impact commercial shipping, data trackers are warning.

The Houthis, who have de facto control over much of Yemen, have declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia and told ships to avoid the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the gateway to the Red Sea on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz. It provides access to western Saudi coastal cities like Jeddah and Yanbu.

Data provider Kpler said shipping in both waterways was "under pressure," saying traffic in both straits had fallen sharply.

Ship broker Clarksons issued a similar warning, saying four vessels had registered new courses on Wednesday, avoiding the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and heading north through the Suez Canal towards the Mediterranean instead.

"The threat of Houthi hostile actions against Saudi Arabia ... has begun to have an overall effect on tanker activity," Clarksons wrote. "There are reports of several tankers, having ​loaded in Saudi Arabia's Yanbu port in the Red Sea, that have shifted course towards the Suez Canal rather than sail south towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, while ​others are holding their positions waiting for further instruction."

For ships headed to places like India, Pakistan, Indonesia or Australia, doing this would add well over 10,000 nautical miles (more than 20,000 kilometers) and weeks at sea to the typical travel distance.

"Anything that restricts shipping through the Red Sea would be problematic for the same reasons that the Strait of Hormuz is problematic," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on the sidelines of a regional summit in the Philippines on Wednesday.

Pakistan's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday warned that the actions "threaten regional security, undermine freedom of navigation, challenge the rules-based maritime order and jeopardize uninterrupted flow of global commerce."

The Reuters news agency cited an advisory from the European Union's Aspides naval mission in the Red Sea as saying that ships with links to Israel, the United ​States or Saudi Arabia ‌were at a higher risk of being attacked by the Houthis and were advised to avoid voyages through the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden until the threat level decreases.

World.title: US and Saudi Arabia reach historic nuclear energy deal
World.content:
The deal is another sign of growing US-Saudi ties during US President Donald Trump's second term. The agreement, known as a 123 Agreement, would allow Saudi Arabia to build nuclear reactors using US technology.

The United States said on Wednesday it had signed a civilian nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, alongside a separate bilateral safeguards pact.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed the agreements with Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman.

The US Energy Department said the agreements would deepen cooperation between Washington and Riyadh in the civilian nuclear energy sector.

“Together, these two agreements lay the legal foundation for a decadeslong, multi-billion-dollar partnership that advances several priority economic and strategic objectives, including nuclear nonproliferation,” the US Energy Department said in a statement.

Deal allows nuclear reactors and uranium enrichment

The agreement, known as a 123 Agreement, would allow Saudi Arabia to build nuclear reactors using US technology.

It would also permit the Kingdom to enrich uranium and reprocess nuclear waste, activities that can potentially produce material for nuclear weapons.

However, like all signatories to the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, Saudi Arabia has already committed to not developing an atomic bomb and consented ‌to international inspections.

The deal, however, does not include an Additional Protocol that would allow the UN nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, to conduct more intrusive inspections at short notice.

The US administration said the agreement complied with non-proliferation requirements under the Atomic Energy Act.

Washington and Riyadh have discussed nuclear cooperation for years, with Saudi Arabia seeking access to US technology and American companies competing for major contracts.

Why Saudi Arabia is redrawing its global alliances To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What happens next?

The agreement will now be submitted to Congress and will take effect unless lawmakers vote to block it within 90 legislative days.

A two-thirds majority would be required to override a presidential veto.

Several Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns that the agreement could increase proliferation risks and trigger a regional arms race.

“They are allowing Saudi Arabia, a belligerent and authoritarian nation, to develop nuclear weapons technologies while starting a war with Iran under the guise of preventing an Iranian nuclear bomb,” Democratic Senator Edward Markey told Reuters.

“This deal would make us all less safe,” he added.

“This agreement will set off a nuclear race in the region, further disincentivizing Iran from limiting its own program,” Democratic Senator Chris Murphy said on X.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has previously said the kingdom does not want to develop a nuclear weapon but would do so if Iran acquired one.

What we know — and don't know — about Iran's nuclear program To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Saudi Arabia wants nuclear energy to reduce domestic oil use, leaving more crude available for the energy-rich Kingdom to export. Harnassing nuclear power would help Saudi Arabia slash emissions and generate power for energy-intensive services such as desalination and air conditioning.

World.title: US judge sets Maduro trial date for June 2027
World.content:
US prosecutors accuse Maduro of using the power of the Venezuelan state to protect and promote illegal drug smuggling.

A US judge on Wednesday set a date for Venezuelan former President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, to go on trial in New York, where they will face charges of drug trafficking.

The two have been detained since early January, when US forces entered Venezuela and seized them from their Caracas home.

The unprecedented middle-of-the-night raid was hailed by US President Donald Trump as a "surgical law enforcement operation" in a criminal case, which had been brought against the couple six years ago.

Maduro has maintained his innocence, calling himself a prisoner of war and referring to his capture as a kidnapping.

Judge Alvin Hellerstein set June 1, 2027, as the trial date for Maduro and his wife, following a joint request from prosecutors and defense counsel.

Hellerstein also scheduled an upcoming hearing for November 17 to discuss defense motions, including a challenge to the legality of how Maduro and Flores were captured and brought to the United States.

"The ‌parties all ​agree that this is a realistic schedule. We don't think it's going to slip, but obviously if anything comes up we will inform your honor," Maduro's lawyer Barry Pollack told the judge on Wednesday.

Venezuelans want elections — but when will they get them? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Maduro faces life in prison

US prosecutors have accused Maduro of using the power of the Venezuelan state to protect and promote illegal drug smuggling. He has also been accused of forming alliances with cartels to bring tons of cocaine into the United States.

If found guilty, Maduro and Flores face potential life prison sentences.

The pair sat through the 15-minute hearing separately at a defense table, surrounded by their lawyers. They did not speak during the proceedings. But Maduro waved to an unknown person in the courtroom's gallery as he was led out of the courtroom by authorities.

Pollack said his team plans to challenge the indictment on sovereign immunity grounds, saying that if successful, Maduro won't have to continue litigating the case.

Since Maduro was removed from power, Venezuela has been led by his former Vice President Delcy Rodriguez.

Rodriguez reestablished bilateral relationships with the US, with Washington effectively taking over control of Venezuela's oil exports.

In turn, the US has eased sanctions on the country's oil industry, while foreign companies have expanded oil and gas projects.

World.title: Hungary: Ex-PM Orban pledges resistance to Magyar 'tyranny'
World.content:
Hungary's former prime minister alleges that his successor has "dismantled the rule of law and eliminated checks and balances." Peter Magyar has pursued Viktor Orban and his allies since winning April's elections.

Hungary's former Prime Minsiter Viktor Orban accused prosecutors and the new government of sham investigations into his Fidesz party on Wednesday, a day after investigators seized equipment from the party HQ in Budapest as part of a corruption probe.

Hungary's longstanding leader, Orban lost April's general elections in a landslide to conservative rival Peter Magyar, himself a former Fidesz member, in a result hailed by much of Europe but not by the Trump White House.

Since coming to power, Magyar has moved to dismantle what he alleges to be systemic corruption of the Orban and Fidesz era, making a host of sweeping changes. Orban, however, on Wednesday, called these measures signs of "tyranny" and said that he and his opposition party would offer "resistance" by all peaceful means.

Orban chose to appear outside Fidesz's HQ a day after the buidling featured in domestic headlines for other reasons Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

What did Orban say?

Orban's online statement late on Tuesday night, followed by his press conference outside the Fidesz HQ on Wednesday, constituted two of his strongest political statements since returning to a role as leader of the opposition in early May after 16 years in power.

On Facebook, he first issued what he called a "statement of resistance" soon after his party announced that prosecutors had searched the party's HQ and seized computer servers and other materials. This is part of a corruption probe into the country's National Culture Fund, which is alleged to have been a state-run payment center for Orban's inner circle and a shadow election campaign fund.

"The National Culture Fund issue was just a pretext for this [search of the party headquarters]," Orban alleged, denying that there had been any wrongdoing.

He said Hungary had "ceased to be a democratic state" after the new center-right government used its parliamentary supermajority to pass a constitutional amendment ending the mandates of the president and the head of the Constitutional Court — both deemed to be Orban allies. He said he and his party would "employ all peaceful means" to oppose an "illegitimate" political system.

On Wednesday, outside Fidesz's base of operations, Orban said he believed Magyar was trying to hobble his party once and for all.

"By yesterday, I had come to realize what this was all about," he told reporters. "What happened was that this served as a pretext to seize Fidesz's servers ... This is a politically motivated legal proceeding designed to render Fidesz — which has clearly survived even this heavy political defeat and is growing stronger — legally unviable."

New laws on term limits mean Orban will not be eligible to stand in Hungary's next elections, assuming they hold Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

How and when did Magyar win power?

Peter Magyar's new party, Tisza, comfortably won general elections on April 12, claiming more than 55% of the vote against Fidesz's tally of almost 37%.

Because of Hungary's first-past-the-post electoral system, Magyar now enjoys the same supermajority that Orban often did in his pomp, holding 141 of 199 seats despite having only won 55% of the votes. Fidesz holds just 52 seats.

In Hungary, a two-thirds vote in parliament is needed to amend the constitution.

The new prime minister, who had broken away from Fidesz in 2024, lamenting double standards and institutional corruption, took office on May 9. He had pledged rapid reforms if victorious, but the speed and scope of his actions even took some of his supporters by surprise.

Can the 'dancing minister' fix Hungary's healthcare? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What has Magyar done since taking office to Orban and Fidesz's detriment?

As well as taking steps in foreign policy like trying to mend ties with Brussels and free up assistance for Ukraine since taking office, Magyar has moved quickly against alleged Orban-era corruption and misdeeds. Magyar often refers to this as targeting Orban's "mafia."

Magyar opened up former government facilities to the public to showcase some of the opulence he says indicates systemic corruption.

The national public broadcaster M1, which Tisza and others in opposition said had morphed into Fidesz's mouthpiece, was briefly taken off air this month and broadcast a black full-screen apology to launch a reform process.

Several political appointees have been removed from their roles — most notably President Tamas Sulyok via a constitutional amendment and Constitutional Court president Peter Polt. Magyar this week suggested chess star Judith Polgar for the largely ceremonial role as president, only for her to indicate that she was flattered but not interested.

On Tuesday, Prosecutor General Gabor Balint Nagy, appointed only last year, agreed to step down after being called Orban's "puppet" by Magyar.

Tisza has also introduced term limits of 12 years for all lawmakers, including the prime minister and government ministers. Orban says this means most of the veterans in his party, himself included, will be excluded from the next elections.

He told reporters in Budapest on Wednesday that this harkened back to the late 1980s and the latter days of Communist dictatorship "when there was no democracy in Hungary, there was no rule of law."

Corruption investigations, including but not limited to the investigation into the National Culture Fund, have also struck Orban and his allies.

Some other senior Fidesz members have voluntarily stepped out of the political limelight. Last week, parliamentary caucus leader Gergely Gulyas stepped down, while Orban's longstanding former Foreign Minister Peter Szijjarto left to take up an executive position with Chinese electric carmaker BYD.

Surveys suggest that Orban's party has suffered even more in its first few months in opposition, with one poll by Median this week showing 60% support for Tisza and only 18% for Fidesz.
