World.title: Mónica García: “Las lógicas partidistas no deben frenar una ley que busca evitar 140 muertes al día”
World.content:
La ministra de Sanidad se muestra convencida de que la nueva ley del tabaco será aprobada en el Congreso y espera mejorar el texto durante la tramitación parlamentaria

La ministra de Sanidad, Mónica García (Madrid, 52 años), presentó este martes la nueva ley del tabaco como una “gran victoria” para España y equiparó la iniciativa al reciente triunfo de la selección en el Mundial de fútbol. Hace 16 años, recordó, el primer éxito de España en este torneo también coincidió con la pionera ley del tabaco, que erradicó el humo de los espacios interiores de bares, restaurantes y centros de trabajo. Como entonces, sin embargo, el proyecto se ha topado con el rechazo de sectores como la hostelería, industria tabaquera y estanqueros, entre otros. Tras su paso por el Consejo de Ministros, el proyecto deberá ser aprobado por el Congreso de los Diputados, donde necesita del apoyo de formaciones como el PP o Junts, que ya han mostrado sus reticencias. Pese a ello, la ministra se muestra confiada en que la tramitación parlamentaria salga adelante, y que el debate mejore el texto en cuestiones como el empaquetado genérico, que evita que las cajetillas de cigarrillos actúen como un elemento publicitario más. La ministra atiende a EL PAÍS por teléfono.

Pregunta. ¿Por qué ha llegado el proyecto de ley al Consejo de Ministros ahora, justo antes de las vacaciones, y no antes?

Respuesta. Hemos tenido que alinear la ley con las directivas de la Comisión Europea y pasar por una serie de trámites que han alargado el proceso.

P. ¿Teme que el proyecto no pase el filtro del Congreso?

R. Sabemos que existen unos equilibrios parlamentarios que no siempre responden a las necesidades de los ciudadanos, sino a lógicas partidistas. Pero esta es una ley que nos pone otra vez en la vanguardia de la protección de la salud pública y esperamos que prime la responsabilidad y no frenen una norma que busca evitar 50.000 muertes al año, 140 al día. El tabaco en todas sus formas está detrás del 30% de los tumores y el 100% de los cardiólogos dicen que, si pudieran retirar un factor de riesgo evitable, este sería el tabaco.

P. ¿Ha tenido algún contacto con el PP o Junts?

R. No todavía. Lo que sí acabo de escuchar es al señor Alberto Núñez Feijóo diciendo que la ley es una cortina de humo y que va a dividir al país. No sé si se refiere a que dividirá a los que quieren tener cáncer y los que no. No sé exactamente a qué división se refiere. Sí sé que en 2010 escuchamos también augurios catastrofistas que no se han cumplido. Hoy tenemos un país con espacios cerrados sin humo, mucho más saludables. Y me alegra ver que bares y restaurantes siguen gozando de muy buena salud. También queremos que la tengan los trabajadores y usuarios de sus terrazas.

P. ¿Qué les ha llevado a dar el salto de prohibir fumar a los menores?

R. El tabaco en todas sus formas es un tóxico adictivo muy perjudicial para la salud y es nuestra obligación proteger a los menores, al igual que hacemos con el alcohol. Estamos viendo, además, que los dispositivos asociados al tabaco son una vía de entrada a la adicción para los menores y que causan daños como hemorragias pulmonares.

P. La ley prevé sanciones de 200 euros si un menor fuma. Serán los padres quienes hagan frente a la multa, que puede ser sustituida por trabajos a la comunidad. ¿Es esta una forma de implicar a todos contra el tabaquismo?

R. La ley, como las de este tipo, debe incluir un régimen sancionador, pero en términos de salud pública eso nos preocupa menos. El objetivo no es sancionar, es consensuar elementos que consideramos de sentido común y fundamentales. No buscamos perseguir ni recaudar, sino visibilizar, concienciar y dar respuesta a la evidencia científica.

P. Se ha criticado que España será una “excepción” europea al prohibir fumar en terrazas y que esto dañará el turismo y la imagen del país.

R. Más que motivo de crítica, debe ser algo de lo que estemos orgullosos. La Comisión Europea dijo en 2024 que había que extender los espacios sin humo, también a las terrazas. Ser de los primeros en aplicar una medida que protege la salud de la población y que con seguridad seguirán otros países debe satisfacernos. El tabaco también es la principal causa de muerte evitable en Europa y existe un consenso entre las sociedades científicas.

P. ¿Era tan importante equiparar los vapeadores al tabaco tradicional? Los críticos dicen que son menos dañinos...

R. Ese debate es engañoso. Si se pretende que estos dispositivos sean una forma de control de daños, deberían usarse bajo supervisión médica, como los parches de nicotina o las pastillas. La industria sabe que no es así y lo está usando como excusa para atraer a nuevos consumidores jóvenes con presentaciones más amables que crearán nuevos adictos. Lo que más nos ha preocupado de las encuestas es el aumento del consumo de estos dispositivos entre los jóvenes.

Mónica García, en la azotea del ministerio de Sanidad, en Madrid, este miércoles. Carlos Rosillo

P. ¿Cómo valora las reacciones de sectores como la hostelería y la industria? ¿Le sorprende que sean tan parecidas a las de 2010?

R. Me sorprende más que algunos sectores no tengan memoria, pero son minoritarios. Existe una amplia mayoría de la sociedad que apoya este tipo de medidas porque los beneficios logrados en 2010 siguen estando muy presentes. También nos hemos encontrado mucha gente que ha dejado el tabaco o quiere hacerlo y está de acuerdo en que se amplíen las zonas libres de humo porque esto les ayuda a dejar de fumar.

P. Usted decía que se ha retrasado la aprobación del proyecto de ley para alinearlo con las directrices europeas. Pero se les critica no haber esperado a que la Comisión Europea acabe de revisar las directivas sobre la materia.

R. No es cierto, estamos alineados con la Comisión. Hay una cosa en la que todavía no está definida la posición europea, por ejemplo, que es sobre los vapeadores desechables. Lo habíamos introducido en el texto, pero por ahora lo hemos retirado porque en Europa todavía no se ha consensuado. Dicho esto, la ley tiene un trámite parlamentario y hay cosas que, si se acuerdan en este tiempo en Europa, las podemos introducir.

P. ¿Tiene sentido criticar la ley con el argumento de que el tabaco aporta casi 4.000 millones al PIB y genera 60.000 empleos?

R. No existe la dicotomía salud a cambio de economía, es falsa. Si no hay salud, no hay economía. 50.000 vidas al año y el enorme sufrimiento que provocan las enfermedades causadas por el tabaco no tienen precio. Y más allá de los impuestos que puedas recaudar, los costes de la asistencia sanitaria de todas estas enfermedades los triplica. No tiene sentido plantearlo en estos términos. Otra cosa es que haya empresas que defiendan sus intereses económicos, pero nuestra función es proteger la salud de los ciudadanos. No se pueden contraponer los intereses económicos de unas empresas concretas a la vida y salud de toda una población.

P. ¿Por qué se ha quedado fuera de la ley el empaquetado genérico que haga indistinguibles las distintas marcas?

R. Había algunas carteras que no estaban de acuerdo con el empaquetado genérico. Decidimos posponer este punto para el trámite parlamentario. Sabemos que el empaquetado genérico funciona. Ya lo tienen otros países y hay evidencia científica de los beneficios que aporta que la propia cajetilla no sea un elemento de publicidad más.

P. Entonces, ¿el PSOE se opone y Sumar quiere convencerle en el Congreso?

R. Más que oponerse, hay algunas dudas. Esperamos resolverlas y convencer a todas las fuerzas parlamentarias de los beneficios de esta medida.

P. Otra cuestión clave es el precio del tabaco. Seguimos siendo uno de los países de Europa con el tabaco más barato...

R. Es cierto que la evidencia es muy clara y un incremento de precio ayuda a reducir la prevalencia del tabaquismo. Pero la competencia es de otra cartera [Hacienda]. En cualquier caso, es bueno que se abra el debate público, porque la evidencia científica demuestra que poner encima de la mesa estas cuestiones ayuda a que la sociedad reflexione sobre el daño del tabaco y ayuda a algunas personas a dar el paso para dejarlo.

P. ¿Cómo valora que el Reino Unido haya aprobado la “generación libre de humo”, en la que los nacidos a partir de 2009 no podrán fumar nunca tabaco convencional?

R. El objetivo de un futuro libre de la adicción al tabaco es compartido por todos. Nosotros pensamos que podemos llegar al mismo sitio por distinto camino, pero todos podemos aprender de los demás y adoptar medidas que tengan éxito en otros lugares. España llevaba sin tocar la Ley del Tabaco desde 2010 y era imprescindible ahora dar un impulso. Pero todos perseguimos el mismo fin: proteger a los menores de la adicción, ayudar a quienes quieren dejar de fumar y evitar que el humo de quienes aún fuman perjudique al resto de la población.

World.title: “Si no tenemos habilidades para tolerar la frustración o para empatizar vamos a tener muchas dificultades en la vida”
World.content:
La psicóloga y conferenciante Patricia Ramírez reflexiona con su hija Carmen Rodríguez sobre la importancia de aprender desde la escuela la gestión de las emociones. Es la primera charla de ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja para debatir sobre la educación que necesitamos

Patricia Ramírez @Patri_Psicóloga Psicóloga, escritora y conferenciante Cuenta con más de 27 años de trayectoria como profesional de la salud, es doctora en Psicología por la Universidad de Granada y dirige una clínica de consultas online Además de ejercer con sus pacientes, lo divulga: tiene más de un millón de seguidores en redes sociales y ha escrito trece libros. En 2024 publicó Cómo tener tiempo para todo (Grijalbo), sobre el impacto del ritmo de vida en el bienestar psicológico Carmen Rodríguez Representante y 'community manager' Tras estudiar Derecho, abandonar unas oposiciones después de dos años y trabajar en un obrador como repostera, decidió dar un giro a su carrera para incorporarse al proyecto de divulgación de su madre, la psicóloga Patricia Ramírez, de la que hoy es representante. Sus cambios laborales le han permitido comprender las inquietudes que comparten muchos jóvenes; la presión académica, las dudas y, en definitiva, la búsqueda de un camino propio

Hay quien regula las emociones con la comida, quien lo hace con horas de scroll infinito frente a un móvil y quien es capaz de gestionarlas de manera saludable. Ese aprendizaje es, para la psicóloga Patricia Ramírez, la esencia de la educación emocional. “Nos permite una mejor tolerancia a la frustración, responsabilizarnos de nuestra vida, tener mejores vínculos con otras personas y un mayor respeto hacia nosotros mismos”. Una herramienta para conectar con la vida, con otras personas y con uno mismo, dice.

“La gente que busca el perfeccionismo nunca está satisfecha con ella misma. Y esto afecta muchísimo a la autoestima”

Para poder desarrollar la educación emocional, la apuesta de Ramírez es que se introduzca desde los primeros años, en las aulas. “Materias como Matemáticas, Física o Geografía son fundamentales, pero, si no tenemos habilidades para tolerar la frustración o empatizar con otra persona, vamos a tener muchas dificultades en la vida”, asegura. Esa es su propuesta para la educación del futuro: “educar en valores desde que los niños son chiquitos: el respeto, el esfuerzo, la justicia, la bondad, el amor, la responsabilidad, la empatía. Los valores son los superpoderes de niños y adolescentes”, cuenta.

“A un adolescente exigente le diría que tiene que crear un espacio para poder comunicar lo que siente; lo bueno y lo malo, sus decisiones, sus dudas”

A Carmen Rodríguez le costó encontrar su vocación. “¿Tú has pensado alguna vez que yo perdía el tiempo?”, le pregunta a Patricia, que le contesta desde la doble perspectiva de madre y psicóloga: “Yo he pensado que estabas explorando diferentes caminos hasta que poco a poco has ido encontrando el tuyo. Y creo que ahí los padres no podemos influiros en qué decisiones tenéis que tomar, porque tú tienes que vivir tu vida, no la vida que un padre o una madre elige para ti”. Una charla que sirve de inspiración para afrontar retos e inquietudes.

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

World.title: Si decido comprar una vivienda anunciada por una agencia, ¿estoy obligado a pagar una comisión?
World.content:
Pregunta. ¿En qué supuestos existe obligación de pagar comisión por parte del comprador a la agencia inmobiliaria cuando quien contrata sus servicios es el vendedor? J. Ibáñez

Respuesta. En relación con la obligación de abonar los honorarios de la agencia inmobiliaria por parte del comprador, debe partirse del principio de libertad de pacto entre las partes. En las operaciones de compraventa inmobiliaria no existe una norma que imponga de forma general que la comisión de la agencia deba ser asumida necesariamente por el vendedor o por el comprador, ni de forma exclusiva por uno de ellos, por lo que la dependerá de los acuerdos alcanzados entre las partes.

La parte compradora estará obligada al pago de dichos honorarios cuando haya aceptado de forma clara y expresa asumir ese coste. En la práctica, es habitual que las agencias inmobiliarias incluyan esta cláusula en el parte de visitas, documento que se suele entregar al potencial comprador en la primera visita al inmueble y en el que, además de dejar constancia de que ha conocido la vivienda a través de la agencia, se puede incorporar una cláusula relativa al pago de los honorarios profesionales.

Si dicho parte de visitas contiene una cláusula clara sobre la obligación del comprador de abonar la comisión inmobiliaria, y esta ha sido firmada por la parte compradora, podrá entenderse que existe aceptación contractual suficiente para reclamar el pago de la comisión, siempre que la inmobiliaria haya intervenido efectivamente en la operación y la compraventa llegue finalmente a formalizarse.

Por lo tanto, en el caso que se expone habrá que revisar el documento firmado por el comprador, ya sea el parte de visitas, el documento de entrega de señal o el contrato de arras que habitualmente se suscribe antes de la compraventa. Si en cualquiera de dichos documentos consta expresamente la aceptación del pago de honorarios a favor de la inmobiliaria, sí podrá exigirse el abono de la comisión a la parte compradora. La ley únicamente establece la obligación de pago de los gastos de gestión inmobiliaria al propietario en los supuestos de arrendamiento de vivienda habitual, pero no en las operaciones de compraventa.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Erasmus Bridge reopens after Rotterdam tram collision
World.content:
The Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam reopened to all traffic on Wednesday evening after the two badly damaged trams which collided on it that morning were lifted clear of the tracks, broadcaster NOS reported. Trams are running over the bridge again.

Fifteen people were injured, one of them seriously, when a moving tram ran into the back of a stationary one waiting for the bridge to close, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported.

The salvage operation took most of the day, with the trams having to be cut apart, RET director Linda Boot told the broadcaster.

Three investigations are now under way. Police are examining the crash, including with a drone team, transport company RET is carrying out its own inquiry, and the Dutch Safety Board has begun a preliminary investigation to decide whether to open a full one.

RET said initial checks showed the driver of the rear tram had not been under the influence of alcohol or drugs. He was among those taken to hospital. Boot said it was too early to speculate about the cause.

Rotterdam mayor Carola Schouten visited the scene and called it “a terrible accident”. No further information has been released about the condition of those hurt.

World.title: Sixteen councils still without a coalition, four months on
World.content:
Sixteen Dutch councils still have not formed a government coalition 126 days after the local elections on March 18 – the highest number ever recorded, according to local government news site Binnenlands Bestuur.

The summer recess will add another 30 days, meaning coalition talks in those councils will have run for more than 150 days. The average formation now stands at 87 days, up from 83 in 2022, and may rise to 90. By comparison, only four councils were still negotiating after the summer in 2022, and in 2018 just one was.

Binnenlands Bestuur points to three reasons. Coalition-building has become more formal, with councils now holding public debates on the election result and appointing scouts and informateurs, where the process was once settled by senior figures behind closed doors.

Councils have also become more fragmented, so a majority often requires four parties or more. And the shift towards right-wing and far-right parties has made it harder to assemble a stable majority, the site said, while vetting the background of candidates for alderman takes longer than it used to.

The outgoing executive stays in place until a new one is appointed, so no council is left without an administration. But caretaker administrations tend to avoid major or politically contested decisions, so new policy largely waits.

Leiden is the only large city still without a coalition, after talks collapsed last month over a lack of trust between PRO and D66. Of the 324 councils that have completed the process, 182 took longer than in 2022, while 115 were quicker – among them The Hague, which did not have a coalition until late September last time. The record is held by Vlieland, which needed 229 days in 2022.

World.title: Half a million Dutch households in energy poverty
World.content:
Around 503,000 Dutch households were living in energy poverty last year, or 6% of the total – unchanged from 2024, according to figures from statistics office CBS and research institute TNO published on Thursday.

The share had dropped to under 4% in 2023 while government compensation for high energy bills was in place, then jumped back once the support ended. It remains below the 2019 level of nearly 10%.

Researchers looked for the first time at how far people fall short, and found households on low incomes with high energy bills were on average €624 a year short of escaping energy poverty, up from €577 in 2024. Lifting them all out would have cost around €256 million.

Average monthly energy costs rose from €167 to €181 across all households, and from €177 to €188 for those in energy poverty, who now spend 11.5% of their income on energy – more than twice the national average.

The number of low-income households facing high energy bills rose from 385,000 to 410,000, while the number living in poorly insulated homes continued to fall.

Energy poverty is most common in the big cities, north-east Groningen and south Limburg. The deepest shortfalls are in homes with very poor energy efficiency (€1,295 a year) and among owner-occupiers (€967).

World.title: Ivory and a rhino skull among 5,800 items handed to RVO
World.content:
Some 5,800 prohibited objects including elephant ivory have been anonymously handed in to the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO) over the past year, a more than fivefold increase on the previous year.

“Never before has so much been handed in,” says The Hague-based RVO, including “moving boxes with a thousand [pieces of] ivory jewellery, a rhino skull with a gunshot wound, crocodile leather bags, musical instruments and an elephant’s leg.”

The objects also included taxidermy animals such as a long-eared owl, peregrine falcon and turtles. Pictures on broadcaster NOS show ivory binoculars and crocodile leather bags.

The sale and trade of elephant ivory are strictly regulated under European CITES laws (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species), with permits required for the possession and trade of protected plants or animals.

Most of the items, which can be handed in at a drop-off bin in The Hague or even by post, are destroyed to prevent them from (re)entering the illegal trade. The RVO says it uses a small number of the items for research and education.

World.title: Thuisbezorgd hides costs and fakes discounts: consumer group
World.content:
The food delivery platform Thuisbezorgd.nl hides compulsory charges and advertises fake discounts, the Dutch consumer association Consumentenbond said on Tuesday, calling on the company to stop and to compensate affected customers.

Mandatory costs should be clearly shown before a customer starts ordering, the association said, but Thuisbezorgd’s app and website do not reveal compulsory “service” charges – for items such as bags, plastic packaging and sauce – until part-way through or at the end of an order, adding an average of €2 to €4 to the bill.

The association also said the company broke rules on special offers. Under Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM) rules, a struck-through sale price must be the lowest the seller charged in the previous 30 days. In one case, the association found Indian snacks that had previously cost €3.75 being offered “on sale” from €7.50 to €6.

“We have been in talks with Thuisbezorgd since March, but the platform is still confronting customers with hidden costs and fake discounts,” said Consumentenbond director Sandra Molenaar, noting the company has more than six million users in the Netherlands.

Because the practice has probably been going on for years, the association estimates the hidden costs run into the hundreds of millions of euros in total. A Thuisbezorgd spokesperson said the company did not recognise the association’s accusations.

The Consumentenbond said it had also found hidden costs at Uber Eats, which made changes in June, though no fake discounts. The findings are part of a wider campaign against hidden charges and misleading offers that also named Bol and Amazon last week.

The association can press companies to change but cannot impose penalties; that is a matter for the ACM, which has fined firms including Leen Bakker, G-Star and Jysk in the past.

Three men have been arrested over the theft of a shipment of smartphones with an estimated street value of around €5 million from the Schiphol area, the Royal Military Police (Koninklijke Marechaussee) have said.

The suspects are two 24-year-old men from Amsterdam and a 39-year-old from Zoetermeer.

The shipment went missing on June 18, prompting an investigation, led by the Noord-Holland public prosecution department, into an organised crime group.

One of the suspects works for a transport company at Schiphol and is thought to have passed confidential information to the group, the military police said. Further arrests have not been ruled out.

World.title: Two trams collide on Rotterdam’s Erasmus Bridge, 15 injured
World.content:
Fifteen people were injured, one of them seriously, when two trams collided on the Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam on Wednesday morning, the regional safety board has said. One of the trams was derailed by the impact.

The crash happened at around 11.10am, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported. Footage shows one tram coming to a halt as it drove onto the bridge from the direction of the city centre, before a second tram approached from behind and ran into it, apparently without braking.

The seriously injured person was trapped and had to be freed before being taken to hospital. The safety board initially reported 18 injured and two seriously hurt, but later revised the figures.

Transport company RET said it could not yet say what caused the rear-end collision, adding that it was shocked by the footage and that its thoughts were with the victims and passengers. Two cars were also damaged, the fire service said.

The power to the overhead lines was switched off and the bridge closed to traffic, halting tram services on lines 3 and 5.

World.title: Man jailed for 15 months over threats to Groningen butchers
World.content:
A Groningen court has sentenced a 23-year-old man to 15 months in prison for sending death threats to butchers in the province and neighbouring Drenthe.

Prosecutors requested a four-year sentence, saying he had a terrorist motive. But the court ruled there was insufficient evidence for such a charge, saying instead he acted out of radical environmental and animal-rights beliefs.

Because four months of his sentence are suspended, the man, known as Bas V., will be released immediately, having already served his time in pre-trial detention. He is bound by a three-year probationary period.

The crime

Last September, Bas V. sent threatening emails to 12 butcher shops demanding they close. “You get one warning, nothing more. If the shop isn’t closed tomorrow, I will come with a machete and stab everyone to death,” read the email.

The court stated: “The texts on his phone say something about his mindset, but not that he wanted to disrupt society with them.”

Bas V., who admitted to sending the emails, was arrested after seven of the butchers filed a complaint. Police found a machete in his home and notes on his phone saying he also needed a pistol with a silencer to “kill people responsible for the humiliation of animals,” according to broadcaster NOS.

The national broadcaster also says that Bas V. was found by experts to have a gaming addiction, a cannabis addiction, ADHD and autism, and will be placed in a protected living facility to receive treatment.

They said that the German personnel would mainly engage in engineering work, such as digging trenches, laying barbed wire and constructing anti-tank barriers. While the armed forces did not reveal the location of the deployment, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated in a social media post that it was on the Russian border. Poland has a 210-km frontier with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. German public broadcaster Deutsche Welle reports that the activities of the German sappers are focused in particular on improving defences around the so-called Suwałki Gap, a strategically important stretch of land around the Polish-Lithuanian border between Belarus and Kaliningrad. “Together, we are ensuring Europe’s security,” said Lieutenant General Alexander Sollfrank, the Bundeswehr’s operational commander, announcing the deployment today. “Through our engagement in Poland, we are strengthening NATO’s defence capabilities and underscoring the alliance’s unwavering commitment to ensuring peace through unity and credible deterrence.” Poland and Germany have signed a bilateral security agreement that will see the two neighbours and NATO allies increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity https://t.co/6BPX2WxvxH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 SGWP, which shared footage of Polish and German forces installing anti-tank barriers, said the work aims to “hinder and delay an aggressor’s actions in the event of a threat”, thereby “increasing the time for a response from the Polish armed forces and the entire [NATO] alliance”. It also seeks to “create conditions for the efficient reception, deployment and use of NATO forces on Polish territory”. Poland’s climate and environment ministry has inaugurated the first of 11 planned “community forests” around large cities, with the aim of giving residents a place for recreation and contact with nature while also helping to fulfil the government’s pledge to reduce logging. Plans for the forests were announced in 2024, and the first has now been established around Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city. Ten other major urban centres, including Warsaw, Kraków, Poznań and Łódź, are set to follow. Dotrzymujemy słowa. Powołaliśmy pierwsze lasy społeczne w Polsce, to lasy ochronne wokół Wrocławia. Kolejne miasta przed nami. @MKiS_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/RxhsMZShj9 — Paulina Hennig-Kloska (@hennigkloska) July 21, 2026 “This is a historic moment and the beginning of a new approach to forest protection – with residents in mind first and foremost,” said climate and environment minister Paulina Hennig-Kloska at an inauguration ceremony outside Wrocław on Sunday. “Community forests are places where residents can relax, play sports and simply spend time close to nature,” she added. “At the same time, they are crucial to our security and quality of life: they retain water, regulate the climate, purify the air and protect the soil.” An area covering 13,000 hectares (32,124 acres) has been designated as a community forest around Wrocław. Forest management there will now be aimed at “maximising the forest’s social functions”, says the ministry, while timber harvesting is also restricted. The area will be divided into three zones, including “natural forests”, where nature will be left to take its course, and “near-natural forests” with minimal intervention. However, the largest zone, amounting to over 8,000 hectares, will be “social forests”, which the state forestry agency says “will be managed in a way that ensures the comfort of those who use the forest and its benefits related to wellbeing, physical exercise and recreation”. Hennig-Kloska noted that, in the latter area, educational trails as well as hiking and cycling paths would be established. However, given that such facilities already exist in many forests, it remains unclear how the new community forests will differ. The ministry is now conducting consultations and analysis on establishing community forests around ten other designated urban centres: Bielsko-Biała, Tricity (Gdańsk-Gdynia-Sopot), Katowice, Kielce, Kraków, Łódź, Poznań, Szczecin, Toruń-Bydgoszcz and Warsaw. On Sunday, Hennig-Kloska said that the “next in line” to have their community forests established are Kielce and Bielsko-Biała, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Shortly after coming to power in December 2023, the current government announced that it would halt planned logging in some forests. The former Law and Justice (PiS) administration had faced criticism for overseeing an increase in logging, especially in Białowieża Forest. The current government also launched plans to create Poland’s first new national parks in over two decades. However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last year vetoed that move, arguing that it would “block the economic development of the region” and threaten Poland’s security. Poland has joined a European Union project developing a secure satellite internet service that would provide an alternative to networks such as Elon Musk’s Starlink. Warsaw has committed €656 million (2.8 billion zloty) to the IRIS² programme, with the money coming from Poland’s EU post-pandemic recovery funds. In return for joining the project, Poland will gain access to the secure satellite communications network for government institutions, the armed forces and emergency services, while the growing Polish space industry will be eligible to compete for contracts linked to the development of the constellation Today Poland🇵🇱joins the EU🇪🇺space programme #IRIS² w/additional €656 mln. 🇵🇱 is on a remarkable space journey to build a strong space economy & secure connectivity for the defence of Poland, the Eastern Flank & 🇪🇺. IRIS² brings greater unity & strength for the entire Europe. pic.twitter.com/TwS59vpXtm — Andrius Kubilius (@KubiliusA) July 21, 2026 “This is a big day for Poland, the eastern flank and the entire European Union,” declared the EU’s defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, at a signing ceremony in Warsaw on Tuesday. “By investing in space, Poland is investing in its security, its economy and its future.” Speaking alongside him, Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said that IRIS² would help “ensure our security and strategic independence” while “demonstrating that Poland aims to be a leader in the European space industry and remain at the centre of EU security efforts”. “No single country is able to build such a [satellite] constellation so efficiently, which is why we are joining this major project – to be part of it and one of its managers,” he added. The IRIS² programme aims to deploy a constellation of nearly 300 satellites in low and medium Earth orbit, providing encrypted, interference-resistant communications for governments, defence agencies, emergency services and selected commercial users across the EU. First announced in 2022, the project is part of the EU’s efforts to reduce dependence on non-European satellite operators amid growing concerns over cybersecurity, hybrid threats and the resilience of critical infrastructure following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “It is super important for Europe to have a sovereign capacity, and Starlink will never do that,” said Eva Berneke, CEO of Eutelsat, one of the companies involved in the project, quoted by Politico Europe. The project is expected to cost €10.6 billion, including €6.5 billion in public funding and around €4 billion from private investors. IRIS² is expected to become operational in 2030. 🇪🇺 The IRIS program is Europe's replacement for Starlink. The constellation will consist of over 300 satellites to serve Europe alone. It will also build a ground gateway station in Warsaw to connect the satellites with GovNet, the country’s secure government fibre-optic communications network. World.title: Archaeologists uncover synagogue in Warsaw Jewish cemetery destroyed by Germans in WWII
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Archaeological work at a Jewish cemetery in Warsaw has uncovered the foundations of and many objects from a former synagogue and funeral home that was destroyed by the Nazi-German occupiers in 1943. The finds were made at the cemetery on Okopowa Street, which, at around 33.5 hectares in size and with some 250,000 people buried there, is the second largest in Poland, after the Łódź Jewish cemetery, and one of the biggest anywhere in the world. Following the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Germans liquidated the ghetto, sending most of its remaining inhabitants to the gas chambers and destroying the buildings that remained there, including the synagogue and burial houses. In June this year, archaeological work began at the site of the former synagogue, commissioned by Warsaw’s Jewish community, which owns and manages the cemetery. The two-storey building, designed by architect Adolf Schimmelpfennig, a Pole of Dutch Lutheran descent, was constructed in 1877 and existed until 15 May 1943, when it was destroyed with explosives. The archaeological work aims to “uncover, document and preserve the remains of this historic complex, maintaining the memory of this place and passing it on to future generations”, says the office of the conservator of monuments for Masovia, the province in which Warsaw is located and which is supervising the work. Archaeologists have so far discovered numerous items that offer “silent testament to the daily life of the community that was connected to this site for decades”, says the conservator. They include ceramic floor and wall tiles, glass bottles and tiles from stoves used at the funeral home. “Every discovered brick, fragment of flooring or piece of furniture helps reconstruct the history of one of the most important buildings in historic Warsaw,” adds the conservator. Among the finds is an item that relates to a well-known and tragic story from the war, a door plaque from the office of the then-director of the cemetery, Abram Pozner. Pozner brought members of his extended family to the funeral home at the start of the war, where they were initially able to remain in relative safety, away from the horrors of the ghetto that the occupiers forced Jews to live in. As life became ever more brutal and dangerous for Jews, Pozner created an underground hideout within the cemetery. The Germans eventually found the bunker and killed most of those hiding there. However, two of them managed to survive imprisonment in German labour camps, one of whom, Avraham Carmi, remains alive today and lives in Israel. The current archaeological work is expected to be completed by the end of July, after which the foundations will be re-covered with earth. Warsaw’s Jewish community then hopes to restore the previous building, adapted to current conditions and needs, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “The goal is to determine whether the funeral home could be rebuilt on these remains, or whether it would make more sense to display them as a monument within a newly constructed building, and also whether erecting a building on this site is even realistic,” cemetery director Witold Wrzosiński told the newspaper. Archaeologist Szymon Lenarczyk, who has led the work at the site, says he has proposed that the structure of a future building should feature an underground room where discovered artefacts can be displayed. Before World War Two, Warsaw was home to around 350,000 Jews, a third of its population and more than any city in the world other than New York. However, the vast majority were killed in the Holocaust, meaning that only a small Jewish community remains today. A planned metro system in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has moved a step closer after the authorities launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. City authorities say the plans – which will include a feasibility study, environmental report, geological research, and assessment of the project’s impact on existing buildings – are a major milestone in the development of what would be only Poland’s second underground railway network. #Krakow #metro #projektowanie #przetargi 🚇Kraków ogłasza przetarg na opracowanie dokumentacji przedprojektowej dla budowy metra. W ramach uruchomionego postępowania powstaną m. in. dokumenty, analizy i decyzje, które pozwolą przygotować dokumentację niezbędną do finalnego… pic.twitter.com/0jcYL4HGRq — Kraków (@krakow_pl) July 13, 2026 The idea of building a metro in Kraków has been discussed for decades and, in 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the project. However, only in 2024 did the city’s then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, announce plans to build a system. In September last year, the city unveiled the metro’s planned route, with two lines travelling through the city’s historic centre from its southwestern and southeastern suburbs to its eastern outskirts. In May this year, Miszalski, who had made developing the metro part of his election campaign in 2023, was removed as mayor in a recall referendum. But the project has nevertheless continued, with the municipal authorities last week announcing a tender for pre-design of the metro. The work will include confirmation of the planned structure of the system as well as the location of stations, tunnels and other infrastructure. The city has allocated 188 million zloty for the pre-design in its budget for 2026 to 2031. Studies of feasibility and impact are particularly important given that the planned route of the metro envisages it skirting around Kraków’s Old Town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site that contains many historical structures. The tender follows months of preparatory work, initial market consultations, analyses and discussions with experts, said Maria Wojtacha, director of Kraków’s public works department. “Although this process doesn’t yet mean that construction has begun, it is one of the most important steps that the city can take individually,” Wojtacha added. “Our goal is to prepare Kraków for the next stage – the ‘design and build’ phase.” The experiences of other recent major infrastructure projects in Poland, such as a major new airport and transport hub and Warsaw’s second metro line, show that environmental and tender procedures need not slow investments down, said Marek Grochowicz of the city’s strategy and European funds department. However, it is clear that the earlier timeline for Kraków’s metro outlined is slipping. Last September, the city said that it hoped construction would begin in 2030 and that the system would be finished by 2035. However, the current acting mayor, Stanisław Kracik, announced last month that construction is unlikely to start until between 2040 and 2045. Even the current tender for “pre-design” work envisages a timeline of up to 50 months for that work alone. Warsaw has announced 56m zloty for “pre-design” work on a fourth metro line. The mayor says improving public transport is an "absolute priority". But his rival in next month's elections says the mayor is digging up forgotten plans as part of the campaign https://t.co/lg3zkNeW2E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2024 Rafał Solecki, head of Kraków’s department of strategy and European funds, also made clear last week that “construction of the metro exceeds the financial capabilities of the local authorities”, and that therefore financial support from the national government and the EU will be necessary. “The metro should be treated as a national strategic investment, similar to large railway, road, aviation and metropolitan projects implemented in other parts of the country with state participation,” he added. The city also announced that it has received a proposal for a consortium of seven local universities and research institutions to provide scientific and expert support for the metro project throughout its preparation and implementation. “Building a metro in a historic city is an extremely complex undertaking, requiring special attention to the protection of cultural heritage,” said Andrzej Szarata, rector of Cracow University of Technology. “Therefore, the support of the scientific community…is of paramount importance.” Kraków has been named Europe's best city break destination by members of @WhichUK. Poland says that the number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants over the border from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. “The effectiveness of [border guard] officers and the Polish armed forces discourages migrants from taking risks,” says Poland’s interior ministry. Bezpieczeństwo na granicy z Białorusią w pierwszej połowie 2026 r. w liczbach: 📉 Ponad 65-krotny spadek prób nielegalnego przekroczenia (ok. 235 vs ponad 15,5 tys. w pierwszym półroczu 2025 r.) 🛡️ 0 udanych prób nielegalnego przekroczenia granicy 💯 Skuteczność ochrony: 100%… pic.twitter.com/1lTXV56JdW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) July 18, 2026 Since 2021, large numbers of migrants and asylum seekers – mainly from Africa and Asia – have tried to irregularly cross the border from Belarus to Poland with the help and encouragement of the Belarusian authorities. In 2021 alone, just under 40,000 attempted illegal crossings were recorded. While Poland subsequently strengthened border infrastructure and sent thousands of additional officers to bolster security, attempted crossings remained high: there were just under 30,000 in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have now fallen dramatically in the first half of this year, when Poland’s border guard recorded only 235 crossings, compared to 15,500 in the equivalent period for 2025. Meanwhile, the interior minister says that the number of successful crossings by migrants – i.e. those who managed to get across the border and were not apprehended – has fallen to zero so far this year, down from around 1,700 in 2025, 5,000 in 2024 and 12,000 in 2023. However, when presenting such figures on successful crossings, the ministry does not indicate how it calculates them, given that successful crossings are often inherently undetected. Most of those who manage to cross do not remain in Poland, instead heading westwards, in particular to Germany. “The statistics clearly show that the 3 billion zloty (€692 million) investment in the security of the Polish-Belarusian border has delivered the intended results – we are effectively protecting our country from illegal migration organised by the Belarusian regime with the support of the Kremlin,” declared the ministry. Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland. Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 Among the measures taken to protect the border are a 5.5-metre-high steel fence as well as an electronic monitoring system that detects attempts to cross and dispatches officers to the scene. In 2024, following the death of a soldier who had been stabbed by a migrant attempting to cross the border, Poland also loosened the rules on the use of firearms by officers posted there. Since last year, it has banned asylum claims by people who cross from Belarus. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, also praised Poland’s “impressive” efforts “to stop illegal migration” and said that it was vital for the EU to offer financial and logistical support. EU chief @vonderleyen has thanked Poland for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” during a visit with PM @donaldtusk to the border with Belarus. She emphasised the “urgency” of protecting the EU’s frontier from the “predator” Vladimir Putin https://t.co/O9bhmLha44 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2025 However, while Poland has managed to significantly reduce the number of attempted and successful border crossings, there is evidence that Belarus has switched its focus to Latvia, another EU member state with which it shares a border. Last week, Latvian interior minister Jānis Dombrava told Euronews that his country has now “become the main target” for Belarus’s migrant trafficking, instead of Poland and Lithuania. On Thursday, Latvia recorded 111 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, compared to two in Lithuania on the same day and zero in Poland the previous day. World.title: Poland welcomes Zelensky’s five-point plan for resolving dispute over WWII massacres
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has cautiously welcomed an announcement by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of a five-point plan intended to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led massacres of Poles during World War Two. In a statement on Friday evening, Zelensky announced that, following a meeting on Kyiv’s policy towards Poland, “the priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighbourly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect”. He reiterated Ukraine’s gratitude for Poland’s “significant support” since Russia’s full-scale invasion and announced that his administration had “agreed on several key steps” in response to the current tensions. I held a meeting on our policy toward Poland. The priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighborly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect. Poland provided significant support to Ukraine after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, and we are… pic.twitter.com/5dNFQYqi1n — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) July 17, 2026 “First, there will be decisions on the diplomatic track,” said Zelensky, though without indicating what this would mean in practice. “Second, all archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the tragic events in Volyn during the 20th century will be opened.” The latter is a reference to the historical issues that are at the heart of the dispute. The historical region of Volhynia, which is now mostly in Ukraine, was part of Poland in the interwar period. There, and in some neighbouring areas, the UPA, a nationalist partisan formation, led massacres of around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, during World War Two, when the region was under Nazi-German occupation. Poland recognises those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine vehemently rejects that label, and also points to anti-Ukrainian measures in the region by the interwar Polish state as well as massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during the war. As his third pledge, Zelensky announced that there would be “decisions to grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. From 2017 to 2025, Ukraine prohibited searches for and exhumations of Polish massacre victims on its territory, where it is believed that tens of thousands remain buried in unmarked mass graves. In a diplomatic breakthrough, such work was allowed to resume last year. However, Ukraine has so far only approved a small number of requests for searches and exhumations, prompting some complaints from Poland. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 As a fourth point, Zelensky said that his team had “discussed possible formats for expanding dialogue between the societies of Ukraine and Poland”, though again without providing details as to what this would involve. Finally, he said that he had agreed with the head of the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINP), Oleksandr Alfyorov, to expand the institute’s capabilities and funding, so that it can “properly represent Ukraine’s interests”. Alfyorov caused anger in Poland earlier this year when he said that the Volhynia massacres are viewed in Ukraine as “just a local historical episode” and suggested they did not constitute a genocide. That prompted a rebuke from Poland’s own Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). Poland's state historical institute has criticised remarks by the head of its Ukrainian counterpart about massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. He said they are regarded in Ukraine as a "local episode" and suggested they do not constitute a genocide https://t.co/MAi6RhpRDL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 11, 2026 In response to Zelensky’s announcement, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he “accepted the words and decisions with satisfaction and hope”. He reiterated that Poland is “ready for a serious and friendly dialogue on the matters that unite us and those that divide”. However, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, a deputy prime minister, emphasised that it was important now for “the announcements regarding the opening of archives, exhumations and dialogue to turn into concrete actions”. “Today, Poland and Ukraine have a common enemy: Russia,” added Kosiniak-Kamysz. “That is where the threat lies. Sowing discord between our nations serves the interests of the Kremlin.” Z satysfakcją i nadzieją przyjmuję słowa i decyzje @ZelenskyyUa, dotyczące relacji między naszymi państwami, które muszą być oparte na wzajemnym szacunku i prawdzie. Jesteśmy gotowi do poważnego i przyjaznego dialogu w sprawach, które nas łączą i tych, które nas dziś dzielą. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 Meanwhile, a senior aide to Polish President Karol Nawrocki – who deepened the crisis by last month stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour – also cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement. “Facing the historical truth is the only way to build further relationships,” Bartosz Grodecki, the head of Nawrocki’s National Security Bureau (BBN), told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “The Ukrainian president’s decision to open the entire archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the events in Volhynia, as well as additional permits for search and exhumation work, is a step in this direction,” he added. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland up 30% this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025, newly reported police data show. The figures come following a number of recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians – who are Poland’s largest immigrant group – as well as ongoing diplomatic tensions between Kyiv and Warsaw. 🔴Coraz więcej ataków na Ukraińców w Polsce – wynika z danych @PolskaPolicja https://t.co/6ZnKFILbdL — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) July 17, 2026 The new data, which were reported by the Rzeczpospolita daily, show that police received 180 reports of hate crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of 2026, which was around 30% higher than in the same period last year and around 35% more than in 2024. If the same trend continues, there would be around 360 such reports by the end of the year, more than the 275 recorded in 2025 and 267 in 2024. However, Rzeczpospolita notes that the figures relate to reported incidents of hate crimes, rather than confirmed cases. On the other hand, experts point out that many such incidents are never even reported to the police. “It is generally assumed that hate crimes are underreported,” Jacek Kucharczyk, head of the Institute of Public Affairs, a think tank, told the newspaper. “Some victims don’t want to report a crime because they’re simply afraid.” Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. While Poland welcomed Ukrainian refugees in 2022, there has been growing negative sentiment towards them recently, indicated in polls and through anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from prominent politicians. In particular, two far-right opposition parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have used anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, while the largest opposition group, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has recently taken a tougher line towards Ukraine. Kucharczyk told Rzeczpospolita that the “toxic atmosphere” around Ukrainians is now spreading from political rhetoric into real-life consequences, as seen in the new police data. He added that Russia also seeks to stoke and exploit such sentiment. An 18-year-old Ukrainian will stand trial in Poland accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tension between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of inscriptions in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which massacred Poles in WWII https://t.co/0w0gVYiGpp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2026 In May, five Polish teenagers were detained in Warsaw over a violent attack on a group of young Ukrainians. The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, blamed the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of right-wing politicians for “encouraging thugs” to carry out these kinds of attacks. Tensions with Ukraine have since ramped up even further, amid a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Volodomyr Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after a Ukrainian nationalist group that led massacres of Poles during World War Two. Earlier this month, two Polish far-right activists were charged over an incident in which they confronted a Ukrainian woman who runs a business that offers assistance to other Ukrainian immigrants. Last week, a man was detained after being recorded hurling xenophobic obscenities at Ukrainian children on a bus in the city of Bielsko-Biała. That latter incident prompted Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, to call on “Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians”. Ukraine’s foreign minister has called on "Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians” after an incident in which a man was filmed shouting xenophobic obscenities at Ukrainian girls on a bus in Poland. The perpetrator has been detained https://t.co/AfGCNqtJbj — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Figures from Poland’s government, which is a coalition ranging from left to centre right, have also condemned recent incidents of hate towards Ukrainians. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called last week’s incident in a bus “disgusting” and warned of the potential “disastrous consequences” of inciting national hatred. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński promised that the state would deal with “any form of aggression”, but also blamed the right-wing opposition for stirring antipathy. However, PiS spokesman Rafał Bochenek accused the government of “cynically exploiting” the incident in Bielsko-Biała “for political purposes”. He said it was, in fact, Tusk and Kierwiński who were “responsible for the brutalisation of public life in Poland”. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, hailed the fact that “the entire political class” in Poland had condemned the incident on the bus and expressed hope that the recent wave of attacks is a “temporary symptom” that “will pass”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Two Polish far-right activists have been charged over an incident in which they confronted a Ukrainian woman who runs a business providing services to immigrants.
