World.title: Russia destroyed 40,000 Armenian roses shipped via Belarus
World.content:
Russia destroys Armenian roses

Officials from Russia‘s agricultural watchdog Rosselkhoznadzor in Smolensk Region discovered a shipment of freshly cut roses from Armenia that was being transported via Belarus.

According to the Belarusian outlet Euroradio, the shipment was deemed illegal because Russia has banned the import of nearly all Armenian goods since the spring.

Armenian roses imported via Belarus / 32.fsvps.gov.ru

Moscow says the import ban was imposed in response to what it described as violations of phytosanitary requirements. However, the restrictions were introduced after Armenia declared EU integration as a foreign policy goal, leading officials in Yerevan and the EU to view the move as politically motivated.

Russia has previously imposed similar trade restrictions on Georgia and Moldova to exert economic pressure amid political disagreements.

According to the accompanying documents, the lorry travelling from Belarus’s Minsk Region to Moscow was carrying non-alcoholic carbonated energy drinks. However, an inspection found 39,200 roses instead.

The flowers were being transported without the required phytosanitary certificates or shipping documents.

Rosselkhoznadzor said some of the boxes still bore labels identifying Armenia as the country of origin.

The roses were destroyed, while the carrier was held administratively liable.

Russia suspends flower imports from Iran over suspected re-exports from Armenia

Shortly after the reports emerged that Armenian roses transported via Belarus had been destroyed, Russia’s agricultural watchdog Rosselkhoznadzor suspended the certification of flowers for export to Russia from Iran, also over suspicions that they had been re-exported from Armenia.

The agency said flower shipments from Iran in 2026 had significantly exceeded the volume recorded during the same period last year.

Rosselkhoznadzor also said that although Iran was listed as the exporting country, the appearance of the flowers and their packaging were identical to products previously supplied from Armenia.

Background

Since early spring 2026, Russia has gradually introduced restrictions on Armenian products.

Initially, the measures targeted Jermuk mineral water, followed by a range of alcoholic beverages.

On 30 May, Russia banned imports from Armenia of tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, herbs and strawberries.

This was followed by a temporary ban imposed by the Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance (Rosselkhoznadzor) on the import of flowers and ornamental plants from Armenia.

Rosselkhoznadzor has also reported problems with imports of certain livestock products, as well as fish and fish products.

Armenia also received a letter from Russia warning of the possible termination of an agreement on supplies of natural gas, petroleum products and rough diamonds.

The restrictions imposed by Russia are significant for Armenia, as the Russian market has been the main destination for Armenian agricultural exports for decades.

The Armenian authorities are currently working, with active support from the European Union, to rapidly open alternative export markets for Armenian products.

World.title: Armenia begins recruiting and training border guards for Azerbaijan border
World.content:
Armenia launches border guard recruitment

The Armenian government plans to gradually transfer responsibility for guarding the entire Armenia-Azerbaijan border from the Defense Ministry to the Border Guard Troops of the National Security Service (NSS).

To make that possible, the agency needs additional personnel. The government therefore plans to expand the NSS by introducing the “I Have the Honor“ programme, which the Defense Ministry already runs successfully.

Under the programme, university students sign a contract to undergo military training while completing their studies. After graduation, they perform their military service at the location and under the conditions specified in the contract.

Under the new proposal, participants will first serve as conscripts in the rank of private in Defense Ministry units. They will then transfer to the NSS as commissioned officers.

“The new mechanism will help strengthen the National Security Service, particularly the Border Guard Troops, by recruiting personnel with higher education,” the explanatory note to the draft says.

Under an intergovernmental agreement signed in 1992, the Russian Federal Security Service’s Border Guard Service has been responsible for guarding Armenia’s borders with Turkey and Iran. In recent years, however, Armenia has steadily moved to place the protection of its borders entirely under its own control. In 2024, Russian border guards withdrew from Zvartnots International Airport and from border areas along the frontier with Azerbaijan. On January 1, 2025, Russian border guards also left the border crossing on the Armenia-Iran frontier. Then, on March 1, Armenia’s National Security Service assumed sole responsibility for guarding the Margara border crossing with Turkey. Since the beginning of 2026, only Armenian border guards have been serving at the Akhurik border crossing on the Armenia-Turkey border.

Deferring military service during university in exchange for serving as an officer

The “I Have the Honor” programme allows students to defer compulsory military service while at university. In return, they commit to serving later as commissioned officers.

“Students attend university free of charge, with the state covering tuition fees in full at the rate set by the university for the relevant programme.”

After graduating from university and completing the required military training, participants receive the rank of lieutenant and begin contract service.

Officers receive their assignments through a lottery system.

Those trained as platoon commanders serve for two years and three months.

Those trained for military medical service serve for four years after graduation, followed by one year of clinical residency.

What other changes does the draft propose?

The legislative package also includes amendments to several laws governing military service, the National Security Service’s Border Guard Troops, and the country’s national security agencies.

In particular, the draft would clearly define the circumstances in which NSS officers may use firearms, special equipment and physical force.

Before using force, officers would have to issue a warning and allow enough time for a person to comply with a lawful order, unless any delay posed an immediate danger. The draft also requires officers to use force proportionately to the level of resistance or threat. They would also have to provide first aid to anyone injured.

If parliament passes the legislative package, border guards will also be able to use video and audio recording devices while carrying out their duties.

The draft would also raise the retirement age for senior NSS officers from 52 to 55.

Armenia launches border guard recruitment

World.title: Georgia’s Asian pivot: What does Tbilisi seek in Central Asia?
World.content:
Georgia’s Asian pivot

A section of Georgia’s Baku–Tbilisi–Kars highway. Photo: Reuters

Since the start of summer 2026, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has met the leaders of all five Central Asian states.

Tbilisi has signed strategic partnership agreements with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The Georgian prime minister has also made his first official visits to Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. In July, Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov paid his first official visit to Tbilisi.

The Georgian government says the renewed engagement is aimed at strengthening the country’s role as a regional transit hub. For the Central Asian states, new trade routes are becoming increasingly important alongside those through Russia and China.

Georgia is offering them access from the Caspian Sea to the Black Sea and onwards to Europe.

The growing ties with Central Asia come against the backdrop of an almost complete freeze in relations between Tbilisi and the West. The European Union has significantly scaled back political contacts with the Georgian government and suspended part of its direct assistance.

According to official EU statements, the measures are a response to what Brussels describes as democratic backsliding in Georgia.

Georgia’s EU accession process has effectively been put on hold until the government changes its political course. The EU’s 2026 report states that no political dialogue took place between the EU and Georgia during the reporting period.

Against this backdrop, the Georgian government describes its foreign policy as multi-vector.

Central Asia has become one of the main pillars of that policy. The key question, however, is what lies behind this shift: an effort to expand Georgia’s economic opportunities, or a political response to deteriorating relations with the West?

Economic data present a mixed picture. Exports to Central Asia have increased, but most of the growth is not driven by goods produced in Georgia. Re-exported vehicles account for the bulk of exports to Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.

Moreover, Central Asia’s interest in Georgia is largely based on access to Western markets. If Tbilisi moves away from the European political and economic space, its value as a transit hub could also diminish.

Kyrgyzstan: Exports driven almost entirely by vehicle re-exports

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze visited Kyrgyzstan on 11 June 2026. According to the Georgian government, it was the first official meeting between the two countries at the highest level.

Kobakhidze held talks with President Sadyr Japarov. Bishkek also hosted the second meeting of the Georgian-Kyrgyz Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov.

The two sides signed a series of agreements covering aviation, veterinary services, education, sport, legal cooperation and the management of state property. They also signed an agreement on the advance exchange of customs information.

Trade was the main economic focus of the talks. However, Georgia’s exports to the region remain heavily dependent on re-exports.

According to Georgia’s statistics office, Geostat, the country exported goods worth $355.2m to Kyrgyzstan between January and May 2026, while imports amounted to just $1.2m. In 2025, exports reached almost $1.5bn.

Data for the first four months of 2026 show that passenger cars accounted for 95.5% of exports. Other goods made up only a small share and included alcoholic drinks, soft drinks, lorries and medicines.

In practice, however, Kyrgyzstan is only nominally one of Georgia’s largest export markets. Georgia does not manufacture the cars it exports. Instead, it acts as an intermediary, purchasing, servicing and re-exporting the vehicles.

Direct investment from Kyrgyzstan also remains limited. It totalled $374,000 in 2025, down from $656,000 in 2024.

The most significant long-term project is the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, which will connect the Chinese city of Kashgar with Andijan in Uzbekistan via Kyrgyzstan.

Tbilisi expects the railway to bring additional freight to the Middle Corridor. The cargo would then travel through other Central Asian states, across the Caspian Sea, and onwards via Azerbaijan and Georgia.

According to Mariam Kvrivishvili, a significant increase in cargo volumes is expected from around 2031. However, different completion dates have been cited for the railway project, while the onward route across the Caspian Sea has yet to be finalised.

Georgia and Kyrgyzstan are also considering launching direct flights. In 2025, Georgia received 21,542 visitors from Kyrgyzstan. The figure remained virtually unchanged in the first quarter of 2026.

Tajikistan: Relations beginning to take institutional shape

Kobakhidze visited Tajikistan on 19-20 June in what was the first official visit by a senior Georgian official.

The prime minister held talks with President Emomali Rahmon and Prime Minister Kokhir Rasulzoda. During the visit, the two sides signed 11 agreements. Previously, only three bilateral agreements had been in force.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Tajik President Emomali Rahmon.

Tbilisi and Dushanbe established an intergovernmental commission on economic cooperation. Agreements were also signed in the fields of air transport, tourism and agriculture.

The two sides identified a broad range of potential areas for cooperation, including trade, investment, transport, energy and mining. Pharmaceuticals, artificial intelligence and digitalisation were also mentioned.

However, no specific projects in these sectors have yet been announced.

Trade with Tajikistan has also been boosted by vehicle re-exports. In 2025, Georgian exports totalled $179.6m, while imports did not reach even $1m. Between January and May 2026, exports fell to $47m.

In 2025, Georgia exported 7,592 passenger cars to Tajikistan worth $162.3m. They accounted for about 90% of total exports.

Other exports included medicines, soft drinks, mineral water and heavy machinery, but their combined share remained small compared with cars.

Direct investment from Tajikistan in Georgia is virtually non-existent. Tourist flows are also limited. In 2025, Georgia recorded 4,704 visits from Tajikistan, fewer than in 2024.

The two sides also plan to launch direct flights between Tbilisi and Dushanbe. However, no date has yet been announced for the start of services.

Tajikistan is a landlocked country with no direct access to the Middle Corridor. Its cargo must pass through other Central Asian states before reaching the Caspian Sea. As a result, linking Tajikistan to Georgia’s transit route requires coordination among several countries.

Kazakhstan: Georgia’s most viable economic and energy partner

Irakli Kobakhidze visited Kazakhstan on 29 June, where he met President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov.

The main political outcome of the visit was a joint statement on strategic partnership. Tokayev also awarded Kobakhidze the first-class Order of Friendship.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

The economic talks covered the Middle Corridor, energy, the port of Anaklia and tourism.

Of the five Central Asian states, Kazakhstan has the most extensive economic ties with Georgia. However, passenger cars also dominate Georgian exports to the country.

In 2025, Georgian exports to Kazakhstan reached $910m. Between January and May 2026, they fell to $218.2m, while imports over the same period amounted to $34.5m.

The main reason for the decline was a drop in vehicle re-exports. In the first five months of 2026, car exports amounted to $163.8m.

Georgia also exports mineral water, soft drinks, poultry meat and frozen fish to Kazakhstan. In return, it imports oil, petroleum products, wheat, cotton and metal ores.

Oil transit is another important area of cooperation. According to Tokayev, Kazakhstan plans to increase oil shipments through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline.

Transporting Kazakh oil through the pipeline reduces the country’s dependence on Russian routes, while generating additional transit revenue for Georgia.

According to a BP report, 49m barrels of oil were transported through the pipeline in the first quarter of 2026, equivalent to about six million tonnes.

The port of Anaklia is also important for Kazakhstan. According to Georgia’s Economy Ministry, the port project was one of the main topics discussed during the meetings in Astana.

Kazakhstan is Central Asia’s wealthiest country in terms of natural resources. It has reserves of oil, uranium, copper, tungsten and other important minerals. Western interest in the country is therefore linked not only to transport routes.

In November 2025, Kazakhstan signed a $1.1bn agreement with a US company to develop a tungsten deposit. The deal illustrates the scale of Western economic interest in Central Asia.

Uzbekistan: Strategic partnership and interest in Georgian ports

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev visited Georgia in July 2026. He and Irakli Kobakhidze signed a declaration on strategic partnership.

The two sides also signed agreements covering the economy, finance, customs, education and healthcare. The documents also addressed agriculture, culture and information technology.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev

Following the visit, Uzbekistan’s investment and transport ministers toured the ports of Anaklia and Poti. They also visited the Poti Free Industrial Zone.

Uzbekistan views Georgia as an important partner and transit hub in the South Caucasus. Its main interest lies in trade routes and access to Black Sea ports.

In 2025, Georgian exports to Uzbekistan totalled $220.2m, while imports reached $89.4m. Between January and May 2026, exports amounted to $64.3m and imports to $25.9m.

Investment remains far more limited. Uzbek direct investment in Georgia totalled just $220,000 in 2025. In the first quarter of 2026, it stood at $276,000.

Over the past six years, Georgia has received about $19m in investment from Uzbekistan. Uzbek businesspeople have mainly shown interest in trade, property and the hotel sector.

The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway is also important for Uzbekistan. The project will provide the country with a direct rail link to China. The route could also be extended towards the Caspian Sea and Georgia.

The visits to Georgian ports were a practical sign of this interest. However, no specific Uzbek investments in the ports of Anaklia or Poti have yet been announced.

Turkmenistan: Gas, oil and access to Black Sea

Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov arrived in Georgia on 17 July, where he held talks with President Mikheil Kavelashvili and Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

The main topics of the talks were the Middle Corridor, TRACECA, port infrastructure and energy cooperation. The two sides also signed agreements covering education, industry and healthcare.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov.

The Turkmen president spoke of the joint use of ports on the Caspian and Black seas.

“Serious negotiations are already under way on the use of port infrastructure. This involves using ports on the Caspian and Black seas on a mutually beneficial basis,” Berdimuhamedov said.

He did not name any specific ports or provide details on the scale of investment or the project’s timeline.

In 2025, Georgian exports to Turkmenistan totalled $63.6m, while imports exceeded $39m. Between January and May 2026, bilateral trade fell to about $38.6m.

Georgia mainly imports oil and petroleum products from Turkmenistan, while exporting passenger cars and meat.

Energy expert Murman Margvelashvili sees short-term potential for refining Turkmen oil in Georgia, particularly at the new oil refinery in Kulevi.

A more long-term project is the Trans-Caspian gas pipeline. It would carry Turkmen gas across the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, before continuing through Georgia and Turkey.

“A more strategic and long-term direction could be a project that has been under discussion for many years: the Trans-Caspian gas pipeline,” Margvelashvili said.

Turkmenistan has some of the world’s largest natural gas reserves. However, the Trans-Caspian pipeline has been discussed for several decades and there is currently no firm timetable for its implementation.

Middle Corridor: shared strategic interest for Georgia and Central Asia

One issue featured consistently in Georgia’s talks with all five Central Asian states: the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, better known as the Middle Corridor.

What is the Middle Corridor? The Middle Corridor, officially known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), is an international trade route linking China and Central Asia with Europe while bypassing Russia. The route runs through China, Kazakhstan, across the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, through Georgia and onwards across the Black Sea to Europe. Why is it important? nterest in the Middle Corridor has grown since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as European and Asian businesses have sought alternatives to transport routes passing through Russia. The corridor offers several advantages: — it reduces dependence on Russian transit routes; — provides an alternative to the Northern Corridor; — can be faster than maritime shipping in some cases; — and connects Central Asian economies with European markets. Georgia’s role Georgia is one of the key countries along the Middle Corridor: — it provides the rail and road links connecting Azerbaijan with the Black Sea; — it is home to the ports of Poti and Batumi; — the planned deep-water port at Anaklia is widely seen as central to expanding the corridor’s capacity. Its main advantage is that it would be able to accommodate large container ships, something Georgia’s existing ports cannot fully support.

The Middle Corridor has gained strategic importance since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Central Asian countries are seeking alternatives to transporting goods through Russia, while Western governments and businesses are increasingly interested in supply chains that are less dependent on both Russia and China.

However, the Middle Corridor still faces a number of challenges:

Limited capacity at ports on the Caspian and Black seas;

Customs procedures that differ from one country to another;

A lack of coordinated tariff policies;

Delays at the junctions between maritime and rail transport;

High transportation costs;

Insufficient infrastructure.

As a result, political declarations alone will not be enough to make the corridor competitive. It will require ports, railways, a digital customs system and a coordinated tariff policy.

Anaklia: A project that could benefit Central Asia

The Georgian government has described the deep-water port of Anaklia as the key infrastructure project of the Middle Corridor.

According to the Ministry of Economy, the first phase of construction is scheduled for completion in 2029. The port will have an annual capacity of at least 600,000 TEU and will be capable of handling Panamax-class vessels.

The marine works are being carried out by the Belgian company Jan De Nul. However, the port operator has yet to be selected, and the project’s final financing model has not yet been determined.

The issue of Anaklia was discussed separately during meetings with the Kazakh and Uzbek delegations. Experts suggest that companies from Central Asia could eventually be considered as operators of the port’s terminals. The Georgian government has not announced any such agreement.

Anaklia’s commercial success will depend on securing guaranteed cargo volumes. For Georgia, therefore, agreements with Central Asian countries are not merely a matter of diplomacy. They also form part of the port’s economic rationale.

Western interest in Central Asia

Central Asia is not only a priority for the Georgian government. The United States, the European Union, China and Russia are all deepening their engagement with the region.

In April 2025, the EU and the five Central Asian states upgraded their relations to a strategic partnership. The bloc also announced a €12 billion Global Gateway investment package covering transport, critical raw materials, energy, water and digital connectivity.

In June 2026, the European Commission launched a new platform to develop transport infrastructure linking Europe with Central Asia via the Black Sea and the South Caucasus. Agreements signed with international financial institutions are expected to mobilise up to €2 billion in investment.

The United States’ primary interest lies in critical minerals. Central Asia is rich in uranium, copper, tungsten, gold and rare earth elements.

The countries of the region are using this growing interest to balance their foreign policies. They continue to cooperate with Russia and China while also seeking access to Western capital and markets.

What does closer cooperation with Central Asia mean for Georgia?

Experts agree that cooperation with Central Asia is important for Georgia. At the same time, the government is presenting these ties as a possible alternative to the country’s traditional Western orientation.

According to economist Rati Tsiklauri, the economic relationship between Georgia and Central Asia appears more substantial in official statements than it does in the actual trade statistics.

“Ultimately, all cooperation with Central Asia comes down to our role as a transit country. Unfortunately, our economy is not large enough to sustain a fully fledged two-way exchange of goods with these countries,” Tsiklauri said.

In Tsiklauri’s view, closer cooperation with Central Asia is a positive development. However, it should not become compensation for Georgia’s deteriorating relationship with the West.

“We should not try to build ties with East and Central Asia only to present them as proof that we no longer need the West because we have China, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan. That simply won’t work,” Tsiklauri said.

Nika Alavidze, Georgia’s former deputy economy minister and co-founder of the public movement Georgia First, focuses on the quality of trade. In his view, vehicle re-exports generate revenue, but they cannot serve as a sustainable model for economic development.

“Re-exports do not create industry. Growing oil exports do not mean energy independence. Higher trade turnover does not amount to a technological breakthrough,” Alavidze wrote on his blog.

He argues that “portraying Asia as an alternative to the West is a dangerous political illusion.”

“The circumstances created by the Russia-Ukraine war have opened a temporary trade window for Georgia, but that is not a strategy—especially when it comes with serious reputational risks,” Alavidze said.

In his view, Georgia’s greatest asset is its integration with the Western system. The country can become a reliable legal, financial and transit platform for Central Asia, but only if it remains connected to European rules and standards.

“What matters to Central Asian markets is Georgia’s geopolitical role, not simply its geographical location. They fully understand that geography alone offers them nothing. By contrast, Georgia’s geopolitical weight allows them to integrate their economic model, culture, legal framework and institutions more smoothly with major Western markets. Asia needs a connection to Europe, just as Europe needs a connection to Asia. If we limit ourselves to serving only as a geographical corridor, we will gain nothing, remain merely a transit route and ultimately be left with little more than environmental or infrastructure-related costs alongside short-term benefits,” Alavidze said.

Economist Elguja Khokrishvili also sees Georgia’s geographical advantage as only a temporary opportunity. In his view, cargo owners will continue to use the Georgian corridor only as long as it remains competitive.

Khokrishvili also notes that the Central Asian countries possess other sources of leverage. Kazakhstan offers partners oil, uranium and a large market. Uzbekistan has gold, copper, uranium and a growing economy. Georgia’s main advantage, by contrast, is its geographical location.

“But geographical advantages quickly lose their value once alternative routes are developed,” Khokrishvili wrote.

Zaza Shengelia, a researcher at EPRC, highlights the financial and institutional support associated with Georgia’s EU candidate status. In his view, partnership with Central Asian countries cannot replace that resource.

“It would be a mistake to suggest that this partnership is an alternative or a substitute for the enormous institutional support that was practically within our grasp thanks to EU candidate status,” Shengelia said.

Taken together, the experts reach a similar conclusion: Central Asia is an important market and transit partner for Georgia. However, the economic value of these relationships depends to a large extent on Georgia’s connection with Europe.

Georgia can serve as Central Asia’s gateway to the West. But to do so, it must itself remain integrated into the West’s economic and legal space.

Otherwise, the country will be left with little more than a favourable geographical location. And a good place on the map is not an economic policy.

Georgia’s Asian pivot

World.title: Bystanders hailed as 'heroes' after stopping attempted murder on CCTV
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains vision and details that may distress some readers.

A man who "doggedly" tried to kill a woman outside a Perth apartment complex in a horrific attack captured on CCTV has been sentenced to 16 years in prison.

Mihael Vrhovsek, 29, was convicted of attempted murder for the attack in Rivervale in 2024.

The Supreme Court jury was shown a graphic video of Vrhovsek confronting the woman, which the ABC has published excerpts of.

Loading...

The 29-year-old grabbed the woman by the throat, lifted her off her feet and carried her, before dropping her limp body to the ground.

A man then intervenes, confronting Vrhovsek, which allowed the woman who was walking her dogs an opportunity to drag the victim away.

She was able to walk on her own, but Vrhovsek — having broken free of the man who had confronted him — ran after her and again began to choke her.

The man who had intervened returned, punching and kicking Vrhovsek in a bid to get him to let go, before the woman walking her dogs was again able to drag the victim away.

'Abusive, menacing and sinister'

In court today, Justice Alain Musikanth said Vrhovsek had used extreme violence, including continuing to strangle the woman once she had lost consciousness.

"Your actions involved deliberate and controlled choices … you were doggedly determined to kill her," he said.

A man intervened to stop the attack. (Supplied: Supreme Court of Western Australia)

Justice Musikanth praised the courage of the bystanders who were "instrumental" in saving the woman's life, describing them as "heroes".

In the days leading up to the attack, Vrhovsek called or texted her more than 230 times using multiple mobile phones, many of which Justice Musikanth said were "abusive, menacing, and sinister".

"I accept she was so affected by the avalanche of abusive communications from you she reported your action to police, saying she was scared you were going to kill her," he said.

CCTV video shows man's 'inexcusable' attack on woman The WA Supreme Court releases disturbing CCTV footage of a man attacking a woman on a Perth street, after a trial in which he was found guilty of her attempted murder.

The defence said Vrhovsek had a “troubled upbringing”, and struggled against his “demons”, which “included self-medication”.

They said his conduct was serious but abhorrent, arguing he is not likely to reoffend, and that he had expressed “visceral” remorse when the CCTV footage of the incident was shown to the court.

But Justice Musikanth said he was unable to find Vrhovsek had any true empathy, or remorse for his victim.

He will become eligible for parole in 2038.

World.title: Court hears complainant's evidence challenged in police officer's rape trial
World.content:
The defence team of a former NSW Police officer, accused of raping a teenage girl almost 28 years ago, has told the court the complainant was relying on phone calls made years later to refresh her memory.

David Robert Blackbourne was serving as a police officer when he allegedly raped the 17-year-old in a town near the NSW-Victoria border in October 1998.

He has been charged with two counts of assault with an act of indecency, two counts of sexual intercourse without consent, and one count of holder of public office misconduct.

Mr Blackbourne was arrested in 2023 and has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

His trial began this week at Sydney's Downing Centre District Court, and today his defence team continued to cross-examine the complainant.

The court has heard that on the morning of October 17, 1998, the girl went to a police station where Mr Blackbourne gave her a police hat to be worn at a year 12 muck-up day.

Defence barrister Matthew Johnston SC asked the complainant whether she walked 4.5 kilometres from her home to the police station on the morning of the alleged rape.

"You gave evidence you were picking up a hat; what were the arrangements?" said Mr Johnston.

"I cannot recall the arrangements," the complainant said.

She later went on to say that despite not remembering the arrangements or the exact date, she would not have walked to the police station if it was not pre-arranged.

The complainant told the court earlier this week that in October 1998, she attended a police station, where David Blackbourne gave her a police hat. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Earlier this week the complainant told the court that shortly after she arrived at the station, Mr Blackbourne took her behind the front counter and sexually assaulted her.

She said he then took her to another room and sexually assaulted her again.

Today Mr Johnston asked the woman whether she said anything when her pants were allegedly pulled down by Mr Blackbourne.

"No," she replied.

"Did you say anything when he pulled his pants down?" Mr Johnston asked.

"No," she said.

Mr Johnston later suggested she was not kissed without consent.

"It definitely happened," she replied.

"I want to suggest to you that the man you believed to be Dave did not have sexual intercourse with you," Mr Johnston said.

"It definitely happened," she said.

Covertly recorded call

Mr Blackbourne's defence team questioned the reliability of the complainant's evidence and whether it was influenced by phone calls made years after the alleged rape.

During a cross-examination of the complainant yesterday, Mr Johnston asked whether the woman was relying on phone calls with her former boss in 2020 to piece together what happened.

She agreed that she was.

David Blackbourne's defence team has questioned the reliability of the complainant's evidence and whether it was influenced by phone calls. (ABC News: Adriane Reardon)

"Do you think you adopted these memories … because you want them to be true?" Mr Johnston said.

"That is not correct at all," she said.

Earlier this week, the complainant told the court that months before the alleged rape, Mr Blackbourne showed her a picture of his young daughter at the police station.

In 2021, during a phone call between the complainant and Mr Blackbourne that was covertly recorded by police as part of an investigation, he told the woman he had two daughters.

During cross-examination, the defence suggested Mr Blackbourne never showed her a picture of his child.

"I disagree," the woman said.

"Can I suggest you made it up after he provided you with information during the phone call?" Mr Johnston said.

"That is incorrect," the woman said.

The trial, presided over by Judge Huw Baker SC, is expected to wrap up on Friday.

World.title: Argument over dog leads to shooting murder and 22 years' jail
World.content:
A man found guilty of a shooting murder that was sparked by an argument over a dog has been jailed for 22 years.

Luke Willcockson will spend at least 16 and a half years behind bars, after a jury found him guilty of fatally shooting Paul Davy through the screen door of a Kendall home on November 22, 2023.

Mr Davy's sister said hearing the sentence being handed down was "bittersweet", but it had restored her faith in "the system".

"No amount of time is going to get back my brother," Dona Davy said.

"I'm elated that it's a lot more than we had envisioned and it's wonderful to see the trial process and the outcome.

"He was my guardian, he was my teacher, my big brother in every sense of the word, the biggest clown anyone would meet, the funniest person, so smart on so many levels and cheeky."

CCTV played to the court showed Luke Willcockson (left) leaving the property shortly after the shooting. (Supplied: The Supreme Court of NSW)

Willcockson, 40, pleaded guilty to two counts of intending to pervert the course of justice and guilty to manslaughter, but not guilty of murder.

He was convicted of murdering Mr Davy by a jury in February.

During the trial, Willcockson said he was unaware his gun was loaded, before "accidentally" firing a single shot into Mr Davy's chest at close range.

He remained expressionless while receiving his sentence.

'A box of ashes'

Mr Davy's mother, Sue Magowan, told the court describing the loss of her son was like "trying to describe the colours a blind person is missing out on".

Paul Davy's niece, Lana Davy-Brandon, mother Sue Magowan and sister Dona Davy welcomed the sentence outside Port Macquarie Court. (ABC News: Marina Trajkovich)

"All we've got left is a box of ashes," she said.

Ms Magowan said she was "pleased" with the sentence.

Disputes over a dog

Court facts show on the day of Mr Davy's murder, Willcockson and friends took a dog from a property in Coolongolook.

It was taken to a home on Batar Creek Road, where Mr Davy arrived a short time later.

An argument erupted at the front door when Mr Davy tried to retrieve the dog.

Paul Davy came to the property to retrieve the dog taken from his friend and former girlfriend's house. (Supplied: The Supreme Court of New South Wales)

CCTV footage played to the court showed him saying it was "a child's dog mate, it's not his".

Willcockson then took a rifle from his bag and approached the door, where Mr Davy was heard to say "you won't do it, you won't shoot me".

Moments later, he was shot in the chest.

Paul Davy's family said his death had significantly affected their mental health and the sentence was "bittersweet." (Supplied: Dona Davy)

In delivering Willcockson's sentence, Acting Justice Ian Harrison said Mr Davy's death was "senseless, unprovoked and tragic" as well as "spontaneous and unplanned."

"Yet another example of total and unqualified stupidity that regularly sees expression in criminal cases in this court," he said.

"The consequences are no less tragic for that."

During sentencing, he noted Willcockson's letter of remorse accepting responsibility for Mr Davy's death, his drug dependency, challenging upbringing and current medical conditions, as well as victim impact statements from Mr Davy's family.

Willcockson will be eligible for parole in November 2040.

World.title: Sovereign citizen question to gun owners shut down by senior officer
World.content:
One of Tasmania's most senior cops sought the contrition of a subordinate after they asked suspected sovereign citizens to prove they were "fit and proper" gun owners.

Documents released through the state's right to information (RTI) system show police asked some Tasmanians to confirm or deny in writing if they aligned with sovereign citizen ideology.

Police then visited some of the Tasmanian firearm licence holders and a "small number" of licences were "temporarily suspended".

The head of Tasmania's police association says, "you don't want to be giving them the heads-up [that] you're attending their address". (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

This prompted an internal review, and Assistant Commissioner Doug Oosterloo to point out an increased risk to officers if they visit the property of a suspected sovereign citizen who believes police may be coming to take their guns.

Tasmania Police Assistant Commissioner Doug Oosterloo questioned the strategy. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

The assistant commissioner's intervention was welcomed by the police association and the Australian Lawyers' Alliance, who warned of potential "authoritarian" overreach if groups of people with shared ideologies are targeted.

At least four letters sent to suspected sovereign citizens

'I do not consent': How pseudolaw supports 'sovcit' ideas "Sovereign citizens" believe Australian laws do not apply to them. That's where pseudolaw comes in.

Sovereign citizen ideology contains a broad swathe of beliefs, but in a 2023 briefing the Australian Federal Police said they traditionally "dissociate from society and refuse to engage with societal requirements like paying tax".

The briefing said "the movement itself is generally claimed to be non-violent", but that some members "can be hostile" and should not be considered non-dangerous.

The RTI documents released contain three letters sent in November last year to existing firearms licence holders and one to a firearms licence applicant from a Firearms Services (FAS) team member.

Assistant Commissioner Oosterloo said the letters may create a dangerous situation for any officers visiting suspected sovereign citizens' properties. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

The four letters were contained within 16 pages of otherwise entirely redacted documents.

The letters said the team was "required to take into account the ability of a licence holder to exercise reasonable and responsible control over a firearm".

"Information available to this office suggests you may align with sovereign citizen ideology", the letters said, and requested a written response to that suggestion.

Once received, the letter said, further consideration would be given to the application for, or retention of, a firearms licence.

In a statement, Tasmania Police confirmed some firearms licence holders were visited, and "a small number of firearms licences were temporarily suspended … where there were credible safety concerns."

"Under the Firearms Act 1996, anyone who holds a firearms licence must be able to satisfy Tasmania Police that they are a 'fit and proper' person, can safely and responsibly control a firearm, and do not pose a risk to themselves or others," they said.

" No licences have been cancelled solely because a person was suspected of holding sovereign citizen views. "

Oosterloo intervened, police changed approach

A few months later, Assistant Commissioner Oosterloo sought a briefing from Firearms Services on "what has occurred … relative to the 'sovereign citizen' letters".

In an email published in the RTI documents, he asked, among others, the following questions:

On what basis were [individuals] identified as 'sovereign citizens'?

What is the specific legislative authority for suspending a firearms licence on the basis of the person being considered a 'sovereign citizen'? and

Did FAS consult or seek advice on issues relating to 'sovereign citizens' before taking action?

In the email, Assistant Commissioner Oosterloo also pointed out the letters may create a dangerous situation for any officers visiting suspected sovereign citizens' properties.

"Police attendance at the address may be perceived to be an action to take their firearms and therefore increases risk to police officers," he said.

He went on to ask for a detailed reflection about what mistakes had been made, what lessons had been learned, and what action was being taken or was needed.

"I would appreciate some honest reflection/contrition if it is conceded there were errors made," he wrote.

Since his intervention, letters have not been sent to suspected sovereign citizens and police have introduced mandatory training "to help officers identify relevant behaviours".

"Each case is now assessed individually, with input from police officers and intelligence analysts, and any action is taken after considering operational risks," police said in a statement.

Changes to process welcomed by officers, lawyers alliance

Police Association President Shane Tilley said it was appropriate the FAS letters program had been shut down, and welcomed the mandatory training.

"When you … write to people with these ideologies you really are setting yourself up to fail, in my view," he said.

" You don't want to be giving them the heads-up [that] you're attending their address or something similar. "

He said police risk assessments had improved in recent years in the wake of the killing of Victorian police officers by suspected sovereign citizen Dezi Freeman and the murder of Tasmanian Police Constable Keith Smith.

Australian Lawyers' Alliance spokesman Greg Barns SC said some sovereign citizens had come to the attention of police in the past, but that did not mean all sovereign citizens were going to use firearms illegally.

"It's got an authoritarian element to it and … I think it's a dangerous practice because it sets a precedent," he said.

Mr Barns said, for example, it would be problematic if police began writing letters to members of protest groups for environmental causes.

World.title: Trump went to war to restrict a nuclear program, now he's backing one
World.content:
At the end of February, the US administration and the Iranian regime were taking part in nuclear talks when Washington walked away from the negotiating table and launched a bombing campaign on Iran with Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

One of the many reasons that was given for US President Donald Trump's decision to go to war was to ensure the Iranian regime stopped enriching nuclear fuel.

But on Wednesday, Mr Trump formally approved a deal with a close ally that analysts warned could open the door for another Middle Eastern power to potentially do exactly that.

The US Secretary of Energy and Saudi Arabia's Minister of Energy signed an accord that allows the kingdom to build nuclear reactors using American technology and to enrich uranium.

"These two agreements lay the legal foundation for a decades-long, multi-billion-dollar partnership that advances several priority economic and strategic objectives, including nuclear non-proliferation," the US Department of Energy said in a statement.

The full details of the civil nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia are yet to be released, but US media has reported American companies will be given a central role in developing the state's new power reactors and other nuclear technology.

US in nuclear deal with Saudis Israeli officials and US politicians from both parties have voiced concern that a civilian nuclear project in Saudi Arabia could be used to eventually develop nuclear weapons.

Westinghouse Electric is set to be one of the biggest winners from the arrangement, which will now go to US Congress for approval.

Saudi officials have long argued the kingdom needed an agreement to develop its nuclear industry and meet energy needs at home.

The accord has been years in the making, with talks spanning both Mr Trump's first administration and that of former president Joe ⁠Biden.

It had been the Biden administration's desire for the agreement to include a loftier outcome, that being Saudi diplomatic recognition of Israel, but that was abandoned after the October 7 Hamas attack.

To get the deal over the line with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman this time, US media is reporting that Mr Trump agreed to terms that may limit international inspectors from carrying out intrusive snap inspections of nuclear sites.

The Saudis may also be allowed to enrich uranium or reprocess plutonium on their soil, a stark contrast to the US deal signed with the United Arab Emirates in 2009 in which the UAE agreed to forgo producing nuclear fuel forever.

"Clearly this is meant to signal Iran that the US is willing to basically allow its allies and partners in the region and the Gulf side to gain a nuclear capability … should it [Iran] choose to try and seek a nuclear weapons capability," said Mona Yacoubian, director and senior adviser of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

The controversial deal will bring the United States closer to the Saudi government at a perilous time in the two sides' relationship.

But analysts warn it has the potential to spark "a nuclear arms race in the Middle East".

A testy time for US and Saudi Arabia

For many years, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was a pariah on the world stage, but since returning to the White House, Mr Trump has worked to bring him back into the fold.

US President Donald Trump welcomes Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman, at the White House in Washington, DC, US, November 18, 2025. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

In May last year, the US president flew to the wealthy Gulf Arab state on one of his first major foreign trips abroad and was personally welcomed by the crown prince after he touched down in Riyadh.

Mr Trump then returned the favour in November when Prince bin Salman visited the White House, personally greeting him on a red carpet outside the historic building and offering a tour of the presidential mansion.

Mr Trump also has a personal connection to the country through his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, a businessman with strong ties to the crown prince who benefited from a billion-dollar investment from a fund led by the Saudi leader four years ago.

But America's war in Iran has tested the US-Saudi relationship at various points in the last few months and brought its leaders close to dispute.

During the conflict, as the Iranian regime has sought to broaden the impact of the war throughout the region, Tehran has targeted US bases in Saudi Arabia and disrupted its energy exports.

Jared Kushner has strong ties to Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

The Saudis have been left grappling with how to contain the fallout of a war they did not ask for, and as they sought reassurances from the Trump administration, they have reportedly come to see the US government as unreliable.

More recently, as the US and Tehran inked a memorandum of understanding and worked towards a peace deal, Saudi Arabia has been moving to strengthen ties with other nations in what appeared to be a sign the kingdom could no longer rely only on the US.

But some of those relationships had the potential to be a thorn in Washington's side.

Nuclear deal will 'deny Russia and China' influence

This deal may go some way to repairing the damage the Iran war wrought on US ties, allowing Washington to keep its key ally on side and within its strategic sphere of interest.

"The agreement could … strengthen US-Saudi ties, and deny Russia and China a strategically important role in the Saudi nuclear program," Robert Einhorn, a former longtime senior State Department official who advised both Republican and Democratic administrations on nonproliferation issues, told the Wall Street Journal.

Analysts argue Russia and China use trade in civil nuclear technology to gain influence in regions of strategic value. (Reuters: Sputnik/Vyacheslav Prokofyev)

For some time now, Chinese and Russian state-owned enterprises have been looking to fill the nuclear supply vacuum left by the exit of Western vendors.

And Saudi Arabia presented a lucrative market.

In 2016, China signed a deal to "invest $US2.43 billion ($3.46 billion) to build a nuclear manufacturing equipment industrial cluster in Saudi Arabia", while Russia had made an offer to build nuclear reactors in the country.

Saudi Arabia had also said if it did not partner with the US, it could partner with China or Russia.

The growing interest from these two superpowers had led analysts from the Carnegie Institute to warn that if Washington "cedes the nuclear supply game at this early stage of development in Saudi Arabia, Moscow or Beijing will become the primary stewards of Riyadh’s nuclear ambitions".

Yet with this new deal, Washington has had the final word, for now.

"If you do a deal the right way, you actually reinforce non-proliferation standards by requiring transparency and by requiring that availability to inspection," said John Erath, senior policy director at the Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation.

"You are setting the high standards for a civilian nuclear power throughout the world.

"If done right this is a very good thing. If done wrong it could lead to proliferation."

There is also a significant commercial interest to the deal, because American firms are going to make a lot of money out of it.

"We are talking about billions of dollars here that would go towards US business," Mr Erath said.

Mr Trump values a good deal, especially if it brings in a lot of money, but his opponents argue that the flow of cash into American coffers may come at a steep cost.

A 'signal' to Iran

Critics of the new pact argue it does not include the typical American "gold standard" that would bar Saudi Arabia from enriching uranium and processing spent atomic fuel — both possible pathways to making material for a warhead.

The administration says the nuclear deal abided by nonproliferation agreements in the US Atomic Energy Act, which were among the world's strongest. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

"They are allowing Saudi Arabia, a belligerent and authoritarian nation, to develop nuclear weapons technologies while starting a war with Iran under the guise of preventing an Iranian nuclear bomb," said Democrat senator Edward Markey.

The deal also reportedly fails to include an "additional protocol" of extra international oversight of relevant nuclear facilities from the IAEA.

"The government of Saudi Arabia has indicated it is unwilling to sign an additional protocol, so without that, how do we meet the high standards of non-proliferation?" Mr Erath asked.

"That is really going to be the question people will ask about this deal when the details become known and what will receive the most scrutiny."

The accord is set to go to US Congress for approval and Mr Erath warned members are going to want to know how nuclear assurances are being provided, if not through an additional protocol.

"The assurances and the transparency measures would be to ensure that Saudi Arabia is not enriching uranium to weapons usable levels," he added.

Analysts said the deal has also raised questions over US foreign policy coherence since Mr Trump's argument for going to war was partly fuelled by Tehran's refusal to give up an enrichment programme.

"I think [the deal] will actually serve as a further provocation from the Iranian side," said Ms Yacoubian.

She suggested the deal could also be a signal that Mr Trump accepts the US war with Tehran will be a long conflict.

"I would give you even a darker potential reading, the US in essence acquiescing to the possibility that Iran may indeed pursue a nuclear weapon, or a nuclear weapons capacity, and then we see the beginning of a nuclear arms race in the Middle East, which would be an extraordinarily dangerous development," she said.

Mr Erath said he believed the timing of the Saudi agreement was tied to the war in Iran and the current discussions around a potential peace deal.

"I suspect that there is some sort of parallel that is going on with the talks with Iran right now," he said.

Mr Erath explained that Saudi Arabia may have insisted on having the "same status" on the issue of nuclear facilities as Iran may get under a potential peace deal with the US.

"I can see the two things proceeding in parallel and equalling each other in that respect," he said.

Regardless of a US-Iran deal, the Saudis have managed to secure a nuclear power deal that goes much further than some expected.

World.title: Driver boasted of drink driving, weeks before killing 12-year-old girl
World.content:
A Victorian judge says a man high on drugs played "Russian roulette" when he caused a crash that killed a 12-year-old girl.

Jordan Kenyon, 30, had a lengthy criminal driving record and was on parole when he smashed into a car with a family-of-four inside.

The crash occurred on January 3, 2024 at Stonehaven, on the outskirts of Geelong.

Crash victim Mia Rossiter died at the scene, while her mother, father and younger sister suffered serious injuries.

The Rossiter family's vehicle was extensively damaged in the 2024 collision near Stonehaven, on the western outskirts of Geelong. (Supplied)

Kenyon has pleaded guilty to numerous driving offences including culpable driving causing death, a crime that carries a maximum 20-year sentence.

During a pre-sentence hearing on Thursday, County Court judge Michael Tinney said Kenyon's decision to get behind the wheel after consuming the drug GHB was like playing "Russian roulette".

"If he wants to play Russian Roulette he should do it in a room on his own, not that I recommend that," the judge said.

"It was a matter of time before he killed someone and the Rossiters had the unlucky ticket. It could have been any one of us."

In 2019, Kenyon was jailed for six years over a wild driving spree around Geelong, during which he drove at up to 170kmh in a stolen Mercedes-Benz.

He was released on parole mid-2023 and was wearing an ankle monitoring bracelet.

Judge Tinney said questions would be asked as to why he wasn't sent back to prison before the fatal crash, given his dangerous behaviour weeks beforehand.

Loading...

Footage from Kenyon's phone, played to the court, showed him steering a car with his legs on the wrong side of the road on December 14, 2023,

He held his phone in one hand and a can of Jack Daniel's (bourbon whiskey) in another.

"I am the best f***ing designated drunk driver in the world!" he said, before taking a swig of his drink.

"Oncoming car, oh yes I love it … Shall we kill these c***s?

" I will crash into a pole tonight. "

The court heard on January 3, 2024, Kenyon took GHB and was doing burnouts in the Geelong area.

With his brother in the passenger seat, he later reached speeds of about 150kmh, before losing control on the Hamilton Highway in Stonehaven.

He crashed into a small Holden Barina, carrying the Rossiter family, who were travelling home after dinner.

Crash victim Mia Rossiter was described by her father Paul as 'bright, loyal and loved her animals'. (Supplied)

Mia Rossiter was killed and her mother Danica, father Paul and 7-year-old sister suffered severe injuries that required ongoing treatment.

Kenyon's brother was also critically injured.

Mia's father Paul, who still requires walking sticks and a moon-boot, paid tribute to his daughter on Thursday.

"Mia was a beautiful, kind caring girl who was looking forward to becoming a teenager," Mr Rossiter said in a victim impact statement.

"Mia was bright, loyal and loved her animals."

Mia Rossiter (centre) and her parents. (GoFundMe)

Mr Rossiter then turned to the killer driver, who looked up from the court dock to meet his gaze.

"You and your stupid actions have taken an amazing young human from this earth," he said.

"I hope hell's a shit place and you rot there when you arrive."

Through tears, Ms Rossiter said the loss of her daughter had taken away happiness in daily life.

"Until you have lost your own flesh and blood, you don't know how this feels," she said.

Defence barrister Luke Barker said his client hadn't learned from his previous jail term and other convictions for driving offences.

"It's a stupid, foolhardy, cavalier, nonsensical decision to have driven that night," he said.

Kenyon, who has been in custody since January 2024, will be sentenced on July 29.

World.title: Elite boarding school review uncovers 'normalised' abuse
World.content:
Readers are advised this article includes details of bullying and violent abuse some may find distressing.

An independent review of an elite private school in regional Victoria has described a culture of "normalised" racism, bullying and abuse.

Ballarat Grammar commissioned Intersection to conduct the review following media reports of student violence in the school's boarding houses and other concerns.

The report identified "genuine strengths" and a "deep sense of community" at Ballarat Grammar, but it also found an erosion of trust in leadership, unclear communication and values, and a belief that the school had grown too quickly.

"The review heard evidence of historical and entrenched harmful practices, including physical punishment and hazing rituals carried out by older students against younger boarders," the report said, noting these behaviours dated back to the 1940s.

" Participants described these practices as having become normalised within a hierarchical peer culture that some perceived to be inadequately supervised. "

Intersection said "it heard both from those who felt let down by the school and from those who felt deeply supported by it".

The review heard from 400 students. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

44 recommendations made

The reviewers spoke with more than 400 students, current and former staff, and parents.

The report makes 44 recommendations, including making houses co-educational, overhauling incident reporting systems, and developing a curriculum covering respectful relationships, bystander responsibility, and consent.

Intersection said incidents of boarding students being whipped by older peers "tested the trust and confidence many parents had placed in the school".

"Parents observed a lack of leadership and transparency and questioned the school's capacity to run a school with the right standards and the right accountability," the report said.

One staff member said staff supervision in the boarding houses was also problematic.

"Unfortunately the culture of boarding is so incredibly toxic," they said.

"A lot of these staff end up in middle management, they don't have the right skill set and then their behaviours and their culture really continues into the day school."

The report included a staff survey in which found 44 per cent of respondents reported that they had experienced "harmful behaviours" from colleagues. Almost half said they had also experienced harmful behaviours from parents.

"Bullying by other staff was the most common behaviour experienced by respondents," the report said.

One employee told Intersection the school had a gender issue in particular, noting Ballarat Grammar "has been at times a hostile place as a female leader".

Ballarat Grammar is an Anglican prep to Year 12 school. (ABC News: Charlotte King)

'Significant remedial action'

In April 2025 the Victorian Registration and Qualifications Authority (VRQA) reviewed Ballarat Grammar's compliance with minimum standards for boarding operations and placed six interim conditions on the school's registration.

These included a prohibition on the enrolment of new boarders, strengthened governance and oversight, and mandated progress reports.

Ballarat Grammar said it commissioned the independent review in May 2025.

Intersection found the school undertook "significant remedial action", including a full boarding review that resulted in 32 recommendations, 31 of which were adopted.

These changes included restructured supervising arrangements, introduction of whistleblower and anonymous reporting systems, revised codes of conduct, additional training and physical modifications to boarding facilities.

Strapping culture

But one student told the reviewers not much had changed since the school started making changes.

"I find the boarding side of the school, especially boys, to be absolutely nasty and that whole community to be absolutely brainwashed by each other's egos," the student said.

The student said some peers felt that "strapping should come back, it's totally harmless" and that "people just need to harden up and not complain, take the straps — how else will there be a hierarchy in the house?"

"It makes me sick to my stomach," the student said.

Some students also reported discrimination based on race, sexuality, disability and gender, including directly from teachers.

"One time a white girl asked the teacher for a charger, she said 'yes' then I asked a few minutes later and she said 'no [I know] what you people do, I'm going to give it to you and never get it back,'" one student told Intersection.

Ballarat Grammar commissioned the review following media reporting of incidents of peer-to-peer violence. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

Another student described a culture of "ableism" in which special provisions for students with disabilities were seen as "an excuse and a nuisance".

The report also noted some employees described the support system for neurodiverse students "as stretched".

Intersection found Ballarat Grammar's junior school fared better as a result of "supportive teachers, good friendships, play spaces, fun activities, camps, and the diversity of opportunities available".

But some acknowledged that those values were not always evident in the playground, with a pupil noting: "You are more likely to get told off for going to the bathroom without asking than if you call another student a f***ing gay piece of shit."

There were also reports of racism in the junior school that were "dismissed … as a joke" by teachers.

The review also found a "longstanding pattern of inconsistent or inadequate institutional response" at Ballarat Grammar that has "functioned across year levels as a signal to students that harmful behaviour carries limited consequences".

Ballarat Grammar apologises

In a video statement released by the school, headmaster Adam Heath said the Intersection review had collated honest and at times difficult accounts of more than 850 members of the school community.

Adam Heath says the school plans to adopt all 44 recommendations from the review. (Supplied: Adam Heath)

"The school board has carefully reviewed Intersection's report and accepts in principle all of the 44 recommendations, which will be adopted in careful consultation with our community," Mr Heath said.

"It represents a defining moment for our school … we acknowledge this report contains findings which some of you may find confronting or distressing.

"Some members of our community have felt hurt and excluded during their time at our school, and for that we unreservedly apologise.

"We now have an opportunity to make our school a better place for everyone."

The school did not make anyone available for interview in relation to the independent review.

World.title: Breaking: Insect repellent release leaves 11 staff sick at major SA hospital
World.content:
Eleven staff at a South Australian hospital have become unwell and a dozen emergency hospital beds have been closed, after the accidental release of an "outdoor insect repellent" inside the facility.

The incident occurred at Flinders Medical Centre, one of Adelaide's largest public hospitals, around 2am.

Authorities say no patients have become unwell, with 11 staff reporting "serious to minor" symptoms after the mosquito repellent was accidentally released.

One staff member is in a serious but stable condition and has been admitted to hospital, with two being treated in the emergency department.

SA Health said the substance was a mosquito repellent, and that ambulances were being redirected to balance the load "across the system".

Chief executive Robyn Lawrence said no patients had become sick, and that the staff who were unwell had suffered "predominantly respiratory symptoms", including difficulty breathing.

"My understanding is that it's an outdoor mosquito fogger-type repellent, like a spray, as I understand it," Dr Lawrence said.

"Staff, as they do, were going through somebody's belongings to make sure there was nothing in there that was a safety risk to the patient when they were left alone.

"In doing that, the lid was knocked off the repellent and it released itself."

Dr Lawrence said the Metropolitan Fire Service had attended the scene and had been on site for several hours.

"They've been assisting the staff and ensuring that the area has been cleaned appropriately and trying to determine why there are ongoing symptoms occurring in the staff," she said.

"They're doing a range of atmospheric tests of the air but also all of the surfaces and the equipment in those zones to make sure nothing's left contaminated."

Dr Lawrence described what had occurred as an "unfortunate accident" and said there was currently no timeline for when it would be safe to reopen beds.

World.title: ASX trims gains as jobs data stokes rate hike bets; miners, James Hardie rise
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX trims gains as jobs data stokes rate hike bets; miners, James Hardie rise Staff writers Updated July 23, 2026 — 5:44pm ,first published July 23, 2026 — 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket pared most of its strong early gains after the nation’s latest job market figures came in stronger than expected, keeping the chances of another interest rate rise next month on the table. The S&P/ASX 200 finished 16 points, or 0.2 per cent, higher at 8439, having climbed as much as 1.2 per cent earlier in the day. Mining and energy stocks paced the muted gains, while six of the ASX’s 11 sectors finished in the red. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.03¢ in the late afternoon. Employment surged in June, stoking bets on another interest-rate hike by the Reserve Bank. Louie Douvis The Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday morning reported that employment surged in June, extending the previous month’s gains, underscoring the ongoing strength in the nation’s labour market and stoking bets on another interest rate increase by the Reserve Bank. The Aussie dollar and bond yields climbed after the data showed the economy added 76,300 jobs, more than five times estimates, after an upwardly revised 44,000 gain in May. The jobless rate held at 4.4 per cent, as forecast, reflecting a rise in the participation rate. However, the underemployment rate also lifted, climbing to 6.5 per cent.



Related Article Jobs Rate hike fear grows as nation adds 76,000 jobs in June RBA Governor Michele Bullock said at her June press conference that the central bank is trying to slow the economy to help pull down inflation. Last month’s hiring results suggest activity may be stronger than the bank had anticipated. The bank’s next rate decision is scheduled for August 11. “The jobs report was marginally stronger than we expected,” AMP Economist My Bui said. “We think [the RBA] will hike in August with inflation too far from target band” and amid upside risks like a second-round fuel impact, she said. Higher interest rates tend to slow economies and undercut stock prices as borrowing gets more expensive for businesses and consumers, hitting corporate profits. In major corporate news, Macquarie Group said its chief executive, Shemara Wikramanayake, is retiring after eight years in the job, to be replaced by the head of its banking arm, Greg Ward.



Related Article Opinion

Executive shake-up Eat what you kill: Macquarie’s first-ever female CEO is a tough act to follow Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The investment banking giant said Wikramanayake, who is 64 and has been chief executive since late 2018, will retire from November this year. Ward, 58, is a Macquarie veteran who has run the group’s banking and financial services arm, which houses its rapidly growing retail bank, since 2013. He joined Macquarie in 1996 and previously served as chief financial officer for 14 years. The company’s shares fell 0.5 per cent on the news. Meanwhile, the big four banks all advanced, with CBA up 0.4 per cent, Westpac up 0.8 per cent, National Australia Bank up 1.4 per cent and ANZ Bank up 0.6 per cent. Origin Energy, the largest Australian power company, added 0.8 per cent, recouping some of its 1.9 per cent fall from Wednesday. It confirmed shortly before the market closed that a hacker had gained access to customers’ private information, including names, addresses and partial credit card and bank account numbers. The company said on Thursday it was working to determine how many customers had been affected by the cybersecurity breach.



James Hardie jumped 6.1 per cent after the building materials maker – which makes most of its earnings in the US – said its June quarter sales beat its own forecasts, coming in at between $US1.45 billion ($2.1 billion) and $US1.48 billion, thanks to stronger-than-expected sales of its home sidings. Mining giants BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue extended their strong run from Wednesday, up 1.5 per cent, 0.5 per cent and 1 per cent, respectively, even as iron ore fell as the continued US-Iran hostilities clouds the demand outlook. The gold miners continued to rise as the precious metal extended its gains, supported by dip-buyers who scooped it up after prices had drifted lower in recent weeks on concerns that rising inflation will prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates. Bullion was trading around $US4130 an ounce, after rising 3 per cent over the previous two days as dip-buying supported prices. This came as the US and Iran signalled that they aren’t ready to return to the negotiating table after escalating attacks. Gold miners Northern Star Resources and Evolution Mining were both up 1.9 per cent. Energy stocks had another strong session as oil prices continued to climb, hitting a six-week high. Brent crude spiked in post-settlement trading overnight, rising near $US95 a barrel after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels said they had struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea. That’s up from less than $US72 early this month, which is roughly where it was before the war. Local oil and gas giant Woodside rose 0.5 per cent, while coal producers Yancoal and Whitehaven were up 1.5 per cent and 2.2 per cent, respectively. Santos finished flat after it cut its production guidance for the second quarter due to challenges in the ramp-up of its Barossa and Pikka projects, and the timing of cargo receipts.



Related Article Opinion

AI Money to burn? Big Tech’s AI splurge is blowing out Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Tech stocks slumped after Google parent Alphabet and Elon Musk’s Tesla reported earnings early in the day that raised concerns about their cash-burn as they ramp up their AI investments. Software makers Xero and WiseTech plunged 5 per cent and 7 per cent, respectively, while Technology One fell 3.7 per cent and family tracking app Life 360 lost 5.5 per cent. The ASX’s meagre gain came as US sharemarket futures trended down, suggesting a 0.2 per cent drop in the S&P 500 when Wall Street opens for trade. US indexes were drifting during their Wednesday session, with the S&P 500 slipping 0.1 per cent, coming off its best day in three weeks, after swinging between modest losses and gains for much of the day. The Dow Jones closed flat and the Nasdaq composite lost 0.6 per cent. Tesla released its results after the closing bell, reporting negative free cash flow in the second quarter for the first time in more than two years as the Elon Musk-led EV maker accelerated spending on AI infrastructure, battery capacity, robotaxis and next-generation manufacturing. Its shares were down 1.3 per cent in extended trading. Google parent Alphabet topped Wall Street estimates for its second-quarter revenue, buoyed by strong demand for its cloud computing services from enterprises worldwide.



Revenue at Google Cloud rose 82 per cent to $US24.8 billion during the quarter ended in June, accelerating from the 63 per cent jump reported in the preceding three months. Analysts on average expected a 64 per cent increase, according to data compiled by LSEG. However, its stock also declined in extended trading amid concerns about the scale of its AI spending. The majority of stocks in the S&P 500 rose overnight after more companies reported strong profits. Philip Morris International rose 3.3 per cent after the seller of Marlboro cigarettes reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than expected. Its shipments of smoke-free products rose 7.5 per cent. AT&T climbed 3.5 per cent after reporting a stronger profit than analysts expected. CEO John Stankey said the telecom is accelerating plans to send roughly $US10 billion to shareholders this year through share buybacks. Super Micro Computer soared 20 per cent after the seller of AI servers said it expects to report stronger profit margins for the latest quarter than it had earlier forecast. It, though, also said that revenue will likely come in at the low end of its forecasted range. In other international markets, indexes climbed in Europe following a mixed session in Asia. London’s FTSE 100 rose 1.2 per cent, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves.



with AP, Reuters, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
