World.title: Fair Work Court to assist Australian workers with employment, underpayment issues
World.content:
PoliticsFederalIndustrial relations Fair Work Court to assist Australian workers with employment, underpayment issues Natassia Chrysanthos Updated July 23, 2026 — 5:36pm ,first published 2:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian workers will be able to escalate their employment issues and underpayment claims to a new specialist federal court, under a Labor pledge that delivers on a long-term demand of the union movement while inviting another battle with business. The party also agreed to back compulsory superannuation for teenagers in its platform, regardless of how many hours they work, in a move that will encourage the parliamentary party to change its policy on contributions for young Australians. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has opened the 50th Australian Labor Party Conference with a promise to create a new workers’ court. Dominic Lorrimer Both were signs of the pro-worker focus that heralded the opening of Labor’s 50th national conference – the forum where tank-and-file party members, MPs and unions come together to decide on the next three years of party policy – as the party emphasised it would focus on hip-pocket issues to combat populist politics. But Labor’s announcement of a new industrial relations court drew new battle-lines with business groups, just two months after its contentious budget put many businesses offside. Employers warned against complicating a workplace system already laden with red tape.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said consultations would soon begin on a new Fair Work Court – reinstating a special workers’ court for the first time in almost 30 years – as he gave a speech at the conference’s opening session. Related Article Live

Political leadership Labor National Conference as it happened: PM announces Fair Work Court, expands health student prac support in address to party’s 50th National Conference in Adelaide Former prime minister John Howard abolished the specialist industrial relations court in 1997 and moved its jurisdiction to the Federal Court as part of an industrial relations overhaul that sought to curb union influence. Australian Council of Trade Unions president Sally McManus said the unions had been calling for a national employment court since the last one was abolished. It would become easier, faster and cheaper for workers to recover unpaid wages, she said. “Too many employers can drag out court cases and grind workers into the dust while making them wait to get a fair hearing,” she said. “Justice delayed is justice denied. If your boss owes you money, you should not have to wait one or even two years to get it back.”



The Albanese government said some workers and small businesses were spending more than two years fighting for resolutions that should be simple. “The new federal Fair Work Court will provide a specialist forum for resolving workplace relations disputes that works seamlessly with the Fair Work Commission,” a statement said. “Specialist judges with workplace relations expertise would sit on the court, with the aim of supporting faster, simpler and more accessible dispute resolution.” However, Australian Industry Group chief executive Innes Willox said the federal industrial court would merely put “a Band-aid on a fundamentally broken ... system” and would most likely be stacked with appointees from union backgrounds. “Given unions have pushed for this development, there will be unsurprising scepticism about the prospect of it operating in an entirely balanced manner,” Willox said.



Related Article Political leadership We feel your pain: PM sets election battle lines with One Nation, pledges cost of living relief Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar warned it would become a “lawyer’s picnic” at business’ expense. “A specialist industrial court also opens the door for the adoption of legal doctrines to be made by an isolated jurisdiction detached from broader principles of commercial, administrative, constitutional and statutory law,” he said. Business Council chief executive Bran Black said a new court was no substitute for fixing the complexity of workplace laws under Labor. “Instead of adding another layer of red tape, we need to make the system simpler to understand for both employees and employers,” he said.



Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership The movement behind Andy Burnham has a message for Labor in Australia “For a small business, a case that costs more than its worth is not only unfair, it can be the difference between staying open or closing its doors.” In another looming change for employers, superannuation could soon become compulsory for teenagers, if the party moves quickly to act on the policy embedded in its new platform. “All workers, including those under 18 and regardless of how they are engaged, can accumulate superannuation on every dollar earned,” the platform says. Teen workers are now only entitled to superannuation if they work more than 30 hours a week. The Greens last month tried to introduce laws to that effect in parliament – a move that Labor voted against.



The government made another pitch to young Australians earlier on Thursday, with a promise to expand $340 weekly payments to a large group of health and medical students while they undertook practical work placements to earn a qualification. Albanese told the conference that the government was dealing with rising angst across the globe by helping people with the cost of living. “I understand that, for many Australians right now, looking to the future runs second to the immediate pressures they are under,” he said. “The last decade has inflicted one global shock after another, and people have been given every reason to feel like the economy is simply not working for them. That goes deeper than sentiment, it’s a reality people are up against.That is why our focus remains squarely on helping with the cost of living, on the practical measures that matter to people and make a positive difference to their lives.” With Mike Foley, Brittany Busch Go deeper on Labor’s national conference

World.title: Save our town: Lancelin residents take coastal erosion fight to city centre
World.content:
NationalWAVanishing coast Save our town: Lancelin residents take coastal erosion fight to city centre Indigo Lemay-Conway Updated July 23, 2026 — 5:23pm ,first published July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dozens of Lancelin residents poured into Forrest Place on Thursday morning, armed with signs and banners with one message: “save our town”. Almost 100 residents aged seven to 80 chanted “no surrender, no retreat” as they peacefully protested in Perth city to try and raise awareness of their coastal erosion fight. Lancelin locals jumped on a bus on Thursday morning to take part in the Lancelin Rescue Ride. Indigo Lemay-Conway “A proposed retreat is not an option, Lancelin matters, it’s a beautiful town, these kids live there, people work there, we’ve got nowhere else to go,” Lancelin resident and protester Kirsty Harding said. Over the past 12 months, approximately 50 metres of dune has eroded away, leaving less than 10 metres between the ocean and local homes and businesses.



So locals took it upon themselves to take part in the Lancelin Rescue Ride to bring their message directly to government officials. “There’s been an evolving, serious, and rapidly progressing erosion situation in the town of Lancelin, which has reached crisis point,” Harding said. Loading “There’s now a very small section of sand dune holding back the ocean from one property currently, but also that sand dune is acting as a dam wall, really, to the entire town, which has a lot of low-lying land below sea level. “So there’s a lot of homes and businesses and people’s livelihoods at stake. And despite this situation being known about, and having been progressing over some time, the state and local governments have not acted effectively or intervened effectively, and we’re now at a crisis point.”



Now Harding and other residents say they are at breaking point and are ready to bring their message straight to government officials. “Where’s [Roger] Cook, where’s Basil Zempilas, where’s [John] Carey, there’s no one here. They were all invited by many of us, but no one wants to listen to us,” one local shouted at the protest. Lancelin Rescue Ride organiser Michael Cardy said Carey – who visited the town earlier this month – apologised he couldn’t make the meeting at 11am but has organised a meeting with a group of representatives later this afternoon. Cardy said the group contains Lancelin residents as well as engineers who will bring ideas to the table that could help resolve the erosion issue. Carey told WAtoday on Wednesday that the meeting would help to continue support for the struggling community.



“I recently visited Lancelin because I wanted to see the coastal erosion issue firsthand and meet with those directly impacted,” he said. Related Article Vanishing coast Coastal WA tourism town’s erosion emergency deepens as landmark washes away “[Thursday’s] meeting is a further opportunity to hear from members of the Lancelin community as we continue to support the Shire of Gingin on interim and longer-term responses.” Lancelin Sand Hotel owner Glen Trebilcock told the crowd gathered at Forrest Place that he has been working on a solution to the erosion problem for the past 18 months. “It’s very, very unfortunate that it happened bang smack in front of our property and the caravan park,” he said.



“The lowest it got about three or four weeks ago was 1.5 metres and if that breaches it’ll go straight through the caravan park, straight through the north of Lancelin throughout the rest of the town. This has never just been a pub problem, it’s a town problem and for some particular reason we just all seem to be ignoring it.” Gingin shire president Linda Balcombe told 9 News Perth in June that the local council was advocating for state government support. Lancelin Sand Hotel owner Glen Trebilcock told the crowd gathered at Forrest Place that he has been working on a solution to the erosion problem for the past 18 months. Indigo Lemay-Conway “All we want are the ministers to come here, stand in this spot, get sandblasted like I am today and see the damage that is happening, and we need help,” she said. Locals have also created a GoFundMe page to raise money to build a seawall. The goal is to reach $150,000 with $97,565 in donations so far.



Harding said the town of Lancelin is now calling for the state government to step in and find a broader solution to the problem. “Lancelin has been ignored on this for a long time to get to this critical point, and we were desperate to be heard for fear that our town would be inundated, and properties and businesses washed away by the ocean,” she said. Signs at the Lancelin Rescue Ride protest on Thursday. Indigo Lemay-Conway “We’d like [government officials] to, in a timely manner, given the urgency of the situation, use their expertise and their resources to devise a long-term engineered solution to this erosion crisis that protects the town, protects the people, their properties, and their livelihoods and their businesses,” she said. At a press conference on Thursday, former environment minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said she was hopeful that Carey would be able to help the Lancelin community.



“I know that we have made a number of investments in supporting some of those erosion issues,” she said. “My understanding is that the minister will meet with that community today when they’re in town, and that he is continuing to work closely with the shire on immediate solutions, but also more long-term solutions.” Greens climate change spokesperson Sophie McNeill said the coastal erosion in Lancelin had reached crisis point. “Unfortunately, coastal erosion like what we are seeing in Lancelin is exactly what climate scientists have been warning of for years,” she said. “Over the last decade the [state] government has failed to take any meaningful action to mitigate climate change and now communities like Lancelin are being forced to adapt to survive.”



WA Nationals leader Shane Love also called on the state government to “immediately commence a detailed coastal study and develop a long-term plan to protect Lancelin from coastal erosion.″ “What we need now is the immediate commencement of a comprehensive coastal study and the development of a long-term plan to safeguard Lancelin’s future,” he said.

World.title: The Odyssey
World.content:
Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey was always going to inspire – and enrage – fans. That’s what you get when you take Homer’s words and make them into a blockbuster in Trump times.

Samantha Selinger-Morris

World.title: ‘Makes me sick to my stomach’: Students speak out about strapping scandal
World.content:
NationalVictoriaPrivate schools ‘Makes me sick to my stomach’: Students speak out about strapping scandal Caroline Schelle July 23, 2026 — 5:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Boarders at a prestigious regional school at the centre of a “strapping” scandal were pressured to keep quiet about the claims, an independent investigation has found. Ballarat Grammar last year expelled two senior boarders over allegations that junior students – some as young as year 7 – were assaulted as part of a hazing culture going back decades that included beatings with straps. Ballarat Grammar School. Joe Armao On Thursday, the school released a report by workplace cultural firm Intersection, after they questioned students, staff and parents about the school’s culture and examined the boarding houses where “strapping” happened. The school also said at least five staff members left in the wake of the scandal, although it would not confirm the circumstances of their exit.



Current and former students told the report’s authors that there was an unwritten rule for boarders: “What happens in boarding, stays in boarding.” This was reinforced by peer pressure and speaking up was considered disloyalty, with students who did raise concerns being labelled a “snitch”, the report found. Those students risked social exclusion or retaliation, and parents said children were reluctant to share experiences because it was normalised. This culture of silence limited information to day school staff, parents, some boarding staff and the school’s leadership, while reinforcing the internal cohesion of the boarding house. “It reinforced the internal cohesion of the boarding house by positioning loyalty to the group above individual wellbeing or external accountability,” the report found.



Related Article Education ‘It was a very brutal five years’: A private school scandal decades in the making Students who took part in the review said there was a judgmental atmosphere at the school, with a sharp divide between those who were boarders and day students. Many felt they were unable to raise concerns about bullying or strapping to their teachers. “I find the boarding side of the school, especially boys, to be absolutely nasty and that whole community to be absolutely brainwashed by each other’s egos,” one day student told the authors of the report. “Naming the day students ‘Scrags’ ... the way the girl boarders say people who snitch on child abuse are ‘snitches’ and ‘strapping should come back, it’s totally harmless’, and ‘people just need to harden up and not complain, take the straps, how else will there be a hierarchy in the House’... it makes me sick to my stomach.” Others revealed they experienced sexism and racism from not just students, but teachers.



“[A male teacher] said women are often just better in the kitchen instead of the classroom as they are better at following recipes than learning complex thinking,” one child explained. “The boys laughed and thought it was hilarious, but it truly hurt.” That student told other teachers, but their complaint was never followed up on, and they were not offered support following the incident. Another said a female teacher told girls their dresses were too short, and it was “unfair to the male teachers at the school” because it put them in an uncomfortable position and there was “no control over what they might do”.



Ballarat Grammar principal Adam Heath. Ballarat Grammar. “I also think lining all of the girls in a year level up and walking past, crouching looking at their dress lengths is objectifying them, and when put in these situations I felt overwhelmingly uncomfortable,” the student said. The report also noted that standards of behaviour were not applied consistently and communication was uneven. “Trust in leadership has been eroded, particularly since the boarding incidents became public,” the authors found. Intersection carried out 126 one-on-one interviews and focus groups attended by 107 students. Its investigators also received 198 written submissions, 299 student survey responses and 146 staff responses, and carried out 32 follow-up meetings.



Ballarat Grammar was barred from accepting new boarders in October last year, on the orders of the Victorian Registration and Qualifications Authority. But the body lifted the prohibition for this school year and put interim conditions in place. The school ordered the independent probe after The Age revealed last year that senior students allegedly abused younger pupils in the Dart House boarding facility. Victoria Police were also called in over claims junior students – some as young as 12 – had been assaulted by older students. Four former students were later formally cautioned. The school installed CCTV cameras in its residential areas and hired overnight private security guards to protect the younger children as they sleep. However, students referred to these guards as “night crawlers”, and some described them as strangers who they did not know well enough to approach.



Related Article Exclusive

Private schools Private school boys accused of ‘punishing’ classmates with straps The report made 44 recommendations that were accepted that included the restructure of boarding houses by age band to reduce the power differential, addressing gender dynamics in boarding, and for the school to “reset the parent-school relationship as an educational partnership, not a service-provider arrangement”. Principal Adam Heath said they were committed to the recommendations, and were working tirelessly to nurture safety, wellbeing and dignity. He also apologised for some findings he acknowledged were confronting for members of the school’s community. “We are deeply sorry that some of our current and former students, staff and families have, at times, felt hurt or unsupported.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Most wanted man won’t be extradited from Greece over fatal Sydney stabbing: reports
World.content:
A court in Greece has ruled out extraditing James Dalamangas, one of the nation’s most wanted men, over an alleged stabbing murder in a Sydney nightclub three decades ago. Dalamangas – wanted over the 1999 death of Sydney man George Giannopoulos – was arrested at a farm property in Greece last month on an Interpol red notice after more than 27 years on the run. James Dalamangas is led into a police van by Greek authorities. Flamis Greece Dalamangas, now 56, allegedly stabbed Giannopoulos in the stomach and neck at the Pariziana nightclub in Belmore, while Giannopoulos was attempting to break up a fight at the venue in Sydney’s south-west. An arrest warrant for Dalamangas was issued one day after Giannopoulos’ death, but Dalamangas was never found.



He allegedly fled the country and became one of the nation’s most wanted men, with his face splashed across Interpol websites and at press conferences by both NSW and the Australian Federal Police. After nine hours of deliberations, a Greek court has ruled that James Dalamangas will not be extradited to Australia to face charges. Nine Australian detectives suspected he moved to Greece shortly after the alleged stabbing, and went by many different names as he found work as a farmer. James Dalamangas leaving a Sydney court before the 1999 stabbing. Nine News His arrest in June triggered a request from Australian authorities to extradite Dalamangas back to Sydney to face the murder charge.



George Giannopoulos, who died after he was stabbed in Belmore in 1999. NSW Police But the Patras Council of Appeals on Wednesday ruled Greece’s 25-year statute of limitations had passed and Dalamangas could not be extradited, according to local media. “The decision was made because the offence is statute-barred in Greece. Our arguments were accepted, particularly the fact that the offence had become time-barred under Greek law,” one media outlet quoted Dalamangas’ lawyer, Giannis Apostolopoulos, as saying. “Under both our country’s criminal procedure and the Greece–Australia treaty, if the offence has become time-barred in either country, that constitutes a mandatory ground for refusing extradition.” Australian authorities pushed for the extradition, reportedly citing Australian laws in which murder carries no statute of limitations.



The NSW Police State Crime Command, which has taken charge of the extradition request, was still attempting to contact its Greek and overseas law enforcement partners on Thursday afternoon (AEST), following the ruling. It will consider its further options after reviewing the decision.



The Australian Federal Police have also been contacted for comment. The Greek court had deliberated for nine hours to reach their decision, local media reported. Giannopoulos’ sister Toula said her family felt “let down” by the court decision, but vowed she was “not giving up” on the bid to extradite Dalamangas. “We’re looking at other avenues, legal avenues, because this is not a fair decision,” Toula told Nine News on Thursday. “I still have hope, not losing hope yet … that was not a fair decision yesterday, in a court that we didn’t even know it was happening.”



Greek media outlet Tempo24 reported that Dalamangas lived under the name Antonis Tzimas for 18 years in the rural village of Alsos. Authorities believe he purchased property in the village and was known as a farmer who lived a quiet life with his partner. Dalamangas’ identity was revealed after he reportedly shared false information during a police check and eventually confessed that he was wanted in Australia. A crossbow and more than a dozen phones were seized in a raid of James Dalamangas’ home. Tempo24 via Hellenic Police Police raided Dalamangas’ home, allegedly finding a crossbow, three knives, 13 mobile phones, a computer and three USB sticks. Australian police had offered $200,000 for information leading to Dalamangas’ capture in January 2024, as the 25-year deadline approached in April that year. World.title: ‘I want to kill her’: Jail for horrific strangling of woman on a Perth street caught on CCTV
World.content:
NationalWACourts ‘I want to kill her’: Jail for horrific strangling of woman on a Perth street caught on CCTV Rebecca Peppiatt July 23, 2026 — 5:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains violent footage that some readers may find distressing. A FIFO worker who carried out months of stalking, abuse and harassment towards a woman in Perth has been jailed for attempting to kill her in a horrific assault captured by nearby CCTV cameras. Mihael Vrhovsek, 29, repeatedly strangled a woman who was known to him in February 2024 before passersby intervened and stopped him, saving her life. Loading Vrhovsek mounted a campaign of abuse at the woman for five months that included changing his number 18 times after she blocked each one so he could repeatedly call and abuse her.



During a Supreme Court trial in March this year, prosecutors told the jury Vrhovsek tried to contact the woman 234 times via text messages and phone calls over a three-day period in the lead up to the incident that culminated with him “lying in wait” in his car outside her apartment block for eight hours. Mihael Vrhovsek, 29, was found guilty of trying to kill a woman. Facebook “Killed yourself already?“, “This is your last warning”, “You’re a spectacular piece of s---”, “Go f--- yourself, politely” and “I would have killed myself already but the hatred towards you is keeping me alive” were just some of the text messages he sent her. By January 2024, the victim said the communication “got darker” with one email reading, “thanks for another sleepless night, I much prefer pretending you are dead in that apartment”. He also texted her “good night attention seeking s---” and later “you’re dead to me”. By the end of February, the woman said she felt too scared to return to her apartment after she was told by a neighbour that Vrhovsek had parked in her car space and slept in his car “like a predatory animal waiting for me”.



The woman told the jury she was “freaked out”, had called the police and explained he was in her basement. “The officer went off and made some calls or something and when he came back he said, it’s a private property, we’ve got no access. He said, ‘We can’t help you’. Mihael Vrhovsek waited outside his victim’s apartment before launching a violent attack on her which only came to an end when bystanders stepped in. Picture: WA Courts WA Courts “I walked out to my car and I just broke down. “I thought, what the f--- do I do? No one is helping.”



Hours later she went back to the apartment briefly to grab a change of clothing with a friend, but when she ran into Vrhovsek she immediately called triple-zero. “I saw him walk out of the doors at me - he was looking down, targeted, coming at me,” she told the jury. Mihael Vrhovsek waited outside his victim’s apartment before launching a violent attack on her which only came to an end when bystanders stepped in. Picture: WA Courts WA Courts In the triple-zero call, the woman can heard yelling “get the f--- away from me, get the f--- away from me” before the call goes quiet. During Vrhovsek’s sentencing on Thursday, Justice Alain Musikanth criticised the operator who took her call, calling it “woeful handling” before launching a scathing assessment of Vrhovsek’s behaviour.



The 29-year-old strangled the woman three times, on the last occasion putting her into a choke hold on the ground while a third party repeatedly punched him and tried to pull him off. He told her she did not deserve to live and that she was a waste of air before stating that “she’s f---ed my life and stole from me” and then saying “let me go, I want to kill her”. “You used extreme violence, you went back and attacked her, you stayed focused on her, placed your fixed attention on her, your actions involved deliberate and controlled choices,” Musikanth said. “You knew exactly what you were doing.” An evaluation of Vrhovsek found him to have narcissistic and insecure traits, as well as possible autism. He had a prior diagnosis of ADHD, for which he took medication, and had been taking testosterone, as well as occasional ketamine use.



Muskinath said he could not find that Vrhovsek showed any signs of empathy or remorse and called the members of the public who stepped in to help the woman “the true heroes of this traumatic and terrifying ordeal”. He sentenced Vrhovsek to 16 years behind bars with a non-parole period of 12 years. Anyone needing support can contact 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732), National Sexual Abuse and Redress Support Service 1800 211 028 or Lifeline 13 11 14.

World.title: ASX trims gains as jobs data stokes rate hike bets; miners, James Hardie rise
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX trims gains as jobs data stokes rate hike bets; miners, James Hardie rise Staff writers Updated July 23, 2026 — 5:44pm ,first published July 23, 2026 — 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket pared most of its strong early gains after the nation’s latest job market figures came in stronger than expected, keeping the chances of another interest rate rise next month on the table. The S&P/ASX 200 finished 16 points, or 0.2 per cent, higher at 8439, having climbed as much as 1.2 per cent earlier in the day. Mining and energy stocks paced the muted gains, while six of the ASX’s 11 sectors finished in the red. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.03¢ in the late afternoon. Employment surged in June, stoking bets on another interest-rate hike by the Reserve Bank. Louie Douvis The Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday morning reported that employment surged in June, extending the previous month’s gains, underscoring the ongoing strength in the nation’s labour market and stoking bets on another interest rate increase by the Reserve Bank. The Aussie dollar and bond yields climbed after the data showed the economy added 76,300 jobs, more than five times estimates, after an upwardly revised 44,000 gain in May. The jobless rate held at 4.4 per cent, as forecast, reflecting a rise in the participation rate. However, the underemployment rate also lifted, climbing to 6.5 per cent.



Related Article Jobs Rate hike fear grows as nation adds 76,000 jobs in June RBA Governor Michele Bullock said at her June press conference that the central bank is trying to slow the economy to help pull down inflation. Last month’s hiring results suggest activity may be stronger than the bank had anticipated. The bank’s next rate decision is scheduled for August 11. “The jobs report was marginally stronger than we expected,” AMP Economist My Bui said. “We think [the RBA] will hike in August with inflation too far from target band” and amid upside risks like a second-round fuel impact, she said. Higher interest rates tend to slow economies and undercut stock prices as borrowing gets more expensive for businesses and consumers, hitting corporate profits. In major corporate news, Macquarie Group said its chief executive, Shemara Wikramanayake, is retiring after eight years in the job, to be replaced by the head of its banking arm, Greg Ward.



Related Article Opinion

Executive shake-up Eat what you kill: Macquarie’s first-ever female CEO is a tough act to follow Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The investment banking giant said Wikramanayake, who is 64 and has been chief executive since late 2018, will retire from November this year. Ward, 58, is a Macquarie veteran who has run the group’s banking and financial services arm, which houses its rapidly growing retail bank, since 2013. He joined Macquarie in 1996 and previously served as chief financial officer for 14 years. The company’s shares fell 0.5 per cent on the news. Meanwhile, the big four banks all advanced, with CBA up 0.4 per cent, Westpac up 0.8 per cent, National Australia Bank up 1.4 per cent and ANZ Bank up 0.6 per cent. Origin Energy, the largest Australian power company, added 0.8 per cent, recouping some of its 1.9 per cent fall from Wednesday. It confirmed shortly before the market closed that a hacker had gained access to customers’ private information, including names, addresses and partial credit card and bank account numbers. The company said on Thursday it was working to determine how many customers had been affected by the cybersecurity breach.



James Hardie jumped 6.1 per cent after the building materials maker – which makes most of its earnings in the US – said its June quarter sales beat its own forecasts, coming in at between $US1.45 billion ($2.1 billion) and $US1.48 billion, thanks to stronger-than-expected sales of its home sidings. Mining giants BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue extended their strong run from Wednesday, up 1.5 per cent, 0.5 per cent and 1 per cent, respectively, even as iron ore fell as the continued US-Iran hostilities clouds the demand outlook. The gold miners continued to rise as the precious metal extended its gains, supported by dip-buyers who scooped it up after prices had drifted lower in recent weeks on concerns that rising inflation will prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates. Bullion was trading around $US4130 an ounce, after rising 3 per cent over the previous two days as dip-buying supported prices. This came as the US and Iran signalled that they aren’t ready to return to the negotiating table after escalating attacks. Gold miners Northern Star Resources and Evolution Mining were both up 1.9 per cent. Energy stocks had another strong session as oil prices continued to climb, hitting a six-week high. Brent crude spiked in post-settlement trading overnight, rising near $US95 a barrel after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels said they had struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea. That’s up from less than $US72 early this month, which is roughly where it was before the war. Local oil and gas giant Woodside rose 0.5 per cent, while coal producers Yancoal and Whitehaven were up 1.5 per cent and 2.2 per cent, respectively. Santos finished flat after it cut its production guidance for the second quarter due to challenges in the ramp-up of its Barossa and Pikka projects, and the timing of cargo receipts.



Related Article Opinion

AI Money to burn? Big Tech’s AI splurge is blowing out Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Tech stocks slumped after Google parent Alphabet and Elon Musk’s Tesla reported earnings early in the day that raised concerns about their cash-burn as they ramp up their AI investments. Software makers Xero and WiseTech plunged 5 per cent and 7 per cent, respectively, while Technology One fell 3.7 per cent and family tracking app Life 360 lost 5.5 per cent. The ASX’s meagre gain came as US sharemarket futures trended down, suggesting a 0.2 per cent drop in the S&P 500 when Wall Street opens for trade. US indexes were drifting during their Wednesday session, with the S&P 500 slipping 0.1 per cent, coming off its best day in three weeks, after swinging between modest losses and gains for much of the day. The Dow Jones closed flat and the Nasdaq composite lost 0.6 per cent. Tesla released its results after the closing bell, reporting negative free cash flow in the second quarter for the first time in more than two years as the Elon Musk-led EV maker accelerated spending on AI infrastructure, battery capacity, robotaxis and next-generation manufacturing. Its shares were down 1.3 per cent in extended trading. Google parent Alphabet topped Wall Street estimates for its second-quarter revenue, buoyed by strong demand for its cloud computing services from enterprises worldwide.



Revenue at Google Cloud rose 82 per cent to $US24.8 billion during the quarter ended in June, accelerating from the 63 per cent jump reported in the preceding three months. Analysts on average expected a 64 per cent increase, according to data compiled by LSEG. However, its stock also declined in extended trading amid concerns about the scale of its AI spending. The majority of stocks in the S&P 500 rose overnight after more companies reported strong profits. Philip Morris International rose 3.3 per cent after the seller of Marlboro cigarettes reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than expected. Its shipments of smoke-free products rose 7.5 per cent. AT&T climbed 3.5 per cent after reporting a stronger profit than analysts expected. CEO John Stankey said the telecom is accelerating plans to send roughly $US10 billion to shareholders this year through share buybacks. Super Micro Computer soared 20 per cent after the seller of AI servers said it expects to report stronger profit margins for the latest quarter than it had earlier forecast. It, though, also said that revenue will likely come in at the low end of its forecasted range. In other international markets, indexes climbed in Europe following a mixed session in Asia. London’s FTSE 100 rose 1.2 per cent, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves.

World.title: Fair Work Court to assist Australian workers with employment, underpayment issues
World.content:
PoliticsFederalIndustrial relations Fair Work Court to assist Australian workers with employment, underpayment issues Natassia Chrysanthos Updated July 23, 2026 — 5:36pm ,first published 2:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian workers will be able to escalate their employment issues and underpayment claims to a new specialist federal court, under a Labor pledge that delivers on a long-term demand of the union movement while inviting another battle with business. The party also agreed to back compulsory superannuation for teenagers in its platform, regardless of how many hours they work, in a move that will encourage the parliamentary party to change its policy on contributions for young Australians. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has opened the 50th Australian Labor Party Conference with a promise to create a new workers’ court. Dominic Lorrimer Both were signs of the pro-worker focus that heralded the opening of Labor’s 50th national conference – the forum where tank-and-file party members, MPs and unions come together to decide on the next three years of party policy – as the party emphasised it would focus on hip-pocket issues to combat populist politics. But Labor’s announcement of a new industrial relations court drew new battle-lines with business groups, just two months after its contentious budget put many businesses offside. Employers warned against complicating a workplace system already laden with red tape.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said consultations would soon begin on a new Fair Work Court – reinstating a special workers’ court for the first time in almost 30 years – as he gave a speech at the conference’s opening session. Related Article Live

Political leadership Labor National Conference as it happened: PM announces Fair Work Court, expands health student prac support in address to party’s 50th National Conference in Adelaide Former prime minister John Howard abolished the specialist industrial relations court in 1997 and moved its jurisdiction to the Federal Court as part of an industrial relations overhaul that sought to curb union influence. Australian Council of Trade Unions president Sally McManus said the unions had been calling for a national employment court since the last one was abolished. It would become easier, faster and cheaper for workers to recover unpaid wages, she said. “Too many employers can drag out court cases and grind workers into the dust while making them wait to get a fair hearing,” she said. “Justice delayed is justice denied. If your boss owes you money, you should not have to wait one or even two years to get it back.”



The Albanese government said some workers and small businesses were spending more than two years fighting for resolutions that should be simple. “The new federal Fair Work Court will provide a specialist forum for resolving workplace relations disputes that works seamlessly with the Fair Work Commission,” a statement said. “Specialist judges with workplace relations expertise would sit on the court, with the aim of supporting faster, simpler and more accessible dispute resolution.” However, Australian Industry Group chief executive Innes Willox said the federal industrial court would merely put “a Band-aid on a fundamentally broken ... system” and would most likely be stacked with appointees from union backgrounds. “Given unions have pushed for this development, there will be unsurprising scepticism about the prospect of it operating in an entirely balanced manner,” Willox said.



Related Article Political leadership We feel your pain: PM sets election battle lines with One Nation, pledges cost of living relief Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar warned it would become a “lawyer’s picnic” at business’ expense. “A specialist industrial court also opens the door for the adoption of legal doctrines to be made by an isolated jurisdiction detached from broader principles of commercial, administrative, constitutional and statutory law,” he said. Business Council chief executive Bran Black said a new court was no substitute for fixing the complexity of workplace laws under Labor. “Instead of adding another layer of red tape, we need to make the system simpler to understand for both employees and employers,” he said.



Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership The movement behind Andy Burnham has a message for Labor in Australia “For a small business, a case that costs more than its worth is not only unfair, it can be the difference between staying open or closing its doors.” In another looming change for employers, superannuation could soon become compulsory for teenagers, if the party moves quickly to act on the policy embedded in its new platform. “All workers, including those under 18 and regardless of how they are engaged, can accumulate superannuation on every dollar earned,” the platform says. Teen workers are now only entitled to superannuation if they work more than 30 hours a week. The Greens last month tried to introduce laws to that effect in parliament – a move that Labor voted against.



The government made another pitch to young Australians earlier on Thursday, with a promise to expand $340 weekly payments to a large group of health and medical students while they undertook practical work placements to earn a qualification. Albanese told the conference that the government was dealing with rising angst across the globe by helping people with the cost of living. “I understand that, for many Australians right now, looking to the future runs second to the immediate pressures they are under,” he said. “The last decade has inflicted one global shock after another, and people have been given every reason to feel like the economy is simply not working for them. That goes deeper than sentiment, it’s a reality people are up against.That is why our focus remains squarely on helping with the cost of living, on the practical measures that matter to people and make a positive difference to their lives.” With Mike Foley, Brittany Busch Go deeper on Labor’s national conference

World.title: Save our town: Lancelin residents take coastal erosion fight to city centre
World.content:
NationalWAVanishing coast Save our town: Lancelin residents take coastal erosion fight to city centre Indigo Lemay-Conway Updated July 23, 2026 — 5:23pm ,first published July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dozens of Lancelin residents poured into Forrest Place on Thursday morning, armed with signs and banners with one message: “save our town”. Almost 100 residents aged seven to 80 chanted “no surrender, no retreat” as they peacefully protested in Perth city to try and raise awareness of their coastal erosion fight. Lancelin locals jumped on a bus on Thursday morning to take part in the Lancelin Rescue Ride. Indigo Lemay-Conway “A proposed retreat is not an option, Lancelin matters, it’s a beautiful town, these kids live there, people work there, we’ve got nowhere else to go,” Lancelin resident and protester Kirsty Harding said. Over the past 12 months, approximately 50 metres of dune has eroded away, leaving less than 10 metres between the ocean and local homes and businesses.



So locals took it upon themselves to take part in the Lancelin Rescue Ride to bring their message directly to government officials. “There’s been an evolving, serious, and rapidly progressing erosion situation in the town of Lancelin, which has reached crisis point,” Harding said. Loading “There’s now a very small section of sand dune holding back the ocean from one property currently, but also that sand dune is acting as a dam wall, really, to the entire town, which has a lot of low-lying land below sea level. “So there’s a lot of homes and businesses and people’s livelihoods at stake. And despite this situation being known about, and having been progressing over some time, the state and local governments have not acted effectively or intervened effectively, and we’re now at a crisis point.”



Now Harding and other residents say they are at breaking point and are ready to bring their message straight to government officials. “Where’s [Roger] Cook, where’s Basil Zempilas, where’s [John] Carey, there’s no one here. They were all invited by many of us, but no one wants to listen to us,” one local shouted at the protest. Lancelin Rescue Ride organiser Michael Cardy said Carey – who visited the town earlier this month – apologised he couldn’t make the meeting at 11am but has organised a meeting with a group of representatives later this afternoon. Cardy said the group contains Lancelin residents as well as engineers who will bring ideas to the table that could help resolve the erosion issue. Carey told WAtoday on Wednesday that the meeting would help to continue support for the struggling community.



“I recently visited Lancelin because I wanted to see the coastal erosion issue firsthand and meet with those directly impacted,” he said. Related Article Vanishing coast Coastal WA tourism town’s erosion emergency deepens as landmark washes away “[Thursday’s] meeting is a further opportunity to hear from members of the Lancelin community as we continue to support the Shire of Gingin on interim and longer-term responses.” Lancelin Sand Hotel owner Glen Trebilcock told the crowd gathered at Forrest Place that he has been working on a solution to the erosion problem for the past 18 months. “It’s very, very unfortunate that it happened bang smack in front of our property and the caravan park,” he said.



“The lowest it got about three or four weeks ago was 1.5 metres and if that breaches it’ll go straight through the caravan park, straight through the north of Lancelin throughout the rest of the town. This has never just been a pub problem, it’s a town problem and for some particular reason we just all seem to be ignoring it.” Gingin shire president Linda Balcombe told 9 News Perth in June that the local council was advocating for state government support. Lancelin Sand Hotel owner Glen Trebilcock told the crowd gathered at Forrest Place that he has been working on a solution to the erosion problem for the past 18 months. Indigo Lemay-Conway “All we want are the ministers to come here, stand in this spot, get sandblasted like I am today and see the damage that is happening, and we need help,” she said. Locals have also created a GoFundMe page to raise money to build a seawall. The goal is to reach $150,000 with $97,565 in donations so far.



Harding said the town of Lancelin is now calling for the state government to step in and find a broader solution to the problem. “Lancelin has been ignored on this for a long time to get to this critical point, and we were desperate to be heard for fear that our town would be inundated, and properties and businesses washed away by the ocean,” she said. Signs at the Lancelin Rescue Ride protest on Thursday. Indigo Lemay-Conway “We’d like [government officials] to, in a timely manner, given the urgency of the situation, use their expertise and their resources to devise a long-term engineered solution to this erosion crisis that protects the town, protects the people, their properties, and their livelihoods and their businesses,” she said. At a press conference on Thursday, former environment minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said she was hopeful that Carey would be able to help the Lancelin community.



“I know that we have made a number of investments in supporting some of those erosion issues,” she said. “My understanding is that the minister will meet with that community today when they’re in town, and that he is continuing to work closely with the shire on immediate solutions, but also more long-term solutions.” Greens climate change spokesperson Sophie McNeill said the coastal erosion in Lancelin had reached crisis point. “Unfortunately, coastal erosion like what we are seeing in Lancelin is exactly what climate scientists have been warning of for years,” she said. “Over the last decade the [state] government has failed to take any meaningful action to mitigate climate change and now communities like Lancelin are being forced to adapt to survive.”



WA Nationals leader Shane Love also called on the state government to “immediately commence a detailed coastal study and develop a long-term plan to protect Lancelin from coastal erosion.″ “What we need now is the immediate commencement of a comprehensive coastal study and the development of a long-term plan to safeguard Lancelin’s future,” he said.

World.title: ‘Makes me sick to my stomach’: Students speak out about strapping scandal
World.content:
NationalVictoriaPrivate schools ‘Makes me sick to my stomach’: Students speak out about strapping scandal Caroline Schelle July 23, 2026 — 5:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Boarders at a prestigious regional school at the centre of a “strapping” scandal were pressured to keep quiet about the claims, an independent investigation has found. Ballarat Grammar last year expelled two senior boarders over allegations that junior students – some as young as year 7 – were assaulted as part of a hazing culture going back decades that included beatings with straps. Ballarat Grammar School. Joe Armao On Thursday, the school released a report by workplace cultural firm Intersection, after they questioned students, staff and parents about the school’s culture and examined the boarding houses where “strapping” happened. The school also said at least five staff members left in the wake of the scandal, although it would not confirm the circumstances of their exit.



Current and former students told the report’s authors that there was an unwritten rule for boarders: “What happens in boarding, stays in boarding.” This was reinforced by peer pressure and speaking up was considered disloyalty, with students who did raise concerns being labelled a “snitch”, the report found. Those students risked social exclusion or retaliation, and parents said children were reluctant to share experiences because it was normalised. This culture of silence limited information to day school staff, parents, some boarding staff and the school’s leadership, while reinforcing the internal cohesion of the boarding house. “It reinforced the internal cohesion of the boarding house by positioning loyalty to the group above individual wellbeing or external accountability,” the report found.



Related Article Education ‘It was a very brutal five years’: A private school scandal decades in the making Students who took part in the review said there was a judgmental atmosphere at the school, with a sharp divide between those who were boarders and day students. Many felt they were unable to raise concerns about bullying or strapping to their teachers. “I find the boarding side of the school, especially boys, to be absolutely nasty and that whole community to be absolutely brainwashed by each other’s egos,” one day student told the authors of the report. “Naming the day students ‘Scrags’ ... the way the girl boarders say people who snitch on child abuse are ‘snitches’ and ‘strapping should come back, it’s totally harmless’, and ‘people just need to harden up and not complain, take the straps, how else will there be a hierarchy in the House’... it makes me sick to my stomach.” Others revealed they experienced sexism and racism from not just students, but teachers.



“[A male teacher] said women are often just better in the kitchen instead of the classroom as they are better at following recipes than learning complex thinking,” one child explained. “The boys laughed and thought it was hilarious, but it truly hurt.” That student told other teachers, but their complaint was never followed up on, and they were not offered support following the incident. Another said a female teacher told girls their dresses were too short, and it was “unfair to the male teachers at the school” because it put them in an uncomfortable position and there was “no control over what they might do”.



Ballarat Grammar principal Adam Heath. Ballarat Grammar. “I also think lining all of the girls in a year level up and walking past, crouching looking at their dress lengths is objectifying them, and when put in these situations I felt overwhelmingly uncomfortable,” the student said. The report also noted that standards of behaviour were not applied consistently and communication was uneven. “Trust in leadership has been eroded, particularly since the boarding incidents became public,” the authors found. Intersection carried out 126 one-on-one interviews and focus groups attended by 107 students. Its investigators also received 198 written submissions, 299 student survey responses and 146 staff responses, and carried out 32 follow-up meetings.



Ballarat Grammar was barred from accepting new boarders in October last year, on the orders of the Victorian Registration and Qualifications Authority. But the body lifted the prohibition for this school year and put interim conditions in place. The school ordered the independent probe after The Age revealed last year that senior students allegedly abused younger pupils in the Dart House boarding facility. Victoria Police were also called in over claims junior students – some as young as 12 – had been assaulted by older students. Four former students were later formally cautioned. The school installed CCTV cameras in its residential areas and hired overnight private security guards to protect the younger children as they sleep. However, students referred to these guards as “night crawlers”, and some described them as strangers who they did not know well enough to approach.



Related Article Exclusive

Private schools Private school boys accused of ‘punishing’ classmates with straps The report made 44 recommendations that were accepted that included the restructure of boarding houses by age band to reduce the power differential, addressing gender dynamics in boarding, and for the school to “reset the parent-school relationship as an educational partnership, not a service-provider arrangement”. Principal Adam Heath said they were committed to the recommendations, and were working tirelessly to nurture safety, wellbeing and dignity. He also apologised for some findings he acknowledged were confronting for members of the school’s community. “We are deeply sorry that some of our current and former students, staff and families have, at times, felt hurt or unsupported.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Most wanted man won’t be extradited from Greece over fatal Sydney stabbing: reports
World.content:
A court in Greece has ruled out extraditing James Dalamangas, one of the nation’s most wanted men, over an alleged stabbing murder in a Sydney nightclub three decades ago. Dalamangas – wanted over the 1999 death of Sydney man George Giannopoulos – was arrested at a farm property in Greece last month on an Interpol red notice after more than 27 years on the run. James Dalamangas is led into a police van by Greek authorities. Flamis Greece Dalamangas, now 56, allegedly stabbed Giannopoulos in the stomach and neck at the Pariziana nightclub in Belmore, while Giannopoulos was attempting to break up a fight at the venue in Sydney’s south-west. An arrest warrant for Dalamangas was issued one day after Giannopoulos’ death, but Dalamangas was never found.



He allegedly fled the country and became one of the nation’s most wanted men, with his face splashed across Interpol websites and at press conferences by both NSW and the Australian Federal Police. After nine hours of deliberations, a Greek court has ruled that James Dalamangas will not be extradited to Australia to face charges. Nine Australian detectives suspected he moved to Greece shortly after the alleged stabbing, and went by many different names as he found work as a farmer. James Dalamangas leaving a Sydney court before the 1999 stabbing. Nine News His arrest in June triggered a request from Australian authorities to extradite Dalamangas back to Sydney to face the murder charge.



George Giannopoulos, who died after he was stabbed in Belmore in 1999. NSW Police But the Patras Council of Appeals on Wednesday ruled Greece’s 25-year statute of limitations had passed and Dalamangas could not be extradited, according to local media. “The decision was made because the offence is statute-barred in Greece. Our arguments were accepted, particularly the fact that the offence had become time-barred under Greek law,” one media outlet quoted Dalamangas’ lawyer, Giannis Apostolopoulos, as saying. “Under both our country’s criminal procedure and the Greece–Australia treaty, if the offence has become time-barred in either country, that constitutes a mandatory ground for refusing extradition.” Australian authorities pushed for the extradition, reportedly citing Australian laws in which murder carries no statute of limitations.



The NSW Police State Crime Command, which has taken charge of the extradition request, was still attempting to contact its Greek and overseas law enforcement partners on Thursday afternoon (AEST), following the ruling. It will consider its further options after reviewing the decision.



The Australian Federal Police have also been contacted for comment. The Greek court had deliberated for nine hours to reach their decision, local media reported. Giannopoulos’ sister Toula said her family felt “let down” by the court decision, but vowed she was “not giving up” on the bid to extradite Dalamangas. “We’re looking at other avenues, legal avenues, because this is not a fair decision,” Toula told Nine News on Thursday. “I still have hope, not losing hope yet … that was not a fair decision yesterday, in a court that we didn’t even know it was happening.”



Greek media outlet Tempo24 reported that Dalamangas lived under the name Antonis Tzimas for 18 years in the rural village of Alsos. Authorities believe he purchased property in the village and was known as a farmer who lived a quiet life with his partner. Dalamangas’ identity was revealed after he reportedly shared false information during a police check and eventually confessed that he was wanted in Australia. A crossbow and more than a dozen phones were seized in a raid of James Dalamangas’ home. Tempo24 via Hellenic Police Police raided Dalamangas’ home, allegedly finding a crossbow, three knives, 13 mobile phones, a computer and three USB sticks. Australian police had offered $200,000 for information leading to Dalamangas’ capture in January 2024, as the 25-year deadline approached in April that year.
