World.title: ‘I want to kill her’: Jail for horrific strangling of woman on a Perth street caught on CCTV
World.content:
NationalWACourts ‘I want to kill her’: Jail for horrific strangling of woman on a Perth street caught on CCTV Rebecca Peppiatt July 23, 2026 — 5:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains violent footage that some readers may find distressing. A FIFO worker who carried out months of stalking, abuse and harassment towards a woman in Perth has been jailed for attempting to kill her in a horrific assault captured by nearby CCTV cameras. Mihael Vrhovsek, 29, repeatedly strangled a woman who was known to him in February 2024 before passersby intervened and stopped him, saving her life. Loading Vrhovsek mounted a campaign of abuse at the woman for five months that included changing his number 18 times after she blocked each one so he could repeatedly call and abuse her.



During a Supreme Court trial in March this year, prosecutors told the jury Vrhovsek tried to contact the woman 234 times via text messages and phone calls over a three-day period in the lead up to the incident that culminated with him “lying in wait” in his car outside her apartment block for eight hours. Mihael Vrhovsek, 29, was found guilty of trying to kill a woman. Facebook “Killed yourself already?“, “This is your last warning”, “You’re a spectacular piece of s---”, “Go f--- yourself, politely” and “I would have killed myself already but the hatred towards you is keeping me alive” were just some of the text messages he sent her. By January 2024, the victim said the communication “got darker” with one email reading, “thanks for another sleepless night, I much prefer pretending you are dead in that apartment”. He also texted her “good night attention seeking s---” and later “you’re dead to me”. By the end of February, the woman said she felt too scared to return to her apartment after she was told by a neighbour that Vrhovsek had parked in her car space and slept in his car “like a predatory animal waiting for me”.



The woman told the jury she was “freaked out”, had called the police and explained he was in her basement. “The officer went off and made some calls or something and when he came back he said, it’s a private property, we’ve got no access. He said, ‘We can’t help you’. Mihael Vrhovsek waited outside his victim’s apartment before launching a violent attack on her which only came to an end when bystanders stepped in. Picture: WA Courts WA Courts “I walked out to my car and I just broke down. “I thought, what the f--- do I do? No one is helping.”



Hours later she went back to the apartment briefly to grab a change of clothing with a friend, but when she ran into Vrhovsek she immediately called triple-zero. “I saw him walk out of the doors at me - he was looking down, targeted, coming at me,” she told the jury. Mihael Vrhovsek waited outside his victim’s apartment before launching a violent attack on her which only came to an end when bystanders stepped in. Picture: WA Courts WA Courts In the triple-zero call, the woman can heard yelling “get the f--- away from me, get the f--- away from me” before the call goes quiet. During Vrhovsek’s sentencing on Thursday, Justice Alain Musikanth criticised the operator who took her call, calling it “woeful handling” before launching a scathing assessment of Vrhovsek’s behaviour.



The 29-year-old strangled the woman three times, on the last occasion putting her into a choke hold on the ground while a third party repeatedly punched him and tried to pull him off. He told her she did not deserve to live and that she was a waste of air before stating that “she’s f---ed my life and stole from me” and then saying “let me go, I want to kill her”. “You used extreme violence, you went back and attacked her, you stayed focused on her, placed your fixed attention on her, your actions involved deliberate and controlled choices,” Musikanth said. “You knew exactly what you were doing.” An evaluation of Vrhovsek found him to have narcissistic and insecure traits, as well as possible autism. He had a prior diagnosis of ADHD, for which he took medication, and had been taking testosterone, as well as occasional ketamine use.



Muskinath said he could not find that Vrhovsek showed any signs of empathy or remorse and called the members of the public who stepped in to help the woman “the true heroes of this traumatic and terrifying ordeal”. He sentenced Vrhovsek to 16 years behind bars with a non-parole period of 12 years. Anyone needing support can contact 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732), National Sexual Abuse and Redress Support Service 1800 211 028 or Lifeline 13 11 14.

World.title: The House: MPs return after two-week break
World.content:
When MPs return to Parliament after a two-week break, the first day or so in the debating chamber can involve a surprising amount of catch-up on the endless business awaiting attention, and on rejuvenated arguments and debates, as well as on not losing ground in the inch-by-inch battles over procedural interpretation. Some of the catch-up is official business, some is tactical and some is political.

Select Committees don't experience the same level of catch-up. They typically lose so many sitting days to extended sittings in the House that many keep working across the sitting breaks, at least to some degree.

Refreshed MPs add new debates to business backlog The House Download MP3 5m

Parliament's 'mail box'

Each sitting day the Clerk of the House informs MPs of what you might describe as mail. New bills, reports from committees, papers from entities (things like Annual Reports or Statements of Intent), and newly arrived petitions. Most days there are a few, but after a two week break, the weight of new reading is staggering.

On Tuesday the Clerk announced 13 petitions, 64 papers, 15 select committee reports, and two new bills. Just reading the titles of that two-lozenge-worthy list took six and a half minutes. Thank goodness most are now electronic and can be found on Parliament's website. Papers can be found here, petitions are here, committee reports are here, and bills are here.

Labour MP Camilla Belich tried to add an extra item to the mailbox, when she asked the House to agree to introduce a new member's bill - the Crimes (Consent Reform) Amendment Bill. The bill would establish "affirmative consent as New Zealand's approach to consent to sexual activity". She wanted it debated on member's day. Permission would need to be unanimous, and was never likely to be given. The move was a political response to National's promise to introduce consent law post-election. Belich was saying something like 'if you care, why wait?'

Noting events

When MPs return there are also often events that need mentioning in the House. This week there were four.

The recent deaths of Bill Birch (a senior National Party MPs from the 1970-80s), and Sam Neill were both given brief attention. The recent triumph of Ryan Fox at the British Golf Open was also noted. Arguably, if only one of those events had occurred it might have resulted in some speeches, rather than a motion.

A recent policy decision was also given an airing when the Speaker agreed to the requested urgent debate into the Government's decision to give financial assistance to New Zealand's remnant cement company.

The procedural recap segment

Something else that often happens after a break is a series of reminders of where things stand in any ongoing procedural tussles. These reminders might come from the Speaker or the Opposition.

This is the parliamentary version of the 'previously on...' segment at the beginning of a TV episode.

This week, for example, Shadow Leader of the House Kieran McAnulty made a gentle point early in the week's first Committee of the Whole House. Labour supports the bill being considered, but the Government has offered substantial amendments to it half way through the parliamentary process. McAnulty wanted to remind everyone that the Speaker had spoken about this kind of thing recently - regarding the importance of giving fair notice.

"We are faced with, at this stage, an Amendment Paper from the Minister that is just as large as the bill. I'd like some reassurance from him that ...the Finance and Expenditure Committee has considered all aspects of this and that the inclusion of this amendment bill is not contrary to the guidance that the Speaker gave the House only last sitting week."

New stakes in the ground

With a new sitting block there are also often new issues to raise, new issues raised by media across the break, maybe newly scandalous events to pick up on, or political feuds to continue or begin. For example, this week there have been various (sometimes oblique) responses to comments by Shane Jones and Stuart Nash.

There was also a new squabble over a privilege issue. During Tuesday's debate on the Arms Bill, Labour's Ginny Andersen accused the Minister in charge of the Bill (ACT's new deputy leader Nicole McKee), of having broken parliament's rules by sharing privileged information with a gun lobby group. McKee was outraged by the claim and demanded a retraction, and while Andersen professed herself happy to provide evidence, matters of privilege shouldn't be raised or debated in the House, nor can they be retracted in the House. They have to be raised directly with the Speaker.

New energy

At the end of the previous sitting block MPs were visibly drained after long days of urgency. Their speeches did not sparkle. Humour was a rarity.

After a week or two with family in their home electorates, MPs have more zest, better humour, and sharper snark. So for example, Labour MP Camila Belich typically debates the careful nuance and detail of law. But on Tuesday, considering New Zealand First's English Language Bill she was refreshingly acerbic. The bill is, at its core, just eight words long, and boldly asserts that English is officially allowed in New Zealand.

Bellich called it "statutory recognition of a fundamental truth. What is the Government going to legislate for next? That it should get dark at night, that the sun should rise in the morning, that the sky is blue, and that flowers should bloom?"

All of that on just the first day back.

World.title: Man charged with stealing police-issued Glock pistol in Whanganui
World.content:
A man has been charged with stealing a police-issued Glock pistol.

According to court documents, he is alleged to have stolen the police firearm, valued at $1204, in Whanganui on 11 February.

In addition to the theft charge, the man, in his 40s, faces a charge of unlawful possession of a firearm arising from the same incident.

NZME understands the man, who cannot be named, tried to sell the Glock to a gang member.

The man has made his first appearance in the Whanganui District Court on the charges and was remanded to reappear in August.

He faces a maximum penalty of seven years' imprisonment on the theft charge and four years on the possession charge.

The court has confirmed there are broad interim suppression orders in place restricting what can be reported about the case.

NZME asked police how the firearm was allegedly taken, how the loss was discovered, whether it had been recovered, whether it had been used in any further offending, and whether there were any public safety concerns arising from the incident.

Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett said police could not comment further than confirming the charges while the matter was before the court.

The alleged theft is one of only a handful of reported cases in recent years involving stolen police-issued firearms.

In 2019, two police-issued Glock pistols were stolen after a patrol car was taken in Gore. The offender was sentenced the following year.

In an earlier case, two police Glocks were stolen from the evidential lock-up at the New Plymouth courthouse in 2013.

World.title: Arthur Easton murder: Lawyers give closing arguments against former police officers
World.content:
A "conscious and deliberate" act to help police secure a conviction, or a legitimate decision to exclude evidence that was deemed unreliable?

Those are the key questions that a judge will consider as he determines whether two former officers attempted to pervert the course of justice in their handling of a 40-year-old murder.

Alan Hall spent 17 years in prison for the 1985 murder of Arthur Easton.

He was later exonerated by the Supreme Court, which found a significant miscarriage of justice had occurred.

Now the former officers, who have name suppression, are facing charges over their role in Hall's conviction.

Lawyers made their closing arguments in the High Court at Auckland on Thursday.

On 13 October 1985, Arthur Easton and his teenage sons, Brendan and Kim, were at home when one heard an intruder in their home.

Closing arguments made in Alan Hall case Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Crown prosecutor John Billington KC recounted what happened next.

"There was a fight and in the course of that fight Mr Easton was fatally wounded and Brendan Easton was seriously wounded. The offender escaped by leaving the home through a hedge into a walkway and made his way down Alma Crescent to Shirley Crescent and close to Clevedon Road."

Later that night, a man called Ronald Turner phoned the Papakura Police Station to reported seeing a hooded Māori man running across Clevedon Road around the time of the attack.

His description tallied with what the Easton brothers had told police in their 111 call - that they were attacked by a six-foot-tall Māori man wielding a bayonet.

Although the brothers would later cast doubt on their recollection, two further witnesses also described seeing a man of a similar description.

"Mr Hall, by reason of his ownership of a bayonet and a hat found at the scene was interviewed on 11 December, 1985. He gave a number of explanations as to why the bayonet and hat were not in his possession on the night of the murder. He was also questioned in relation to his ownership of a blue sweatshirt which was similar to that seen by Mr Turner," Billington said.

"Now obviously, Mr Hall did not match the description given by Mr Turner. Mr Hall is a Pākehā, somewhere close to five-foot-eight in height, frail build and clearly not Māori."

Billington questioned why police only presented some of Ronald Turner's evidence to the jury at Alan Hall's trial, excluding his description of the offender's ethnicity.

And why did the former officers not provide his original statement to Hall's defence team when they requested all relevant evidence?

"By modifying the Crown case, the defendants denied the defence lawyers, the trial judge, the jury, the Court of Appeal access to the prior statements.

"They each carried out an act which was intended to and had the obvious effect of preventing the courts from doing justice."

John Billington said it was difficult to accept that their conduct was anything but "conscious and deliberate".

But defence lawyer David Jones, KC, said police had "very real concerns" about Turner's recollection of the man he saw.

"What someone says in a statement to a police is not evidence. It is a statement they have made which could or could not be used as evidence in the case," he said.

"That has to go through a filtering process. And that is exactly what happened here."

Furthermore, Jones said, it was ultimately for the Crown to decide on what evidence was admissible in court.

"What we have is a recreation of events by the Crown which is castling a sinister light on an investigation which is carried out in an entirely normal and logical and legal way.

Jones urged Justice Gault not to rely on the findings of the Supreme Court when it quashed Alan Hall's conviction in 2022 because, he argued, the Crown had "capitulated" during the appeal.

Acting for the second defendant, Paul Wicks, KC, said there was no statutory framework guaranteeing pre-trial disclosure in the mid-1980s, as there is today.

"The Crown in this case has endeavoured to weave a few loose threads into a tapestry of guilt working backwards from the Supreme Court judgement," he said.

"It has failed, in my submission, to establish to the required standard that [the former officer] acted with any intention to pervert the course of justice and ultimately the only correct and safe verdict is one of not guilty."

World.title: NRL: NZ Warriors squash reports of Nathan Cleary recruitment
World.content:
Barely has one wave of free agency speculation passed, when another blindsides NZ Warriors coach Andrew Webster.

Last week, the Auckland NRL club secured veteran second-rower Kurt Capewell for another season, perhaps the last big name taken off the market for next season. Only centre Rocco Berry remains and he has two months to shake off his injury woes to push his claims for a contract extension.

This week, more names have popped up on social media channels as potential Warriors targets, including two of the biggest in rugby league - Nathan Cleary and Joseph Manu.

Webster is adamant they have spoken to neither and, in Cleary's case, they cannot do so for another three months, until the 1 November free-agency window opens.

"We're definitely not in talks with Nathan Cleary and none of his representation have contacted us - and it's not even legal," he said. "It can't even happen.

"Everyone's trying to guess what Nathan's doing, I guess, and they can see the romance in the Warriors. I see the romance in that scenario.

"He went to school here, he was a ballboy here - I can see why they would put two and two together, but there's certainly nothing in that at all."

Cleary, 28, spent much of his childhood at Mt Smart, while dad Ivan played and then coached at the club, helping it to the only two grand final appearances in its history. Both have since created a dynasty at Penrith Panthers, including four straight championships.

Younger brother Jett is working his way through the grades at the Warriors and is due to take up a full contract next season, as part of his development.

Nathan Cleary's contract ends at the Panthers next season and Ivan has also indicated he will step down as coach at that time, so speculation over their futures is rife.

The Warriors roster is currently stacked with halves, but incumbents Te Maire Martin and Chanel Harris-Tavita have only extended for next season, leaving a potential opening there, if Cleary were to cross the Tasman.

"I can't give it any more fire, because it's not existent," Webster said.

Playing mainly at centre, Manu, 30, logged 180 games for Sydney Roosters between 2016-24, winning two premierships, before switching codes to play rugby in France.

Kiwi Joseph Manu is considering his options, after three seasons in French rugby. Andrew Cornaga / www.photosport.nz

With his season at Racing 92 over, he has visited Papua New Guinea and seems likely to sign the newest NRL expansion team, when they enter the competition in 2028. That would leave him a gap year, if that's the decision he makes.

"I'm guessing, if it's about money, then no-one's going to compete with Papua New Guinea, but if it's about football, I hope he would like to contact us and say, 'Do you guys want my services?'.

"I don't know what his plans are around rugby - I don't have a clue."

While these two possible additions are mouthwatering, the prospect of losing a couple has also been floated.

Hooker Wayde Egan, who has made 138 appearances for the Warriors since 2020, has been linked with a possible move to St George-Illawarra Dragons or Brisbane Broncos.

Again, that conversation can't legally take place until 1 November and the Warriors have a chance to trump that before then.

"Everyone told me all year we were going to lose all these players, and I was confident we would chat through that and have the right conversations at the right time," Webster said. "Put it this way, we have no intention for that to happen.

"I'm not nervous about it, simply because the rumour around Nathan is not right as well. Wherever these are coming from, I'm sure people are bored and come up with them."

One player that may be looking elsewhere is promising forward Kayliss Fatialofa, who reportedly had a clause in his current contract that allowed him to test the market, if he hadn't made his first-grade debut by Round 15 this season.

The Warriors first-grade line-up has been hit by injury and Origin absences over the past two months, and Fatialofa has been named on the interchange bench a few times, without ever quite making it onto the field.

Webster confirmed the 'out' clause, but also hoped his player would choose to stay.

Kayliss Fatialofa hasn't quite made it onto the field for the Warriors first-grade side, but has starred for their reserves. AAP/Photosport

"We want Kayliss to stay, but he has an opportunity to look around, that's the truth," he said. "He hasn't debuted yet, but his long-term pathway looks exciting, so we're hoping he stays."

Webster agreed the NRL's continued expansion had created an active market that suited players like Fatialofa looking to fast-track their careers.

The Dolphins entered the competition in 2023, Perth Bears will arrive next season, with the PNG Chiefs due the year after.

"If anyone knows Kayliss, he has a good head on his shoulders and he assesses the situation," Webster said. "I know he enjoys it here.

"I want them to be patient, because I genuinely see the path forward for them, but they may see their path different and I can't begrudge them that.

World.title: PNG and NZ commit to deeper defence co-operation
World.content:
Papua New Guinea and New Zealand have committed to deeper defence cooperation, particularly in the maritime domain.

The two countries have signed a statement of intent on defence cooperation for the next three years.

The statement, signed in Port Moresby by New Zealand's Defence Minister Chris Penk and his PNG counterpart Elias Kapavore, notes an intensifying geostrategic environment in the Pacific.

It affirms that PNG will first seek support from the Pacific Islands Forum in times of crisis, including a security threat.

The agreement commits to expand joint maritime operations, and the deployment of assets to undertake surveilance activities in PNG waters.

It is also set to increase defence dialogue, training exercises and personnel exchanges between the two forces.

NZDF / Supplied

New Zealand's Defence Force had most recently come to PNG's aid during Cyclone Maila.

World.title: New Zealanders warned to leave Iran as soon as possible if they can
World.content:
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has renewed its warning to New Zealanders in Iran after Donald Trump threatened further military strikes.

The US President on Wednesday said that the United States would bomb Iranian civil infrastructure every time Tehran fires at ships in the Hormuz Strait.

A Safe Travel advisory issued by Mfat said New Zealanders should leave Iran as soon as possible if it is safe to do so.

A limited number of flights are still operating from Khomeini International Airport in Tehran but airspace closures could occur at any time, it says.

Land routes out of Iran via Turkey and Armenia are still viable and have been successfully used by other New Zealanders to leave the country.

Anyone who cannot leave Iran should follow the advice of local authorities and move to or remain in a safe place and ensure they have essential supplies such as food, water, torches, batteries or power banks and any medications.

The advisory says there are a number of steps people should take if they are at risk of drone or missile attacks.

Know how advance warnings are communicated in the area

Follow all local authority instructions

Identify the nearest shelter or safest locations

If no shelter is available, move to a basement or interior room away from windows

Avoid any potential target locations, including military sites, airports and oil and energy infrastructure

Keep in contact with family and friends where possible

New Zealanders who need urgent consular assistance should contact the 24/7 consular emergency line on +64 99 20 20 20.

World.title: Forcing 'cameras on' work meetings could be problematic - employment expert
World.content:
Forcing employees to turn webcams on an 'invasion of privacy' Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Making workers turn their cameras on during Zoom or Teams calls could potentially be discrimination, an employment expert says.

An employment tribunal in the United Kingdom has recently ruled that not letting a worker with anxiety turn off their camera during a meeting was a type of disability discrimination.

Barrister and employment expert Barbara Buckett told Checkpoint forcing employees to have their cameras on in meetings did present a lot of issues.

"As for this person it was overwhelming, the question is 'camera's on rights off'."

Buckett said employers needed to think about why they were making the request and if someone didn't feel comfortable with it, was it reasonable for them to ask.

In some cases, Buckett could see an argument for having cameras on in a meeting - including client meetings and team engagement - but it shouldn't simply be a blanket policy.

"People might not want an intrusion into their private space at home."

Buckett said she thought digital mediums like Zoom, Teams and Slack were causing concerns for workers as people often did feel less comfortable on them.

"They're quite intrusive and people feel like they're on screen and they do feel it's more invasive."

She said there were all sorts of reasons why someone may not be comfortable including cultural reasons, personal ones or even their living conditions.

"I remember in Covid times we were in people's bedrooms....I found that quite odd.

"You can perfectly have constructive engagement without that camera on."

Another issue with video meetings was recording, Buckett said, and urged anyone to announce if a meeting was being recorded.

World.title: Religious artwork stolen from Wellington church
World.content:
A Wellington church is asking for the return of two icons stolen from their altar on Tuesday.

Religious artworks of the Virgin Mary and baby Jesus and a copy of the famous Icon of Christ and the Abbot Mena in the Louvre were taken from St Peter's Church on Willis St.

Reverend Jean Malcolm, who made the image of Mary and Child herself, said they seemed to "have grown legs and walked".

The church leaves its doors open during daylight hours.

St Peters Church, Wellington. RNZ

She said the items did not have monetary value, but that they were "an important part of our environment of the church".

Believers use icons to help them pray as the holy people in the images let worshippers feel God's presence, she said.

"They leave a big hole, and we're hoping that by advertising their loss, we might be able to get them back."

The church decided not to involve police in the matter.

"We don't want to take anyone to court about it; we just want our icons back."

She hoped for a reconcilation with the person who took them but understood if they were too shy or scared to come themselves.

The church would close for a day if the icons were not returned by Tuesday. She said they would be "mourning for the loss of the icons and also mourning that this kind of hospitable space has been kind of harmed in this way".

She said the church understood life was hard for many at the moment, "but actually, the only way out of this difficult time is if we reach out to one another, if we remain open to one another".

World.title: Bomber Caddy to face Hawks after heart scare
World.content:
Essendon interim coach Dean Solomon says Nate Caddy will play in Saturday's match against Hawthorn following his recovery from a heart scare.

Caddy was taken to hospital during last Sunday's three-point win over GWS due to an elevated heart rate.

Bombers star cleared for return Nate Caddy is expected to fully train and play next weekend despite experiencing an elevated heart rate during Essendon's win over GWS.

The 21-year-old was released from hospital after being given the all-clear.

The club's medical staff has since given its approval for Caddy to face the Hawks.

"He'll be good to go," Solomon said.

"They said there's no risk with what happened and he's fully good to go. I trust our medical staff, and Nate's in a good headspace as well.

"He spent a lot of time with the docs and medical staff, gone through it all and has a good understanding that there's no risk at play here, and he's really confident.

"So we've just got to trust our medical staff."

Essendon has lost Xavier Duursma (hamstring) for the rest of the season, while Kyle Langford will miss the Hawthorn match due to suspension.

McKay sits out Blues training

Star Carlton forward Harry McKay failed to participate during the Blues' main training session on Thursday.

McKay suffered a minor tear to his meniscus, as well as bone bruising to his knee, during Saturday night's 21-point defeat to Collingwood.

The 28-year-old was ruled out early in the match after his knee knocked into teammate Sam Walsh.

Harry McKay was forced from the field against the Magpies last weekend. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

But speculation around McKay ran rampant, with Fox Footy commentator David King questioning the one-time Coleman medallist's injury.

The Blues were privately seething with McKay's character being criticised, before the severity of the injury was confirmed on Sunday.

Interim Blues coach Josh Fraser said he "didn't spend a lot of time thinking about" the commentary surrounding McKay.

"Whenever there's an injury, your mindset goes to the care and support for the player," Fraser said.

"We act on the information we're given from our medical team, the commentary around all of that, I probably push it to the side.

"I can only judge him on the way he's presented and he's presented his usual self.

"Great energy around the group, trying as hard as he can to play and leading internally around the club."

Carlton's wildcard hopes will go on the line on Saturday when it host out-of-form Gold Coast at Docklands.

World.title: Aussie captain relishes 'special' chance 'to take time to be a dad'
World.content:
Water polo is a brutal sport.

Relentless swimming. Incessant wrestling. Elbows and fists flying around as if the combatants were half-submerged within a flooded UFC cage.

To put it mildly, it is not a place for the faint of heart.

So it is somewhat incongruous, then, to see Australian Sharks captain Nathan Power sitting on the side of the Griffith University pool on the Gold Coast with his son, Sebastian in his arms, feeding him a bottle.

Power, 33, will lead the Australian men's water polo team at the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup event in Sydney this week, with the Sharks taking on reigning world champions Spain on Thursday.

He is also on six months of parental leave from his role as a manager with KPMG, giving him valuable time to be a dad as well as skippering his nation.

Nathan Power will skipper the team in his home town of Sydney. (Supplied: Water Polo Australia)

"It's been fun to get to do this," Power told ABC Sport, with Sebastian still in his arms.

"To get an opportunity to take time to be a dad, it's really special."

It's created some changes within the team environment too.

"This is the first time in my time with the men's team that there's been a baby on tour — and there's actually two at the moment, Blake Edwards has his son Jude here as well," Power said.

"It makes for a bit of a shift; even at breakfast time now, the boys all roll in and it's a case of, who's gunna take hold of the baby and who wants to look after a baby.

"It's amazing to see how a large group of men have all very quickly clicked into dad mode to help out where they can."

Australian Sharks Water Polo coach Tim Hamill (left) says the addition of kids to camp has been great. (Supplied: Zac Hudson)

Head coach Tim Hamill, who has led the Sharks since taking the reins post-Tokyo in 2021, also made note of the positive changes to the dynamic young children can have.

"It's a first for us," the former international player told ABC Sport.

"One of our values as a team is around family, so we talk to that in having those families here.

The 'precious' bond driving the Stingers to success Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, were the most successful Australian team at the Paris Olympics, winning a stunning silver medal. This is the secret to their success.

"We're really fortunate to have a nice balance of the group, we've got the spectrum covered in terms of interests and ideas and for the first time, in this preparation, we've got two of our players who have children, which we've never had before.

"So that changed the dynamic of the group.

"A lot of people have spoken about Paris and how do we get those results [that we got] and I'm conscious to talk culture because it's that overused word in sport at the moment.

"But for me, culture as a word is derived from that care, there's real care in this team.

"We know that our culture needs to be the best in the world, we know that our team care needs to be the best in the world, otherwise we can't compete, so we invest time in all of that, and that's conversations with those 18s all the way through to 30 plus year olds and now fathers."

The topic of keeping mothers in sport has been a hot one in the Australian space for a while now.

In December, the Australian Olympic Committee created the Olympians Future Fund, with a key pillar of that designed to help support female Olympians return to high-performance sport after giving birth, making them eligible to receive $10,000.

Although Power's situation is different, he noted that the support that he has received from KPMG and Water Polo Australia was just as valuable to him in order to allow both he and his partner Maddy to continue their careers.

Water polo is not exactly a gentle sport, as Power shows while wrestling Spain on their way to the world championship title last year. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

"That's kind of the thing that can maybe get lost at times, but really it's support for the family," he said.

"With the support that I get through my work at KPMG, that then enables Maddy to get back into work; the support I get from Water Polo Australia, that enables us as a family to be here.

"We both get to keep on pursuing what we want to pursue, but also get to spend some really meaningful time with Sebastian too.

"It's been awesome to come home from training and the first thing I see is a silly smile from the window, him looking out at me.

"It's a new, fun way to come home from training when you're a bit cooked and tired and maybe a bit grumpy."

Power beamed with joy when recounting how much Sebastian was enjoying finding his feet in the water during his lessons, adding that fatherhood has "massively" changed his perspective.

Nathan Power has competing priorities now. (Supplied: Water Polo Australia)

"I think, obviously parenthood becomes that key identity that you have and you see yourself as," he said.

"It's also something which for me, at 33, I guess we can probably confidently say I'm closer to the end than the start of my career, so it means you also get to take some moments and really appreciate that this isn't normal to get to do this and to share this experience with your family.

"It gets you to appreciate these experiences you have with the team too, because they can be very fleeting."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The World Cup Final is the first time Australia has hosted a major water polo championships since the 2007 World Championships in Melbourne, and the first time Sydney has hosted a combined event since the 2000 Olympics.

Power said the opportunity to compete in front of friends and family will never be undervalued by the squad.

"The importance of it and the rarity of it is not lost on us," Power said.

"I've had teammates who've started their career and gone through their career and finished their career and didn't get that opportunity to be able to play in an event at home like that.

"Obviously, as we move towards Brisbane, this is one of those good examples of something which can hopefully lead to more of these events occurring as well."

World.title: Nina Kennedy knows now is the time to soak it all in — if she remembers to
World.content:
For most of us, falling for 5 metres is terrifying. For Nina Kennedy, provided there's no bar following her down, the fall is the fun part.

But last year introduced her to a fresh fear: the fear that it might all be over.

The reigning Olympic and world champion in pole vault tore her hamstring early in April last year.

Despite the long recovery from surgery, Kennedy was initially named in the Australian squad for the World Athletics Championships in September, but a strained muscle just a couple of days later dragged her back to reality.

How we got to Glasgow 2026 The bumpy road to Glasgow 2026 has produced a Commonwealth Games that will look a little different than the ones that came before.

She had to watch as American rival Katie Moon won outright the title they shared two years earlier.

Yesterday, she was named Australia's flag-bearer for the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony, which felt like a long shot when she was in the depths of rehab less than a year ago.

"Whenever you have a major surgery and you're out for the whole season, there's definitely that doubt of, 'Will this get fully better and will I return to my best and better?'" she said after flying out of a pre-Games athletics training camp early to accept her flag-waving honour.

"You have those thoughts, but you put in the work you do the rehab, you listen to your team, speak to your sport psychologist and never stop dreaming.

"I'm so proud of myself. Of course there were doubts, but I'm lucky enough to do this as a job and I'm pretty damn good at it. I work my arse off every day. So I'm not surprised but I am really proud of myself.

Kennedy has warmed back into the 2026 season after a torn hamstring last year. (Getty Images: Marco Mantovani)

"As athletes we try and get the best out of ourselves, so my mind always goes to, 'What if I don't get to defend my Commonwealth title? What if I don't make it back to the Olympics? What if this hamstring goes again and my career's over and I haven't really soaked up the last few years like I should have?'"

Kennedy has been representing Australia on the world stage for more than a decade, but the past five years since turning to the sport full time have seen her conquer the world and set the Australian women's pole vault record 10 times, including just two weeks ago in Monaco.

The 29-year-old admitted the Brisbane 2032 Olympics would probably be a bridge too far for her, so it was time to look around and enjoy what was happening while she was still on the field.

"Sport can be so fleeting so I've really learned to enjoy every step and this is such a special honour. I'm really going to try and soak this in and make some good memories," she said.

Unfortunately, she knows herself too well and is pretty sure she will not nail it when she leads her teammates into Glasgow's Hydro for the opening ceremony tomorrow morning (AEST).

"I'll be thinking, 'Soak this in, soak this in, soak it in,' and then I won't soak it in," she said.

"That's what will happen."

World.title: Why netball is growing into a sport of choice for men and boys
World.content:
When Daniel Statton was plotting a move from Far North Queensland to Geelong, the prospect of playing more competitive netball was part of the attraction.

The 19-year-old is one of a growing number of Australian men and boys taking up the sport.

He has now been selected for Australia's national men's netball team, the Kelpies.

"I'm just still hungry for more," he said.

"There's still more to achieve in netball, and I'm just wanting to get after it."

Daniel Statton looked forward to more competitive netball after moving to Geelong from Cairns. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

Statton has represented Australia at under-18 level and played for Queensland in the Australian Mixed and Men's Netball Association national championships in Perth earlier this year.

"I'm pretty athletic and agile, so the coaches love that,' he said.

" I always love to get up and get a bit of an aerial ball and get the crowd going a little bit. "

Born and raised in Cairns, Statton was the only boy playing netball in his sister's teams until he was about 12.

After that, age restrictions for boys forced him to switch to football and basketball.

Lynton McKay helped found the Cairns men's netball league. (ABC News: Bridget Herrmann)

He was not able to return to the game outside of mixed competitions until he was about 16.

"It was really exciting to know there were more like-minded athletes who enjoyed playing netball," he said.

Taking a shot

Before moving to Victoria for further study, Statton played in the Cairns men's netball league, one of the only men's competitions in Queensland.

Now in its third season, the Cairns competition has grown to four teams.

Lynton McKay grew up playing basketball, but after trying netball more than a decade ago, he never looked back.

Daniel Statton has represented his state and country in netball. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

He founded the Cairns men's competition so he could continue playing the sport after moving back to the region from Melbourne.

"There wasn't really anything on the scene other than mixed indoor [netball]," he said.

He said once men and boys had the netball itch, the sport was hard to give up.

"It's not as easy as it looks; it's quite tactical," he said.

Lots of talent emerging

Mr McKay said one of the biggest challenges to growing netball in regional areas was the smaller pool of players with competition from many other sports.

He said there was still a stigma about netball being a female sport, "probably more so in a regional place than a big city like Melbourne or Brisbane".

"But I do think that stigma is dropping," he said.

The popularity of netball among boys and men in Australia is growing. (Supplied: Queensland Suns)

"I'm also a teacher, and I do find there's huge participation now among boys. They all seem to really enjoy netball when they come down and give it a try."

Mr McKay said the Cairns men's competition was "still a work in progress" but said the region had some "really talented players", including some recent high school graduates who had represented their state.

"Considering we've only got four teams, it's a testament to the talent we have here in Cairns," he said.

Leprechaun Netball Club men's team co-captain Damian Nowak said the sport was a safer option for people's joints.

He said the social aspect was also a big drawcard.

Netball has to compete with other sports such as football and basketball for male talent. (Supplied: Clusterpix)

"We're just down here to have fun, a good bunch of mates, a good bunch of dads," Mr Nowak said.

Mr McKay said the best way for netball competitions to attract more players was to "keep pushing".

"I've noticed when we have school carnivals there are a lot of schools now starting to enter boys' teams," he said.

"This didn't happen five years ago."

World.title: Sharks 'happy to take underdog tag' ahead of blockbuster World Cup
World.content:
Australia's men's water polo team are set to take on some of the biggest teams on the planet this week at the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup Finals.

The Sharks get their campaign underway on Thursday evening against the most daunting of opponents, reigning world champions Spain.

For most, the sight of the world champions lining up poolside at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre would send shivers down your spine.

The Sharks, though, are not familiar with being daunted by anyone.

"I think if you were to ask anyone else in the world outside of our group, they would call us underdogs," goalkeeper Nic Porter told ABC Sport during the Sharks' pre-tournament training camp on the Gold Coast.

"But I think you ask any one of us in our group, we'd give you a very different answer.

"As Australians, as we all know, we're more than happy to take the underdog tag. I actually think Australians relish that.

"We'll take the underdog tag, that's fine, we understand where we're ranked in the world.

"But I also remember where we were ranked in the world in Paris 2024 and what happened there."

Paris run and quarterfinal pain fuelling drive for LA

Marcus Berehulak played when the Aussies stunned Serbia at the Olympics. (Getty Images: Clive Rose)

Ah yes, the Paris Olympics. There, the Sharks made a pledge to stun the world and, by and large, they did just that.

Eventual gold medallists Serbia were beaten by the staggering scoreline of 8-3 in the group stages.

"The way we approached the game against Serbia was, we had no fear," Porter said.

"And I think we must do the same in this tournament.

"The key for us and everything that we're focusing on now is those first four minutes against Spain.

"Dominate those first four minutes and then let's have a look at the rest of the game after that.

"I think if we can start really hot with a home crowd backing us, supporting us, giving us a bit of extra energy, I think it's going to be a really difficult night for the Spanish.

"And we're certainly going to be doing everything we can to make it as difficult as possible for them."

Nic Porter is relishing playing in front of a home crowd. (Supplied)

The Serbia game was not even the high point for Australia in Paris.

Hungary, the nine-time champions and most successful nation in the history of men's water polo at the Olympics, and hosts France were also beaten, by identical 9-8 scorelines.

The world could safely be considered to have been suitably shocked, especially the French, who were backed by an enormously parochial crowd at the Paris Aquatic Centre.

"That was a special night, the French night," coach Tim Hamill recalls.

"Among others, that was really special."

How the Aussies silenced the French crowd The Australian men's water polo team is hell-bent on riding a wave of good form all the way to the knockout rounds, after a hard-fought, dramatic 9-8 victory over hosts France and their legions of fans.

Tim Putt, who has returned to the squad after narrowly missing out in Paris, noted that the victory against the French was a real litmus test on how far the Australians had come in a relatively short space of time.

"For that Paris cycle, one of the great metrics I look at is France," the 27-year-old said.

"France was always our crossover game where we had to beat them to go through in the tournament and for like the first three tournaments we always just lost.

"But we all knew we could still beat them and we were gonna beat them next time.

"We had an official training match against them at the start of the Paris tour and we lost I think and then, leading into the Olympics, we were playing really good games, we came second at a tournament in Serbia and in the Olympics we had France as our last group game.

"I thought, 'Oh, they're going to pump them, they're going to absolutely pump them,' and they did.

"It took three years to show on the scoreboard what we were doing, but it did show in the end."

Australia's win over France was a thriller in Paris. (Getty Images: Clive Rose)

Alas, that victory against the French was the pinnacle of the Games for the Aussies, who fell in a heartbreaking quarterfinal defeat to the USA on penalties.

"That was the one, that's the heartbreaker," Hamill said.

"That's the one that we still lose a little bit of sleep over — and I say that only half jokingly.

"It was a huge moment for us that we ultimately didn't grab to its full potential at the time, but we got huge learnings out of that.

"We were one shot away from playing for Olympic medal, but we've learned from that, we've taken a huge number of lessons from that and we intend to use those for Sydney World Cup and as we get close to the LA Olympic Games."

'The next big Everest'

Tim Hamill has enjoyed the home build-up ahead of the World Cup. (Supplied: Water Polo Australia)

Hamill has been coach of the Sharks since 2021, taking over from Croatian international Elvis Fatović after the Tokyo Games.

The quarterfinal appearance at the 2024 Olympics was a spectacular high point of his tenure so far.

However, Hamill was clear that he only sees Australia improving on the way to Los Angeles in 2028, and beyond to the Brisbane 2032 Games.

"We know that on our day we can beat any team in the world, but doing it consistently across a tournament like the World Cup in Sydney or the upcoming Olympic Games is the next big step for us, that's probably the next big Everest for this group," Hamill said.

"The Sydney World Cup provides a great opportunity for some really high-level international exposure and we'll back-end our investment to make sure that 2027 and 2028 are heavily towards getting enough games.

"We're a long way away from the home of water polo [southern Europe], so we've got to get over there and get that international dosage over the next couple of years."

The Sharks were left gutted after their quarterfinal defeat against the USA in a shootout. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Skipper Nathan Power, who played a key role in the Sharks' run to the Olympic quarterfinals in Paris, noted that the time to switch on and take the next step was now.

"I think as a country, we've always done a really good job of being up and ready to go when it gets to a major tournament," Power said.

"But if we want to be, I guess, in Olympic terms, taken seriously as a second-week team, it really is a matter of starting to string together these results into a complete tournament.

"For us, there's a mental resilience thing there. While we can lean into the joys we had from Paris, we can also lean into the heartbreak we had there too.

"The stage we're getting to here [at the World Cup] starts at the quarterfinal stage and the quarterfinals is where we fell down in Paris, so even that in itself is a good pick-up point to start and coming forward with a positive result this time round."

The Sydney World Cup offers a fantastic opportunity for Australia to compete on home soil and use a home advantage that is rarely available to them.

Australian fans often have to travel. (Getty Images: DeFodi Images/Marcel ter Bals)

But Hamill noted that it's not just about getting results at this tournament, but continuing to build.

"High-performance sport and Olympic sport will always be about outcomes," Hamill said.

"We haven't hidden from the fact that what we want to achieve in LA is significant, we want it to be more than Paris.

"But for us as a group, there is more to it than that.

"This program has struggled for a number of years to get some traction in sport, so having a stand full at the Sydney World Cup, with young boys and young girls and families and inspiring the next generation and legacy and program depth, they're all really, really important for this team.

"The players themselves talk about leaving the cap in a better place moving forward, so legacy is a word that's come a lot through this group.

"So yes, we want to achieve what we want to achieve in Sydney World Cup and LA and hopefully beyond.

"But we're trying to build something long-term and sustainable with this water polo program in this country."

Sharks call on crowd to bring the passion

Nic Porter is known for wearing his heart on his sleeve. (Getty Images: Clive Rose)

Ticket sales for the World Cup have been hugely promising according to Water Polo Australia, setting the stage for what should be an electric atmosphere poolside over the next five days.

"My concern is that a lot of it's going to be for the Greeks and the Hungarians and the other countries," Hamill said, half-jokingly.

He probably has cause to be concerned.

Water polo is a huge deal in Europe and by all accounts, the expat communities of those nations in Sydney are set to really embrace the tournament as a rare chance to see their heroes in the flesh.

"That's probably the thing that we're probably the most excited for," Porter said.

"For us, when we go overseas and we play against these European countries or even America or Japan or wherever we play, we've always faced such a passionate home crowd that are cheering against us, and that can be pretty daunting sometimes, particularly when you go into some of these European nations where water polo is the number one sport.

"It can be very hostile there sometimes. So for us, we're hoping to create a bit of a hostile environment for our opponents.

Marcus Berehulak and Nic Porter are thrilled to be playing at home in Sydney. (Getty Images: Clive Rose)

"We want to have some deafening support, we want the classic Aussie spirit on display in the stands because we really feel like that'll help push the men's and women's teams over the line.

"We really can't wait to see a sea of green and gold in the stands, Australians love to get rowdy in a respectful way and support the athletes, and we can't wait to see that transferred over to water polo in a couple of weeks."

Marcus Berehulak noted that although crowds in major events such as the LEN Champions League Final Four were "hectic," that energy could be beneficial to everyone.

"It's pretty crazy, some of those events, especially Final Four, you've got flares and banners and everything chucked into the pool and whatnot in the end," he said.

"It's definitely a hostile environment."

Hamill noted that Porter, who played in Greece for Panionios last year and has just signed for French powerhouse Marseille, is one player who relishes a frenetic atmosphere.

"Nic's a really great example of utilising energy from the crowd and family support to make you perform, he wears his heart on his sleeve.

"It's not for everyone, playing up to the crowd, but the tournament that he put together at Paris was, from a goalkeeping point of view, as good as you'll see and that reflected in our results."

'Underdog' Sharks aim to use the home support

The Sharks feel like they are coming in under the radar. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Hamill was aware that all the players were pumped about playing on home soil.

"Sharing those [ticket sale] numbers with the players, you can see the excitement on their faces," Hamill said.

"Knowing that we're going to have big crowds at home is really exciting for everyone.

"There's often a desire for teams to not get caught up in that emotion and the hype, but often being very much the underdog team that we are, including like we were in Paris, I think of it a little bit differently in terms of finding moments, opportunities.

"We can utilise that energy and crowd noise and not avoid it.

"Everyone talks about ignoring the distractions of the Olympic Games, but I'm more about embracing those so-called distractions and how they can provide momentum for teams, which is something I think we did incredibly well in Paris and we intend to do the same in Sydney.

"We won't avoid the distractions, we won't avoid the people and moments, we'll open our doors to all of that."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Power agreed, noting that embracing the pressure had worked well for the team at the Olympics.

"It's something which as a team we've consciously been trying to do a lot more," Power said.

"In the lead into Paris and beyond there was a 'smell the roses' and take a moment to appreciate those very cool things that you get to experience.

"Some people might view it as a distraction. Instead, you're acknowledging that thing is there and then you're using that to have a positive impact on you.

"It would be silly to go, 'Oh, we're not going to think about it too much,' we're going to be in a crowd full of people cheering for us, which is something very special.

"We've had some really wonderful experiences with the crowds in Brisbane and Perth and now in Sydney, to get a chance to really turn it on in a very iconic venue for Australian sport too.

"It's certainly not lost on us how important that'll be."

World.title: Star footballer's protest over transfer leads to training cancellation
World.content:
Wolverhampton striker Tolu Arokodare allegedly forced the cancellation of a training session after he refused to leave the pitch.

Sources said the 25-year-old Nigerian sat down and demanded the club let him move to Italian club Fiorentina.

Wolves have rejected a bid from the Serie A side, having accepted an offer from Turkish club Trabzonspor.

Arokodare's actions led to new boss Cesar Peixoto terminating the session.

Arokodare will not be involved in Wolverhampton's friendly at Maidenhead United as Wolves continue their pre-season plans.

Arokodare denied the reports on social media.

"I was very surprised and disappointed to see the media reports today, many of which are inaccurate. Throughout my career, I have always taken great pride in conducting myself professionally and maintaining the highest training standards," he wrote on X.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I remain under contract with Wolves, and my only intention is to fulfil my responsibilities professionally by training, doing my job, and contributing to the team in accordance with that contract."

The latest incident is another flashpoint in the forward's career at Wolves after he was disciplined in April following a confrontation with young forward Mateus Mane.

Arokodare signed a massive deal after leaving Genk before last season's EPL, but scored just three league goals as Wolves finished bottom of the Premier League and were relegated.

The incident presents an early challenge for Peixoto just weeks into his reign after he replaced Rob Edwards in a surprise move last month.

World.title: Kiana started weightlifting after an injury. Now, she's a Comm Games athlete
World.content:
Kiana Elliott always knew she wanted to compete in the Olympics.

When she was aged just three, the Sydney 2000 Games captured her attention.

"There was a little seed planted in my head," she said.

She thought gymnastics would be her pathway to the podium, but injury meant she had to retire from the sport at 14.

She discovered weightlifting while looking for another way to keep fit.

"I didn't even know it [weightlifting] existed, and I found it fun," Elliott said.

"I pursued it, and I've kept going and I'm still going."

Kiana Elliott finds weightlifting fun. (ABC News: Sophie Holder)

Elliott has now represented Australia in weightlifting at multiple events, including several Junior World Championships, three Pacific Games and the pandemic-delayed Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games.

She competed at the Birmingham 2022 Games, having suffered an injury just two months earlier.

"There was a big question mark on whether I'd be able to go," she said.

"I lifted about 90-to-94 per cent of my best and that was good enough for fourth.

" That left a little bit of a fire in me. "

According to the Australian Commonwealth Games website, Elliott is among 27 South Australians expected to compete at Glasgow.

'Anything can happen'

Elliott said she was focused on being in a good headspace ahead of the Games.

"I personally don't push too hard in terms of maximal weight and maximal attempts in the gym because I need to keep myself physically intact for competition," she said.

"Sport is like a little microcosm of life, it's the stories of the underdog, the triumph, the adversities, it puts you in a situation where it counts right now, so anything can happen on the day."

Weightlifter Kiana Elliott will compete in the 63kg competition at Glasgow. (ABC News: Sophie Holder)

Elliott said she would compete in the 63kg class against some "really great" athletes and people she respected at Glasgow.

" I just hope that I can put my best foot forward and compete as best as I can. "

Progressing past setbacks

Elliott's physical preparation coach at the South Australian Sports Institute (SASI), Michael Nash, said a lot of work had been put into Elliott's training program.

"That works with, not only what she's previously had with her injuries [but] then building that into the Comm Games as well," he said.

"[We] feel good about [how] she's progressing. She's had a few setbacks with injuries as well, so my main priority with her is to look at what she's been doing and adjusting her sessions to make sure she's getting the most out of [them] so she can perform as well as she can."

He said Elliott was one of the most "technically good" weightlifters he had seen in Australia.

Michael Nash says Kiana Elliott is one of the most "technically good" weightlifters he has seen in Australia. (ABC News: Sophie Holder)

'Geez, what's happening here?'

Elliott said more women and girls had taken up weightlifting since she first started in the sport 13 years ago.

"That's super exciting," she said.

"Maybe I've played a little bit of a part of making that visible, locally I know some other athletes that made [it] visible for me.

"There's nothing better than pursuing your own strength and pursuing your own capability.

"It's in a gym environment, gym environments are very masculine, very ego-based and there's something … amusing, fun, cool … to be in the gym as a female, and the guys are like 'geez, what's happening here?'"

Elliott described weightlifting as fun and simple.

"It's a numbers game so it's really, really easy to measure your progress and its addicting for that," she said.

Kiana Elliott fits her weightlifting training around her work commitments. (ABC News)

Elliott said she fitted training around her job at SA Pathology, where she worked part-time.

"I don't know about balance, it's a bit off-kilter," she said.

"I'm really lucky to have built a really good relationship with my employer. The people that work close to me, they understand what I'm trying to do."

She said the general public tended to believe athletes who represent their country had everything handed to them.

"And you're set up and you're ready to go, and it's really not the case," Elliott said.

"I feel really lucky, proud and happy to have a good bunch of people around me and that include the guys here at SASI.

"I train here at South Australia Sports Institute, just outside of the CBD in Adelaide.

"I live down by the airport, I work in the CBD, if things weren't so close together, I couldn't make it work."

World.title: Philipsen claims Tour de France stage as UCI defends late-night drug tests
World.content:
Jasper Philipsen has capped a fine team performance to win stage 17 of the Tour de France, with defending champion Tadej Pogačar protecting his overall lead.

Mathieu van der Poel led his Alpecin-Premier Tech teammate Philipsen to his first stage victory of this Tour overnight by controlling the pace and containing counterattacks through the last kilometres.

Philipsen finished just ahead of Mauro Schmid and Olav Kooij.

The Belgian rider described a "a roller-coaster of emotions" after what had been a disappointing Tour for him personally.

"I prepared very, very well. I was in the shape of my life, I think, and the first stages, the first 12 days, were just horrible. I couldn't find myself, couldn't find the feeling I was hoping for," said Philipsen, who thanked his team colleagues.

"I was like an angry bird at the table. I was just disappointed in myself, angry that I couldn't take [a] stage win, that I didn't find my feeling. And the team, they had to deal with it, not only the riders, the staff. This one is for them to keep on believing."

Pogačar, who is chasing a third straight Tour title and fifth overall, maintained his lead of just over four and a half minutes over Remco Evenepoel, the winner of the previous two stages.

But it was a bad day for Pogačar's UAE Emirates XRG teammate Adam Yates, who struggled and only made it back within the time limit. The British rider slumped over his handlebars, clearly exhausted.

The race ends on Sunday in Paris.

The relatively flat 174.7km route from Chambery to Voiron was the last favourable stage for sprinters before the Tour takes to the Alps, and it led to a day of attempted breakaways, with many riders vying to put themselves in contention.

Van der Poel was among the leaders after Côte de Saint-Jean d'Arvey, the last significant climb, and they were joined by others before Yates's problems began in the peloton.

Mads Pedersen was the next to attack the leaders with 65km remaining, and the green jersey-holder invigorated the group when he joined them.

More sprinters broke away, swelling the group to 30 riders, before Pedersen, Ben Healy, Michal Kwiatkowski, Felix Engelhardt, Ed Planckaert and Jasper Stuyven struck out 57km from the finish.

Stuyven attacked on his own 26km from the line, leaving his five former co-leaders to chase or wait for the main bunch. They were caught. The only question was whether the 34-year-old Stuyven had the stamina to claim his first Tour stage win.

The Belgian rider was caught with less than 4km remaining, and Van der Poel did the rest for Philipsen.

Support for Tour night doping tests A former cyclist who took performance-enhancing drugs, now a team boss at the Tour de France, supports doping tests in the middle of the night at cycling's biggest race.

Philipsen's stage win moved him just behind Pedersen in the contest for the green jersey awarded to the rider with the most points.

With four stages remaining, Pedersen of Lidl-Trek had 452 points, followed by Philipsen on 445. Biniam Girmay of Eritrea was next with 361 points.

Cycling's governing body, the UCI, responded to criticism of unannounced anti-doping controls after Pogačar and his main rival Jonas Vingegaard were woken in the early hours of Sunday for tests by the Swiss-based International Testing Agency.

Vingegaard subsequently crashed during Sunday's stage and had to abandon the race.

The UCI said it acknowledged the night-time testing "can disrupt riders' rest and recovery" and said it remained an exceptional measure.

"While fully aware of how onerous such a measure is for riders, the UCI nevertheless underscores that these controls serve an overriding interest: the fight against doping," the body said in a statement.

Tech.title: Lego’s Donkey Kong arcade machine lets Mario jump endless barrels — Miyamoto is reportedly happy
Tech.content:
Q: How does the barrel mechanism work, and how many barrels fit inside of it at a time?

The barrel mechanism is essentially a pump. It uses a stack of 14 Barrels going up the side of the model. Each time the barrel lever is pulled, it adds one barrel to the bottom of the stack and one falls out the top. The system holds 20 barrels so there can be 6 barrels rolling down at a time.

Q: Do the barrels roll all the way down to the bottom? Do they fall out of the set, and need to be reinserted into the slot, or does the mechanism bring them back to the top?

The barrels roll all the way from the top to the bottom where they are collected in a hopper that is connected to the barrel pump. This forms an infinite barrel loop which is, by definition, “barrels of fun”.

Q: What was the biggest hurdle in designing and testing that mechanism?

The biggest challenge was getting the barrels to roll down slowly without stopping or getting stuck. This was achieved through a combination of rolling over steps, LEGO studs, slopes, bows and using LEGO Technic beams which are slightly thinner than LEGO Bricks. This allowed us to capture the feeling of the gameplay where the barrel rolls down slowly. I rolled thousands of barrels down those tracks to figure it out… Those barrels drove me bananas!

The second biggest hurdle was finding a way to get the barrel from the bottom to the top again. We built all kinds of stuff; things to shoot one barrel from the bottom to the top, worm gears, force multiplication levers, and more. But it turned the right answer was simply a lot more barrels.

Q: How do the joystick and button make Jumpman/Mario move?

The joystick moves Jumpman from left to right using a long lever up the back of the model, connected to a dingler. The jump button uses a similar mechanism used in a piano key. When it is pressed down in front of the model, the other end of a see-saw lever presses up on a long rod with Jumpman at the top. When the button is released gravity returns Jumpman to the bottom.

Tech.title: Meta won’t have to face the next planned social media addiction trial
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

Less than a week before Meta’s lawyers were set to return to a Los Angeles courtroom, the plaintiff accusing the platform of inflicting harm dropped the case. Brought by 15-year-old Florida plaintiff going by initials R.K.C., the case was set to be the second in a set of bellwether trials meant to test legal arguments that social media giants allegedly broke the law by creating features that hooked and harmed teens.

TikTok, Snap, and YouTube previously settled claims brought by R.K.C. for undisclosed amounts. “In light of the overall successful result of the litigation and his concerns about enduring a grueling weekslong trial, he has elected to withdraw his claims against Meta,” R.K.C.’s lawyers Emily Jeffcott and Rahul Ravipudi said in a statement. “He’s ready to close this chapter and focus on his recovery and engage in therapy as he aspires to have a normal life.” That means Meta got out of this case without having to pay a settlement. “The claims never held up, and this outcome makes clear that we will not back away from defending ourselves against baseless lawsuits,” Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said in a statement.

Meta got out of this case without having to pay a settlement

Multiple cases have already begun to test claims about social media companies allegedly misleading users about the safety of their products and inflicting harm. Meta and Google’s YouTube lost the first bellwether case tried at the courthouse, with a jury finding them to be negligent and ordering them to pay a total of $6 million in compensatory and punitive damages to the single plaintiff. Separately, a New Mexico jury ordered the company to pay a $375 million penalty, and the state is preparing for the next phase of trial seeking structural business changes.

There’s still seven more bellwether cases on deck in the California state courthouse in LA, and a separate set of cases pending in a federal court in Oakland. Meta, Tiktok, Snap, and YouTube settled with a school district that was set to be the first in that separate set of bellwether cases seeking money to cover mental health-related costs to students allegedly caused by their platforms. Meta is still set to face claims brought by state attorneys general in federal court next month, alleging that it illegally misled the public about harmful and allegedly addictive features.

Tech.title: Tesla’s revenues are bouncing back, but profits are still weak
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After a dismal two years of weakening demand, falling sales, and damage to its brand by Elon Musk’s political activities, Tesla’s road to recovery continues apace. On the heels of an impressive delivery report, the company released its earnings for the second quarter of 2026 — giving us the latest glimpse at the EV company that Musk has said he wants to transform into a leader of AI and robotics.

Despite that mission, Tesla remains a car company. And in the second quarter, it sold an impressive 480,126 vehicles, about a 25 percent increase compared to the second quarter of 2025. (For a direct-to-consumer company like Tesla, deliveries are a proxy for sales.)

Tesla certainly did a good job shrinking its inventory, which is good for the balance sheet. But what about those numbers?

Tesla certainly did a good job shrinking its inventory, which is good for the balance sheet. But what about those numbers?

Tesla said it earned $1.11 billion in net income on $28.2 billion in revenue in the quarter that ended June 30th. That’s a 26 percent increase in revenue but a 5 percent increase in profits over the second quarter of 2025, when the company earned $1.17 billion in net income on $22.5 billion in revenue. Tesla exceeded revenue expectations from Wall Street, which assumed approximately $26.4 billion in revenue.

But there were still signs of trouble. The company reported negative free cash flow of $1.1 billion, a sign that Tesla’s operating revenues are insufficient to cover its capital expenditures. Basically, Tesla is spending more — on AI infrastructure, robotics, and manufacturing — than its earning on car sales and energy installations. Last year, some analysts predicted that negative free cash flow could trigger a steep drop in share price. (Tesla’s share price is down 14 percent so far this year.) The company said it had $43.5 billion in cash on hand, but its capital expenditures were up year over year 142 percent to $5.7 billion this quarter.

In a shareholder deck, Tesla said it “generated over $100B in revenue on a trailing twelve-month basis for the first time.” It also touted Cybercab production at its Gigafactory in Texas, and said Tesla Semi production “remains on track” at its Nevada facility later this year. And it said it began construction for its Optimus humanoid robot production at the factory in Fremont after decommissioning the assembly line for the Model S and X.

“Tesla is in its largest and most exciting period of investment,” the company states. “From here, there remains much hard work as we aim to revolutionize transportation, energy and productivity through our leading real-world AI. Scaling will be non-linear, and we are focused on long-term value creation. We’ve never been more optimistic about the future.”

Automotive gross margins, which measures revenue minus the direct cost of manufacturing the vehicle, remains an important number for Tesla. They fund the company’s multi-billion dollar investments in AI, autonomous driving, and robotics, while also providing a buffer for Tesla to slash vehicle prices when demand slumps.

In the second quarter, Tesla said its automotive gross margins were 16.3 percent, minus revenue from the sale of regulatory credits (a revenue stream that will soon cease to exist, after the Trump administration’s elimination of penalties for automakers who exceed emission standards). That’s up over the 15 percent margins in Q2 2025, but down from 19.2 percent in Q1 of this year.

YANTAI, CHINA - JULY 03 2026: New IM5 electric cars wait for shipment to overseas market in a port in Yantai in eastern China’s Shandong province, Friday, July 3, 2026. (Photo credit should read stringer/ Feature China/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

Tesla’s energy business remained a bright spot for the company. It reported $3.1 billion in energy generation and storage revenue, a 13 percent increase over the same period in 2025.

The earnings report is the latest evidence that Tesla was starting to turn the corner on a dismal two years of declining sales and falling profits. It also comes as the company faces tough questions about its slow progress in expanding its robotaxi operations. Tesla’s autonomous vehicle project has fallen far short of Musk’s prediction of covering 50 percent of the US population by the end of 2025. The company recently launched robotaxi operations in two Florida cities, Orlando and Tampa, but a crowdsourced tracker shows only a handful of cars were available.

Tesla rolled out a new update to Full Self-Driving (v14 Lite) for its vehicle owners, bringing personalized driving preference learning to individual Teslas. But the number of crashes involving Tesla drivers using Autopilot and FSD continues to grow at an alarming rate, with Electrek reporting 207 crashes in May 2026 alone.
